items.title: A fair amount of slop: generative artificial intelligence and carelessness made cheap, unbounded and unattributable

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: In this paper the author argues that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has not created a new form of academic misconduct. Rather, it has taken the least-policed form of misconduct we had, that of cutting corners, and stripped it of the three properties that made it survivable. This 'sloppiness' was coupled to effort, bounded to one paper, and attributable to someone who lacked diligence. Fluent prose was once an 'honest signal', because it was costly to fake, and the apparatus of peer review built upon that cost. GenAI has broken that signal. Other things have broken too, including the evidence chain. 'Citation laundering' is where a fabricated claim, cited once by an author linking it to a real source, acquires a provenance despite it being unreachable by any reference check. The author highlights research in health professions education in which various authors have admitted to citing work they have not read, and argues that current GenAI use declarations are largely uncalibrated instruments. The closest look health professions education scholars seem to have taken at their own reference lists appears to predate these tools, and because syntheses inform guidelines and guidelines inform curricula, a fabricated claim can travel from a 'prompt' to what a clinician teaches at the bedside. Because journals' workflows have not traditionally involved verification, blame for abuses all too often falls on reviewers, who are ill equipped to carry it. Ultimately, the use of GenAI means that much of our cognitive effort needs to be relocated from the act of writing into a deliberate act of adjudication. The author describes how this paper was itself produced using GenAI to bring back effortful, bounded and attributable practice leading to a worked example of disclosure that describes practice rather than certifying intention.

items.title: AI-powered human action recognition of functional activities in stroke: a systematic review

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI)-based human activity recognition (HAR) is a promising approach for detecting functional activity in individuals with stroke, potentially enabling objective and ecologically valid assessment, monitoring and treatment. We aimed to synthesize current evidence on AI-based HAR for functional activity recognition after stroke, focusing on sensing technologies, target activities, settings, and model architectures. PubMed, Embase, WOS, and Scopus were searched and seventeen studies involving 224 individuals with stroke met the inclusion criteria. Inertial measurement units were the predominant sensing modality (12/17, 70.6%), with several studies demonstrating the feasibility of recognizing relevant functional activities using a single device. Single-sensor approaches were also used in home-based and simulated-home settings, suggesting potential for scalable and unobtrusive monitoring outside clinical environments; however, most studies were conducted in controlled clinical settings (11/17, 64.7%), with limited real-world validation to date. Convolutional neural networks were the most frequently used deep learning architecture, while Random Forest was the most common traditional machine learning method. Multimodal sensing may enrich activity characterization, although greater sensing complexity may reduce feasibility for prolonged home monitoring. Methodological and reporting limitations, including concerns regarding confounding and reproducibility, should be considered when interpreting the current evidence. Overall, single-sensor AI-based HAR appears promising for low-burden, continuous, and ecologically valid monitoring. Future research should prioritize longitudinal validation in everyday environments, transparent reporting of code and data availability, and inclusion of acute and severely impaired stroke populations to facilitate clinical translation toward objective monitoring, personalized rehabilitation, and remote care.

items.title: Deep learning–driven learning analytics for enhancing digital literacy skills of media students using an explainable BiLSTM-attention framework

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The increasing adoption of digital technologies and online learning platforms has transformed higher education, making digital literacy an important competency for media students. However, existing learning analytics approaches primarily focus on academic performance prediction while providing limited attention to digital-literacy-related behavioral patterns and the interpretability of predictive models. Furthermore, conventional machine learning techniques often fail to capture the temporal behavioural patterns generated through learner interactions within Learning Management Systems (LMSs). To address these challenges, this study proposes an Explainable BiLSTM-Attention Learning Analytics Framework for predicting MDLA-derived digital-literacy behavioral proxy categories using learner behavioural data extracted from the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD). Because OULAD does not contain independently measured digital-literacy scores, the Low, Medium, and High target categories are derived from LMS behavioral information through the proposed Media Digital Literacy Analytics (MDLA) representation and are treated as behavioral proxy categories rather than directly measured levels of digital literacy. The proposed framework combines a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network with an attention mechanism to model sequential learner behaviour, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and attention visualization improve model transparency and interpretability. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework obtained higher scores than the evaluated baselines in a single run on OULAD, the evaluated machine learning and deep learning baseline models, achieving an Accuracy of 95.8%, Precision of 95.1%, Recall of 94.7%, F1-score of 94.9%, and a ROC-AUC of 97.2%. Explainability analysis identified engagement duration, assessment performance, resource usage, forum participation, and interaction frequency as the most influential behavioural factors contributing to the prediction of the MDLA-derived proxy categories. The findings suggest that integrating sequential deep learning with explainable learning analytics can model digital-literacy-related behavioral profiles in this OULAD setting. MDLA is a behavioral representation and has not been validated against a standardized digital-literacy assessment. The findings are based on a single dataset (OULAD) and a single experimental run, and should not be generalized to other institutions, LMS platforms, or learner populations without external validation. items.title: Exploring adaptive learning challenges and AI opportunities through educational professionals practices

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Despite its promise, adaptive learning faces significant technological, pedagogical, and infrastructural challenges that hinder its large-scale adoption. This study explores pedagogical obstacles from the perspectives of educators and instructional designers, focusing on their practices, perceptions, and specific needs. A mixed-methods approach combined a quantitative survey with qualitative data. Data were collected from 90 education professionals (teachers, instructional designers, and trainers) reached through LinkedIn and academic networks. Most participants (82.2%) identified situations requiring adaptation, yet only 55.6% had implemented adaptive measures. The qualitative analysis identified four main categories of adaptation practices. Participants expressed strong interest in AI-powered features to support instructional design tasks. The study proposes actionable recommendations to bridge the gap between technology and pedagogy, including the use of AI-assisted tools combined with human expertise, the development of adaptive interactive content and investment in professional development. This balanced approach aims to address critical barriers while maintaining educational quality and effectiveness, contributing to a better understanding of how AI can be integrated into adaptive learning systems to address current challenges.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence usage by university students in the light of Diffusion of Innovations theory

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, has fundamentally transformed the landscape of higher education. This study investigates the factors influencing the adoption of generative AI by university students through the theoretical lens of Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory. Drawing upon Rogers’ seminal framework, this research examines how five perceived attributes of innovation-relative advantage, compatibility, simplicity, trialability, and observability-is related to students’ behavioral intention to use generative AI tools in their academic pursuits. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among students from multiple Polish universities, and the collected data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory psychometric properties, with all constructs achieving acceptable levels of internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. The structural model results indicate that relative advantage, simplicity, observability and compatibility are significantly related to behavioral intention, while trialability demonstrates a non-significant effect. The model explains approximately 48.7% of variance in behavioral intention. These findings contribute to the theoretical understanding of technology adoption in educational contexts and provide practical implications for higher education institutions seeking to integrate generative AI tools into their pedagogical frameworks. The study concludes with recommendations for fostering responsible AI adoption while addressing concerns regarding academic integrity and critical thinking development.

items.title: Prompt engineering knowledge predicts ethical AI awareness and learning outcomes among tertiary students in Bangladesh

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: This study examines the relationship between prompt engineering literacy and academic learning outcomes among tertiary-level students in Bangladesh, with particular attention to the ethical dimensions of artificial intelligence (AI) integration in higher education. Using a concurrent mixed methods design, data were collected from students across public, private, and National University-affiliated institutions through online forms, telephone surveys, and messaging-platform surveys, complemented by key informant interviews with students and educators. The findings show that students with stronger prompt engineering knowledge achieved substantially larger gains on a post-intervention knowledge assessment, and that this knowledge, together with the frequency and perceived usefulness of AI engagement, was the strongest independent predictor of learning outcomes, ahead of institutional type. Ethical concerns, most notably academic dishonesty, algorithmic bias, and overreliance on automation, were widely recognized by students, yet formal institutional guidance on ethical AI use remained rare and was almost entirely absent among National University-affiliated colleges. These results carry direct implications for policy and practice. They suggest that prompt engineering merits treatment as a foundational academic literacy rather than a technical add-on, that AI ethics training needs to reach under-resourced institutions as a matter of priority, and that closing the gap between how quickly students adopt AI and how slowly institutions govern it is now an urgent task for Bangladeshi higher education.

items.title: Confidence and trust in artificial intelligence mediate the relationship between performance expectancy and students’ behavioral intention to use ChatGPT

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract This study investigates the factors influencing university students’ behavioral intention to use ChatGPT in higher education, focusing on the mediating role of confidence and trust in artificial intelligence (CTAI) as a second-order construct integrating self-efficacy and trust. Using a cross-sectional quantitative design, data were collected from 199 students at the University of Jeddah through purposive sampling and analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM) with AMOS. The results indicate that performance expectancy (PE) and effort expectancy (EE) significantly predict CTAI, while CTAI significantly predicts behavioral intention (BI). However, the direct effects of PE and EE on BI are not significant. Mediation analysis using bootstrapping reveals that CTAI fully mediates the relationship between PE and BI, whereas the indirect effect of EE on BI is not significant. These findings suggest that students’ perceptions of performance benefits are associated with their behavioral intention to use ChatGPT through confidence and trust in AI, whereas this mediating mechanism was not supported for effort expectancy. The study contributes to technology acceptance research by conceptualizing CTAI as an integrative higher-order construct and providing initial empirical evidence of its mediating role specifically in the relationship between performance expectancy and behavioral intention.

items.title: Source transparency and accuracy warnings support more selective reliance on generative-AI answers in a randomized online experiment

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative-AI systems increasingly provide answers to everyday questions, but users need to decide not only whether to accept an answer, but whether acceptance should depend on answer correctness. This randomized online experiment tested whether visible source information and an accuracy warning supported more selective reliance on AI-style answers. A final analytic sample of 800 adult participants was assigned to one of four between-subjects cue conditions in a 2 × 2 × 2 mixed design crossing source transparency (absent vs. present), accuracy warning (absent vs. present), and answer correctness (incorrect vs. correct, within participant). Each participant evaluated 24 AI-style answers, yielding 19,200 trial-level observations. The primary analysis used all trials and modelled acceptance as a function of source transparency, accuracy warning, answer correctness, and their interactions. Participants accepted correct answers more often than incorrect answers, and the correct-incorrect acceptance gap was largest in the source-plus-warning condition. In the applied-risk model restricted to incorrect-answer trials, acceptance of incorrect answers was highest in the control condition (1080/2400, 45%) and lower in the source-only (864/2400, 36%), warning-only (672/2400, 28%), and source-plus-warning conditions (504/2400, 21%). Verification behaviour was highest in the combined condition (2496/4800, 52%). These results indicate that brief on-screen cues lowered erroneous-answer acceptance and encouraged verification in low-risk information-evaluation tasks, while the distinction between response bias and sensitivity remains an important boundary condition.

items.title: Exploring the evolution of AI ethics in CS ethics courses

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background and Context Building on a previous study analyzing CS ethics course requirements across CS undergraduate programs at 250 universities, this paper explores the content of a subset of computing ethics courses from US universities.Objective We aim to examine the evolution of content related to artificial intelligence (AI) and AI ethics in these courses, and hypothesize that the growth of AI in both academic and industrial settings has precipitated an increased focus on the ethics of AI in undergraduate CS courses.Method Through an online search, we manually construct a data corpus consisting of 116 CS ethics courses from 93 universities in the United States. Subsequently, we conduct both a keyword analysis of course titles, descriptions, and syllabi for these courses, and qualitatively evaluate the subset of 54 courses for which a course syllabus or course website could be found.Findings We find that, while the introduction of content on AI in ethics courses takes many forms, the majority of content only started to be added beginning in 2020. In the years since, more courses have revised their syllabi to address the social implications of AI, while some courses that already incorporated AI content have begun to deepen their engagement with the ethical challenges posed by AI.Implications Synthesizing our findings, we propose a three-phase classification of the integration of AI ethics content into the curriculum, and advocate for increased attention to the legal, policy, and governance frameworks necessary to guide the development and use of “responsible” AI systems.

items.title: Different Logics, Similar Intentions: Heterogeneity in How Employees Evaluate AI Adoption

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) adoption at work has documented heterogeneity in user attitudes and adoption profiles, but less is known about whether employees differ in how they weight adoption-relevant information. In a within-subject structured-profile experiment, 446 employees provided 7,136 intention judgments across 16 profiles that varied AI adoption benefits, barriers, replacement vulnerability, and anticipated work harm. Multilevel regression mixture model analysis identified four latent decision-policy classes with different estimated weights on opportunity and threat cues; class mean intentions were not statistically distinguishable. Drawing on multiple-cue judgment theory, we interpret this pattern as heterogeneity in cue utilization rather than simply in attitude levels. Explaining and managing AI adoption therefore requires attention to latent decision policies, because aggregate effect estimates and profiles based on mean levels can conceal differences in cue responsiveness that shape how employees evaluate AI.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and online participation: feasibility analysis in Sao Paulo's participatory budgeting
items.venue: Innovation The European Journal of Social Science Research

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: This paper presents essential, globally relevant insights to guide smart cities in scaling Artificial Intelligence (AI) effectively to achieve enhanced civic engagement. This conceptual study contributes to emerging literature on AI in democratic innovation and participatory democracy. It addresses feasibility analyses as a critical bottleneck in participatory processes such as participatory budgeting: ad-hoc feasibility shows the transformative potential of AI in participatory initiatives. Through an exploratory case study on São Paulo's participatory budgeting, our analysis identifies how manual feasibility assessments create significant delays and high rejection rates for citizens’ proposals, where more than every tenth proposal was rejected. The research demonstrates how AI can support the process, including data retrieval systems and automated summarization. The main focus is on ad-hoc real-time feasibility checks. Furthermore, we analyse the required state capacity and capabilities for implementation. While AI offers substantial potential to improve participatory governance, it also demands organizational transformations.

items.title: Does ChatGPT influence metacognitive calibration during undergraduate physics problem solving?

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract We present a controlled pilot study examining how access to generative Artificial Intelligence influences metacognitive calibration, the alignment between perceived and actual learning. Second-year undergraduate physics students of the University of Bath were split into a control group, completing three successive first-year exam problems of comparable difficulty under standard exam conditions, and an experimental group, in which ChatGPT access was permitted during the intermediate problem. We quantify the performance improvement of students via a partial-credit marking scheme, while their perceived improvement is recorded through self-assessment questions. Students with access to ChatGPT show a ∼ 60% improvement in calibration accuracy, primarily associated with a reduction in underconfidence. Our exploratory study suggests that the educational value of generative AI may extend beyond performance by supporting students in forming more accurate assessments of their own performance, and in turn, understanding.

items.title: Consent to passive sensing in artificial intelligence-personalized interfaces: perceived surveillance, transparency, and trust

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Artificial intelligence-personalized interfaces increasingly use passive behavioral signals generated during ordinary interaction. Such sensing can support personalization but may also heighten perceived surveillance and reduce users’ sense of control. Across two sequential experiments, we tested how data collection type (active sharing vs. passive sensing) and consent design quality (low vs. high transparency/control) shape privacy appraisals, trust, and consent. Study 1 (N = 855) showed that passive sensing increased perceived surveillance and creepiness and reduced trust, consent willingness, and behavioral acceptance, particularly under low transparency/control. High transparency/control increased perceived control and attenuated these effects. Study 2 replicated the principal self-report pattern in a laboratory setting and added eye tracking and galvanic skin response (GSR)/electrodermal activity. Passive sensing increased attention to data-use and decision-relevant elements and produced greater baseline-adjusted electrodermal arousal, with the clearest transparency/control buffering during the decision window. Process measures did not add explanatory value for trust or consent willingness, although an exploratory model indicated that GSR measures improved prediction of behavioral acceptance. Passive sensing should therefore be treated as a consent and privacy design issue, not only as a technical mechanism for personalization.

items.title: Speak before the reveal: a practical method to protect clinical reasoning from artificial intelligence scribe deskilling, never-skilling, and mis-skilling

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
items.abstract_text: Abstract Objective Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes are rapidly becoming normalized in clinical practice, yet governance frameworks focus on accuracy, privacy, consent, and medicolegal status. Risks to clinician capabilities have received less attention. Speak before the reveal is a proposed method in which clinicians verbalize critical cognitive steps, such as synthesis and plan, before note generation. Discussion Recent work distinguishes deskilling in senior clinicians, never-skilling from premature offload in trainees and mis-skilling, the internalization of AI errors and inappropriate use as sound practice. This Perspective builds on emerging evidence that reasoning before seeing AI output may protect unaided reasoning. Training implementation, evaluation, adherence challenges, validation methodology, and governance strategies for training bodies, health services, and scribe vendors are discussed. Conclusion Speak before the reveal is a low-cost, testable approach to maintaining clinical reasoning for individuals or organizations. Successful AI scribe adoption requires preserving clinicians’ ability to work without AI support.

items.title: Implementing AI-CDSS in Low-Resource Maternal Care: Lessons Learned from the Preeclapp Deployment

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are one of the leading causes of maternal morbidity and mortality in Colombia, particularly in rural regions with limited access to specialized care. In this context, Preeclapp was developed as a clinical decision support system grounded in expert-system logic, designed to provide guideline-based support for maternal care in settings with limited resources and connectivity. This proof-of-concept implementation study analyzes the integration of Preeclapp into clinical practice and the factors that influenced its adoption. The main barriers identified included unstable connectivity, lack of data interoperability, high staff turnover, and initial skepticism toward AI-based technologies. Nevertheless, the project showed preliminary feasibility of use by non-specialized personnel in obstetrics and gynecology, even in low-connectivity environments. To overcome these challenges, the project relied on training sessions, embedded educational resources, continuous technical support, and iterative software adaptations. Our implementation suggests that these strategies were perceived by users as supporting adherence to obstetric protocols, reinforcing clinical decision-making, and enhancing staff confidence, particularly in facilities with limited specialist availability. As a proof-of-concept implementation study, this work did not evaluate diagnostic accuracy or clinical effectiveness; instead, it focused on early implementation feasibility, usability, acceptability, and perceived usefulness. The findings suggest that sustainable adoption of AI-CDSS systems requires strengthening digital literacy and promoting a culture of innovation. Our experience with Preeclapp indicates that adoption and implementation benefited from a modular design, low-connectivity functionality, flexibility, and co-creation with local teams, which helped adapt the tool to each institution’s context.

items.title: Markets embedded in publics: information-processing social systems under the attention economy

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract This article theorizes financial markets and democratic publics as collective information-processing systems embedded in shared communicative infrastructures, such that markets can even be said to be embedded in publics. Bringing the efficient market hypothesis into dialogue with the liberal marketplace of ideas and the Habermasian public sphere, I identify four epistemic conditions these traditions depend on: diversity, independence, aggregation, and correction. I argue that price discovery is epistemically embedded in the same media environment through which public opinions form. The attention economy of engagement-driven media brings this into view by degrading that environment: it privileges affective arousal over informational quality, correlates judgements, and suppresses correction, in effect creating corrupted marketplaces of ideas. The comparison also shows a specific difference between the domains: market correction through arbitrage operates through market transactions as well as media communication, whereas counterspeech and persuasion in publics are more reliant on media, arguably rendering publics more vulnerable to media impairment.

items.title: AI-mediated teacher learning in Chinese lesson study: regulating cognitive demands in EFL pre-service teachers

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal for Lesson & Learning Studies
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study, guided by the cognitive theory of multimedia learning (CTML), investigates how multimodal large language models (MLLMs) mediate the professional learning of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) pre-service teachers within Chinese lesson study (CLS). It aims to elucidate the cognitive and dialogic mechanisms through which AI-supported mediation shapes teacher learning processes and participation. Design/methodology/approach A three-month intervention integrating MLLMs into CLS was conducted with 50 EFL pre-service teachers at a Chinese normal university. Adopting an interpretive qualitative design, data were collected from longitudinal reflective journals, MLLM interaction logs, field notes and two rounds of semi-structured interviews with 5 purposively selected focal participants. Data analysis combined deductive coding based on CTML (intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load) with inductive thematic analysis to capture emergent patterns of AI-mediated learning and interaction. Findings The findings reveal that MLLMs functioned as cognitive-dialogic mediators in three key ways: (1) reducing linguistic and organizational barriers, thereby lowering extraneous cognitive load; (2) redistributing cognitive resources to support meaning-making and pedagogical reasoning; and (3) enabling deeper engagement in collaborative knowledge construction and reflective inquiry within CLS. However, participants also reported tensions related to epistemic reliability and the risk of overreliance on AI-generated outputs, indicating a shift in cognitive demands from knowledge construction to evaluation and regulation. Originality/value This study advances the field by proposing a cognitive-dialogic framework that brings CTML into dialog with sociocultural perspectives on mediation, offering a nuanced account of how AI reshapes teacher learning in practice-based settings. It contributes empirical evidence on the role of MLLMs as mediating tools in CLS and provides design implications for cognitively and ethically informed AI integration in teacher education.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how algorithmic monitoring shapes gig workers’ psychological well-being through passive and active algorithmic resistance. It further investigates whether algorithmic fairness alters the relationship between algorithmic monitoring and resistance behaviors. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a two-study quantitative design. Study 1 applies a three-wave survey of 224 gig workers in Pakistan, with four-week intervals between each wave. Algorithmic monitoring and algorithmic fairness were measured at Time 1, passive and active algorithmic resistance at Time 2 and psychological well-being at Time 3. Study 2 uses a 2 × 2 experiment with 115 participants, manipulating algorithmic monitoring and algorithmic fairness and examining resistance responses and psychological well-being. Findings Study 1 shows that algorithmic monitoring is positively related to passive and active algorithmic resistance, and that both forms of resistance are negatively related to psychological well-being. Passive and active resistance also mediate the relationship between algorithmic monitoring and well-being. Algorithmic fairness weakens the relationship between monitoring and active resistance. Study 2 shows significant interactions between algorithmic monitoring and algorithmic fairness for passive resistance, active resistance and psychological well-being, although the observed resistance patterns differ from the hypothesized form. Originality/value This study advances algorithmic human resource management (HRM) research by showing that gig workers do not merely experience algorithmic monitoring passively but respond through distinct forms of resistance that have implications for psychological well-being. By integrating labor-process theory, organizational justice theory and a stress-and-coping perspective, the study explains how algorithmic monitoring becomes psychologically consequential and how fairness shapes workers’ responses to platform control.

The framework method was used to analyse the data. Findings AI adoption remains limited and uneven, and is rarely embedded in everyday management control. Under uncertainty, controllers link AI to better forecasting and faster access to information, but worry about data quality, privacy and overreliance. In complex settings, they expect AI to help integrate diverse information and enable more systemic control, provided processes are standardised and human oversight remains. items.abstract_text: Purpose Agentic AI systems execute procurement decisions, reroute shipments and renegotiate supplier contracts at speeds that preclude real-time human review. The existing literature offers limited analytical attention to the risks that arise when decision authority is delegated to agents. This paper develops a risk taxonomy for agentic AI in supply chains and traces the hierarchical dependencies and influence magnitudes among the identified risks. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of literature, analyzed through theories–characteristics–contexts–methods framework, produces the risk taxonomy. A hybrid modified total interpretive structural modeling and fuzzy decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory methodology is then applied to structured expert judgments to establish the causal hierarchy and quantify inter-risk influence. Findings Three risks, namely workforce skill gap, data quality and reliability and ethical misalignment occupy the deepest level of the causal hierarchy. Lack of accountability and governance and data privacy emerge as terminal outcomes. All three analytical methods converge on a conclusion: agentic AI risks originate at the institutional layer, with technical risks acting as transmission mechanisms. Practical implications The findings indicate that effective governance requires that workforce capability, data integrity and objective-function alignment are addressed before deployment. The stratified agentic AI governance framework is proposed that translates hierarchical structure into a sequenced intervention architecture, providing practitioners with governance priorities organized by risk-propagation logic. Originality/value This paper contributes a systematically derived risk taxonomy and a causally weighted governance map for agentic AI risks in supply chains. Five propositions are derived from the causal structure and are advanced as a testable research agenda.

items.abstract_text: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can both enhance and constrain employee creativity, yet the mechanisms underlying these divergent effects remain unclear. This study examines how augmentation and automation motivations for GenAI usage shape employee creativity through distinct knowledge-processing mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on dual-process theory and self-regulation theory, we distinguish augmentation and automation motivations for GenAI usage and propose distinct cognitive mechanisms linking them to creativity. We test the hypotheses using a multi-wave, multi-source field survey and a scenario-based experiment. Findings Augmentation motivation is positively associated with employee creativity through knowledge integration, whereas automation motivation is negatively related to creativity through knowledge dependence. Conscientiousness strengthens the positive indirect effect of augmentation motivation and attenuates the negative indirect effect of automation motivation on employee creativity. Research limitations/implications Augmentation and automation motivations may coexist and vary across tasks and use episodes. Future research could explore these dynamics, examine how other individual differences shape their effects, and assess whether the consequences of GenAI dependence vary across work contexts. Practical implications Organizations should encourage employees to use GenAI to generate and develop ideas rather than replace their own judgment. Training could help employees critically assess AI-generated suggestions and combine them with their own knowledge. Originality/value This research shifts attention from how much employees use GenAI to why they use it. By distinguishing augmentation and automation motivations, it explains when and why GenAI can enhance or constrain employee creativity through distinct knowledge-processing mechanisms.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study investigates the trust paradox in artificial intelligence (AI)-generated content, where efficiency conflicts with perceived inauthenticity. Integrating source credibility theory and congruity theory, it examines how the interplay between ad genesis (AI vs. genuine), strategic context (disclosure, brand authenticity) and consumer mindset (construal level) determines communication effectiveness. Design/methodology/approach A three-study experimental design was employed to isolate specific contingencies. Study 1 manipulated ad genesis and AI disclosure to test engagement. Study 2 examined the moderating role of brand authenticity on purchase intentions. Study 3 tested the congruity between AI message focus (hedonic vs. utilitarian) and consumer construal levels. Findings Genuine imagery generally outperforms AI-generated imagery; however, effectiveness is contingent on strategic fit. Disclosure boosts engagement for genuine ads but reduces it for AI content. AI ads enhance purchase intentions for low-authenticity brands but damage high-authenticity ones. Furthermore, hedonic AI appeals align with high-construal mindsets, whereas utilitarian appeals suit low-construal consumers. Research limitations/implications The experiments used static images in controlled online settings. Future research should test dynamic and multimodal AI content and validate the effects with real-world behavioral metrics, such as click-through and conversion rates. Practical implications AI use should fit the context. Heritage brands should avoid AI imagery, whereas challenger brands can benefit from it. Disclosure helps genuine-image ads but hurts AI-generated ads. Hedonic AI appeals suit abstract mindsets, whereas utilitarian appeals suit concrete mindsets. Originality/value This research advances advertising theory by applying a split-credibility lens to AI-generated advertising, demonstrating that effectiveness depends on source-context congruence.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can function as both “performance accelerators” and “risk propagators” in organizations. This study investigates how AI-enabled work capability, particularly employees' decomposition and evaluation skills, is associated with deliverable quality and rework effort through the behavioral pathway of calibrated reliance on AI. Additionally, it examines task verifiability as a critical boundary condition that shapes the effectiveness of human-AI collaboration. Design/methodology/approach Guided by appropriate reliance and automation trust theories, data from 380 workers were analyzed using SmartPLS 4 (partial least squares structural equation modeling) and hierarchical polynomial regression to test mediation, moderation, and quadratic effects. Procedural remedies and a latent method factor approach were employed to assess common method bias. Findings AI-enabled work capability was positively associated with calibrated reliance on AI. Calibrated reliance on AI was associated with higher deliverable quality and lower rework effort. A double diminishing marginal pattern emerged: as reliance calibration increased, quality gains and rework reductions leveled off, indicating a “too-much-of-a-good-thing” pattern. Task verifiability strengthened the positive association between calibrated reliance and deliverable quality and also strengthened its negative association with rework effort. Originality/value This study shifts the focus from reliance intensity to reliance calibration in explaining AI-enabled work outcomes. It documents a double diminishing marginal pattern, showing that the benefits of calibrated reliance are meaningful but not unlimited. It also identifies task verifiability as a boundary condition that helps explain when calibrated reliance is more strongly associated with improved deliverable quality and reduced rework effort. These findings provide focused guidance for capability development, reliance calibration, and task-specific AI governance.

items.abstract_text: Purpose As artificial intelligence advances and its application scenarios continue to expand, human–artificial intelligence interaction grows increasingly close. While artificial intelligence brings convenience, it also raises concerns that it may weaken users' cognitive autonomy. To investigate this issue. This study aims to explore the composition of AI dependence and its impact on cognitive autonomy and specific aspects of creative performance. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on cognitive evaluation theory and the elaboration likelihood model to construct a dual-pathway model with instrumental dependence and affective dependence as core variables. The model explains the formation mechanisms of the two types of artificial intelligence dependence and their differential effects on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily examines their potential role in the elaboration dimension of creative performance. A two-stage mixed-method design was employed to test the model. Findings Study 1 found that perceived trust mainly had a positive effect on instrumental dependence. Different dimensions of interactivity differentially affected affective dependence and cognitive autonomy. Mediation analysis further confirmed the core mediating role of Dependence. Study 2, a small-sample exploratory experiment, re-tested selected hypotheses and found a possible negative effect of instrumental dependence on the elaboration dimension of creative performance. Research limitations/implications The main theoretical contribution of this study lies in revealing the dual-pathway formation mechanisms of artificial intelligence dependence and the reshaping effects of different types of dependence on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily explores the potential effects of dependence on elaboration performance. Originality/value The dual-pathway dependence model constructed in this study offers practical implications for understanding how long-term use of artificial intelligence affects cognitive autonomy.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how knowledge workers make sense of GenAI-enabled co-production, with particular attention to authorship ambiguity and its implications for competence attribution, self-evaluation and meaningful work. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a qualitative approach based on in-depth interviews with 32 knowledge workers who work directly with GenAI tools, combining inductive coding with abductive interpretation. We used the Gioia methodology to analyze participants' reported experiences and interpretations of human–AI collaboration, with sensemaking informing the interpretation of emergent themes and aggregate dimensions. Findings The findings identify authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. When GenAI contributes to ideation, analysis, drafting, coding or other knowledge-intensive outputs, workers may find it difficult to distinguish their own contribution from that of the technology. Participants responded to this ambiguity differently. Some reconstructed their expertise around judgment, validation and contextualization and experienced GenAI as extending their professional capability. Others struggled to internalize successful outputs as evidence of their own competence and reported impostor-like experiences and reduced meaningfulness. The findings suggest that experiences of GenAI-enabled co-production depend on whether workers interpret and reconstruct their contribution. Practical implications Managers in comparable knowledge-intensive settings may consider making human judgment visible, clarifying legitimate uses of GenAI and recognizing contributions beyond output speed and quality. Originality/value This study identifies authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. It shows how uncertainty regarding the respective contributions of the worker and GenAI can complicate competence attribution and initiate sensemaking about professional contribution. By explaining how workers' interpretations of authorship ambiguity are associated with divergent identity and meaning outcomes, including enhanced capability, impostor-like experiences and changing meaningfulness, the study extends research on human–AI collaboration beyond its predominant focus on performance and productivity.

items.venue: Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Technology
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine how tourists’ perceptions of fairness, accountability and transparency (FAT) in artificial intelligence (AI) recommendation algorithms shape algorithm trust and how trust influences recommendation acceptance and resistance, with tourism product type as a moderator. Design/methodology/approach A scenario-based online survey of 355 Korean adult consumers was conducted via travel-related Naver cafés and KakaoTalk communities. Hypotheses were tested with structural equation modeling in AMOS 23.0, and the moderating role of tourism product type was assessed through multigroup analysis. Findings All three FAT dimensions positively predicted algorithm trust, with transparency showing the largest effect, followed by accountability and fairness. Algorithm trust positively predicted recommendation acceptance and reduced resistance. Indirect effects through trust were significant for accountability and transparency but not fairness; accountability influenced trust only in the utilitarian condition. Research limitations/implications Self-reported, cross-sectional data from a Korean-only sample may limit causal inference and generalizability. Future research could use objective behavioral data, longitudinal designs and cross-cultural samples to extend the FAT–trust–behavior framework. Practical implications Tourism platforms should prioritize explainable AI features, adopt context-sensitive communication – emphasizing accountability cues for utilitarian services and transparency-based emotional appeal for hedonic ones – and focus on building trust at the first AI recommendation touchpoint. Social implications The findings provide empirical grounding for tourism-specific AI governance. The dominant role of transparency suggests that policymakers should consider introducing recommendation rationale disclosure requirements for AI-powered tourism platforms, enabling consumers to understand why specific products are suggested. In addition, the finding that consumers cannot directly evaluate algorithmic fairness highlights the need for independent, third-party fairness audits of recommendation systems to protect consumers from potential algorithmic bias that may systematically favor certain destinations, accommodations or price segments over others. Originality/value This study is one of the few to empirically apply the AI ethics FAT framework to tourism consumer behavior. The findings suggest that the three FAT dimensions may not contribute equally to algorithm trust – with transparency showing the strongest association regardless of context and accountability becoming relevant primarily in utilitarian service settings – which points to the limitations of treating FAT as a uniform construct in AI recommendation design. The resulting framework offers tourism platforms an empirical basis for tailoring AI trust strategies to specific product categories.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study investigates the configurational pathways underpinning digital-green synergistic transformation (DGT) and examines the enabling role of artificial intelligence (AI), thereby advancing understanding of how manufacturing firms navigate the dual imperatives of green development and digital upgrading. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the enabling effect of AI is more pronounced in state-owned enterprises, firms with high market attention and those with high industrial chain integration. It further demonstrates AI’s enabling role in these pathways, providing insights into how firms can embed AI to achieve their strategic goals. By revealing how AI’s effects vary across firm, market and industry contexts, this study advances a contextualized understanding of AI-enabled transformation.

items.abstract_text: Purpose Algorithmic leadership (AL) is an emerging leadership paradigm in higher education. It involves quantitative assessment, logical reasoning, precise calculation and a systematic problem-solving approach. The current study examines research on how AL reshapes strategic decision-making and planning, and how it informs policy recommendations in this domain. Findings The review and bibliometric analysis indicate that AL is an emerging field with growing interest among researchers and recommend further exploration, as the number of authors and organisations working on or adopting AL remains low. items.abstract_text: Purpose Firms increasingly depend on a small number of external providers for artificial intelligence (AI) models, yet that dependence is not only imposed by supplier concentration; it can also be reproduced by a firm’s own technology-integration decisions. This paper aims to examine how provider-specific integration progressively erodes a firm’s ability to switch providers, and what company leadership can do about it. Design/methodology/approach This paper is conceptual. Using resource dependence theory as its base, it draws on transaction cost economics, modularity and real options reasoning, organisational routines theory, and the attention-based view to develop a mechanism and an organisational capability, formalised in four core propositions, a typology matrix and a remedy audit. Findings The paper develops integration drift, a reinforcing process in which locally rational integration decisions cumulatively raise the cost of switching providers. It also introduces architectural hedging capacity (AHC), an organisational capability enacted through three recurring routines: governance-enforced modularity, rehearsed recalibration and sustained managerial attention. And lastly, the argument also identifies a boundary condition in resource dependence theory: where dependence is continuously reproduced through organisational integration, maintaining autonomy requires continuously reproduced exit capacity rather than a one-time remedy. Originality/value The paper extends resource dependence theory to settings where dependence is reproduced inside the firm through its own architecture, not only imposed externally. A typology and a remedy audit checklist give boards and managers a diagnostic for assessing and managing AI-provider dependence.

items.abstract_text: Purpose The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into Italian public administration raises a central question: can person-centred human resource management practices turn technology from a source of psychosocial strain into an enabler of continuous improvement? This paper explores how formalized and participatory governance of AI adoption, structured around three Kaizen principles, is associated with employee participation in digital change and with the technostress reported by public employees. Design/methodology/approach A theory-informed qualitative multiple-case study was conducted in five organizational cases, namely Italian public administrations engaged in digital transformation projects funded by the Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza (PNRR). In each organization, a manager–officer dyad (10 participants in total) took part in narrative interviews held between October and November 2025, focused on lived experiences of AI adoption, perceptions of human resource management and professional engagement. Transcripts were analysed through deductive, theory-driven content analysis based on the three Kaizen principles (process orientation, step-by-step improvement and human capital orientation) and on the technostress dimensions, followed by within-case and cross-case comparison. Findings Across 10 participant accounts embedded within five organizational cases, practices consistent with Kaizen were associated, within the accounts, with distinct narrative profiles of technostress and engagement. Accounts reporting all three principles described active co-authorship, professional empowerment and emerging roles; accounts reporting none described persistent techno-anxiety, disengagement and eroding professional identity. Among the creators, techno-insecurity is the one most closely tied to how adoption is governed, and is typically accompanied by techno-anxiety as an affective strain response, while overload, invasion, complexity and uncertainty appear in association with specific operating conditions. Intermediate accounts varied with the missing principle and its hierarchical level. Originality/value This paper develops the joint Kaizen–STS framework as an original analytical lens for AI governance in public administration. It provides qualitative evidence that Kaizen-consistent HR governance is associated with less salient technostress, particularly in the governance-related dimensions emerging from the analysis, and with stronger reported participation, professional agency and more favourable organizational conditions for continuous improvement. The study therefore contributes to organization and human resource management research by proposing the vertical governance gap between managerial design and operational experience as a sensitizing concept and offers public managers a diagnostic framework for PNRR-funded digital transformation across heterogeneous public-sector settings.

items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, NotebookLM, and DeepSeek have transformed higher education. AI tools are becoming commonplace among university students for academic writing, problem-solving, information retrieval, and self-directed learning. There has been an increase in research on these technologies, but current empirical studies remain scattered, using a variety of theoretical lenses, research variables, and methodological approaches. This makes it difficult to deepen the understanding of the usage of AI by university students. Relevant articles published from 2022 to 2026 were identified exclusively from the Scopus database and systematically analysed using the Literature Review Matrix, resulting in 35 empirical studies. The review synthesised evidence on theories, research variables, methodologies, and research gaps in the literature. The findings show that the most used theories are the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). Although studies on technology acceptance, student perceptions, and learning outcomes have received attention, the focus on AI literacy, responsible use of AI, and organisational aspects remains under-researched. This review offers a detailed summary of the existing research and suggests future directions for the effective and ethical use of AI technologies in higher education.

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into vocational education creates opportunities to support personalized, authentic, and student-centered learning, yet limited evidence explains how students experience AI when it is embedded in project-based contextual learning, particularly in vocational education. This study aims to examine students’ learning experiences during AI-Assisted Project-Based Contextual Learning (AI-PBCL) and explore the benefits and challenges students perceive when using AI as a learning partner. The study employed an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design involving 113 students at a vocational high school in Madiun, Indonesia. Quantitative data were collected through a learning experience questionnaire covering AI learning support, contextual learning, cognitive engagement, collaborative learning, learning autonomy, reflective learning, and overall learning experience, followed by semi-structured interviews with purposively selected students. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically and integrated to explain the quantitative findings. The results showed positive learning experiences across all dimensions, with contextual and collaborative learning emerging most strongly. Students perceived AI as supporting information exploration, feedback, problem solving, and project completion while facilitating discussion and knowledge construction. However, learning autonomy and reflection remained relatively less developed, alongside challenges related to AI dependence, information accuracy, prompt formulation, and internet access. These findings indicate that AI-PBCL can foster meaningful and authentic learning experiences when AI is positioned as cognitive scaffolding rather than a substitute for student thinking or teacher facilitation.

Because the detection community rarely reports how much energy a particular detector uses, twenty YOLO object detection models were trained on 13,639 aerial and satellite images of illegal mining equipment from Colombia, in three categories, reporting both detection accuracy and the energy required on the same instrumentation. Auditing those experiments allowed us to keep three sets of parameters fixed. Once the parameter set was fixed, architecture became the only free variable. Energy per image spanned a factor of 28, from 0.7 to 19.5 J, against a spread of only 0.14 mAP@50-95 in accuracy, so the detector was selected on marginal accuracy return per joule, at the knee of the Pareto front, rather than on accuracy alone. The knee where accuracy falls off occurred at YOLO26m, which produced 0.7260 mAP@50-95 on a previously unseen test dataset for 2048 mJ. Next, three of these models were compiled to INT8 for a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-8L accelerator, which served as a proxy for a nanosatellite payload. The workstation ranking did not survive compilation. There were changes at both ends: the model that ranked highest on the GPU lost 0.160 mAP@50-95 and finished last, while the two middle-ranked models switched positions. items.abstract_text: As generative AI reshapes professional and educational practice, institutions face a challenge: how to support diverse learners, from non-coders to advanced students, in building confidence and practice with AI-supported problem solving. Most institutional responses bifurcate into conceptual workshops for general audiences or technical courses for computer science majors, leaving few spaces where mixed-ability learners can engage common AI tasks at levels matched to their prior experience. This experience report presents the LearnAI Framework, a two-layer model for just-in-time AI co-creation piloted at a comprehensive teaching university. The Wide-Exposure Layer embeds short presentations in existing courses to build AI awareness at scale, reaching students and faculty across 18 courses in five disciplines. The Customized Co-Creation Layer provides opt-in, one-on-one sessions where clients work with trained undergraduate tutors through a 5-Stage Pedagogical Script: Problem Framing, Tool-Task Mapping, Iterative Co-Prompting, Deployment and Verification, and Ethical Reflection. Over two semesters, 35 clients co-created 36 portfolio websites and over 20 deployed web applications. Interviews with five clients and two tutors suggest a recurring change in how clients described AI use, shifting from treating AI as a passive answer machine to engaging it as a collaborative tool under human direction. A small paired pre/post AI readiness dataset (N=7) provides preliminary descriptive context, and tutor accounts document how the pedagogical script was enacted and adapted across client types. We report on boundary cases including clients who felt overwhelmed and respondents who deliberately rejected AI use. This paper contributes a practical, adoptable framework with initial evidence from a single institution.

items.abstract_text: Silicon Lifecycle Management (SLM) is essential for ensuring the reliability, security, and performance of modern computing platforms. Conventional SLM approaches rely on off-chip or software-only analytics, which lack on-die interpretability. We present X-OCTANE, an explainable on-chip telemetry-based anomaly notification engine. X–OCTANE is a hybrid explainability framework that integrates Causal-Preserving Mutual Information (CP–MI) with SHAP-based feature attribution for interpretable feature ranking and selection. The proposed feature rank-and-selection procedure retains competitive safety-oriented anomaly detection and bolsters security-specific in-field monitoring of compute platforms. For the 7 nm ASAP technology, X-OCTANE achieves competitive anomaly detection performance with less than 0.50% CPU die area and 1.0% non-idle power overhead. In addition, X–OCTANE improves anomaly-driven diagnosis accuracy by over 7% on average. Experimental validation using the PAMPAR benchmark suite on two separate experimental platforms demonstrates enhanced anomaly detection and diagnosis through the proposed explainable feature-rank-and-selection method. X–OCTANE establishes a scalable and transparent foundation for on-chip SLM analytics, unifying detection fidelity with causal interpretability.

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.abstract_text: To address the growing computational demands of high-performance computing (HPC) and machine learning (ML) applications, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) have transitioned from single-chip designs to multi-chip module (MCM) architectures, driven by manufacturing constraints. Simultaneously, GPUs are increasingly deployed in cloud environments to accelerate a wide range of applications for multiple users. Spatial multitasking, which allows multiple applications to run concurrently on a single GPU by executing them on different sets of streaming multiprocessors (SMs), offers an efficient method for sharing GPU resources. However, effectively supporting multitasking in the emerging MCM-GPU architecture presents a significant challenge that remains an open problem. This article presents the key observation that the placement of co-executing applications in MCM-GPUs plays a critical role in system performance. Specifically, for certain multiprogram workloads, co-executing applications achieve better performance when located on the same GPU chip to maximize memory bandwidth utilization. Conversely, other workloads benefit from being distributed across different GPU chips to mitigate memory contention. To address this, we propose a Location-Aware Scheduler (LA-Scheduler) that identifies application characteristics and makes optimized scheduling decisions. The LA-Scheduler performs lightweight workload classification using a k-means-based clustering method and applies multitasking scheduling rules during runtime to determine the optimal placement of applications within the MCM-GPU architecture. Evaluation results show that the proposed LA-Scheduler improves system throughput (STP) by an average of 38.67% compared with single-task operation. Compared with the traditional methods intra-chip scheduling and inter-chip scheduling, the system throughput is improved by an average of 13.51% and 7.14% respectively.

items.abstract_text: Large language models (LLMs) have great potential to enhance productivity in many disciplines, such as software engineering. However, it is unclear to what extent they can assist in the design process of electronic circuits. This article focuses on the application of LLMs to switched-mode power supply (SMPS) design for printed circuit boards (PCBs). We present multiple LLM-based workflows that combine reasoning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a custom toolkit that enables the LLM to interact with the SPICE circuit simulator to receive physical feedback. Two benchmark experiments are presented to analyze the performance of LLM-based assistants on various design tasks. These include parameter tuning and topology adaption, as well as design optimization of SMPS circuits through optimal catalogue component selection to maximize circuit efficiency or balance multiple objectives like size, ripple, and component loss. Experiment results show that SPICE simulation feedback and current LLM advancements, such as reasoning, significantly increase the solve rate on 269 manually created benchmark tasks from 15% to 91%. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that most parameter tuning design tasks can be solved, while limits remain for certain topology adaption and multi-objective optimization tasks. Our experiments offer insights for improving current concepts, for example by adapting text-based circuit representations.

items.abstract_text: Students are adopting LLMs at scale. This poses a question: does unrestricted AI access bypass the cognitive effort required for learning, or does it streamline knowledge acquisition? This paper reports on a study where we compare three designs for user-AI interaction in a learning context: (1) an unrestricted conversational bot like ChatGPT, (2) a pedagogically constrained bot that guides through hints without giving final answers, which we refer to as the Socratic mode; and (3) a non-conversational adaptive tutoring system that adjusts difficulty in real-time based on the user’s cognitive engagement derived from the brain signals. Fifty study participants were tasked with learning about nuclear safety protocols, a domain chosen for its zero-prior knowledge baseline. The participants progressed through an instructional video, a pre-test, an AI-driven assessment phase, which varied in the three conditions, and an immediate post-test. The nature of the questions centered primarily on factual knowledge acquisition, but it still required participants to have a global understanding of the concepts in order to answer the questions correctly. A Muse headband was used to derive the cognitive engagement of all users in all conditions. The unrestricted chatbot produced higher learning gains (delta) than both constrained modes ( p <.03, d > 0.80), while the adaptive condition generated significantly higher EEG engagement ( p =.018). The cluster analysis of chatbot usage and discussion patterns by users showed that most participants in the unrestricted-mode adopted a direct answer-retrieval strategy, while participants in the Socratic-mode initially attempted to reason through the hints before progressively disengaging. Consequently, this also suggests that the success of the unrestricted AI is not an evidence of deeper learning, but rather a result of the immediate post-test evaluation after the training phase.

items.abstract_text: Table Question Answering (TableQA) requires reasoning over natural language questions and structured tables and remains challenging due to noisy evidence and complex multi-step reasoning. Recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based approaches typically adopt decomposition–reasoning–validation pipelines that combine Chain-of-Thought (CoT) decomposition, Direct Prompting (DP), Python Agent (PyAgent) execution, and self-validation. However, these methods still largely rely on unconstrained LLM reasoning during decomposition, which may introduce unsupported sub-questions and irrelevant evidence expansion. We propose EV idence- A ware (EVA), a framework that explicitly grounds decomposition on question-relevant table evidence before reasoning begins. EVA first extracts evidence-aware relational structures that associate question semantics with supporting table attributes, thereby constraining sub-question generation within a grounded evidence space. EVA further introduces relation-guided validation and integrates both DP and PyAgent reasoning to improve robustness across different reasoning patterns. Experiments on datasets across multiple LLMs demonstrate that EVA consistently improves reasoning reliability and achieves strong performance across diverse TableQA settings.

items.abstract_text: The rapid growth of long-form documents presents a fundamental challenge to information retrieval (IR). Their length, dispersed evidence, and complex structures demand approaches that go beyond standard passage-level techniques. This survey provides a comprehensive review of long-document retrieval (LDR) and organizes existing work into three major eras of development. It traces progress from classical lexical and early neural models to pre-trained language models (PLMs) and large language models (LLMs). It highlights core paradigms such as passage aggregation, hierarchical encoding, efficient attention, and LLM-driven re-ranking and retrieval. In addition to methods, the survey summarizes domain-specific applications, available evaluation resources, and the benchmarks that shape empirical study. It identifies open challenges related to efficiency tradeoffs, evidence localization, multimodal alignment, and interpretability. The principal conclusion is that future progress in LDR will depend on hybrid solutions that combine sub-linear indexing, structure-aware modeling, and LLM-based reasoning (resources are available at https://github.com/lmh0921/Long-Document-Retrieval-SURVEY-PLMs-LLMs ).

items.abstract_text: Machine learning models are increasingly proposed for high-risk domains, such as healthcare and public policymaking. However, their growing complexity creates significant obstacles to transparency. This complexity arises from various factors; in this work, we focus on making the organizational development process of a model transparent. A model is often developed over many years and involves multiple version updates, carried out by different individuals, and based on varying subsets of data. To address these issues, we propose a new model reporting framework called a lifecycle narrative, characterized by three dimensions: first, how the purpose of the model has incrementally evolved over time; second, how the data used in the model and the model itself have been developed; and third, what inferences can be made with the model and what the consequences of its use are. We demonstrate these three dimensions using a case study of a high-risk application in healthcare. Our framework complements existing model reporting tools, such as model cards and datasheets, by reconstructing the full lifecycle of the model—a documentation requirement of the EU AI Act. Ultimately, the lifecycle narrative empowers external stakeholders, such as regulators, researchers, citizens, and national competent authorities, to holistically understand a model’s development process.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT now provide novice programmers with instant, personalized support and are reshaping computing education. While a growing body of work has examined AI's immediate impacts, multi-year classroom evidence remains limited on how students’ awareness of AI, student-AI interaction patterns, and course outcomes evolve as GenAI becomes routine in classrooms. To address this gap, we investigate an introductory Python course across three successive AI-supported cohorts (2023-2025). Using questionnaires, coded student-AI dialogue logs, and course assessment records, we examine cohort-to-cohort shifts in students’ AI awareness, interaction practices, and course outcomes. We find clear cohort-to-cohort differences in students’ relationships with GenAI. Across cohorts, familiarity and prior use became increasingly normalized before course entry, and student-AI interaction shifted from more implementation-oriented use toward more iterative workflows centered on verification, debugging, and refinement. At the same time, course outcomes remained broadly stable. Together, these findings suggest that, during a period in which GenAI became increasingly normalized in everyday life and classrooms, the most visible cohort-level differences appeared in how students sought help, verified their work, and coordinated problem-solving with AI, rather than in final course performance. The central instructional challenge, therefore, is not simply whether students use AI, but how courses can cultivate productive, course-aligned, and agency-preserving forms of AI use.

items.abstract_text: Background : Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce fluent, context-responsive explanations and clinical suggestions, but the same fluency can conceal factual, evidentiary, or reasoning errors. Health professions students therefore need more than access skills or generic warnings: they need repeated practice deciding when AI advice is warranted, when it requires verification, and when it should be rejected. Aim : To propose a theory-informed, operational framework for teaching appropriate reliance on GenAI through case-based learning. Approach : A focused critical synthesis integrated four bodies of scholarship: GenAI in health professions education, trust and automation bias in human-AI interaction, metacognition and self-regulated learning, and case-based learning. The purpose was conceptual integration rather than exhaustive evidence retrieval or estimation of intervention effects. Framework : Verification-Scaffolded Case-Based Learning (VS-CBL) is a six-phase cycle: Commit, Consult, Challenge, Corroborate, Calibrate, and Consolidate. Students first make and rate an unaided judgment, then consult a documented AI system. They actively test the response for omissions and counterevidence, verify pivotal claims against authoritative sources, decide whether to accept, modify, or reject the advice, and complete an accountable final response plus an unaided transfer task. Faculty prevalidate cases, vary AI accuracy and error subtlety, preserve patient privacy, and scale oversight to clinical risk. Implications : VS-CBL shifts the educational target from AI use or satisfaction to appropriate reliance. It supports measurement of overreliance, underreliance, verification quality, confidence-accuracy calibration, reasoning quality, and delayed independent transfer. The design is adaptable across medicine, nursing, pharmacy, dentistry, rehabilitation, public health, and allied health programmes, including settings with limited connectivity. Conclusion : The educational question is not whether students should trust GenAI in general, but whether trust is warranted for a particular claim, task, and level of risk. VS-CBL offers a testable curriculum architecture for making that judgment visible and teachable. Its effectiveness and implementation burden require prospective, multicentre evaluation.

In many university settings, the accessibility of AI tools through internet-enabled devices has reduced the need to consult libraries or engage with multiple scholarly sources because users find AI-generated responses so swift, with ready-made content that does not overwork them. The study investigated the growing use of artificial intelligence and the decline of knowledge verification practices among students and teachers in higher education institutions in mid-western Uganda. It explores how AI tools are influencing academic habits, including reduced library engagement, increased reliance on instant digital responses, and the growing perception that information obtained from the internet is fundamentally correct. Using a mixed-methods approach involving questionnaires and interviews, the study examined the extent to which students and teachers verify AI-generated content before incorporating it into academic work. The findings of this study highlight the emerging culture of unquestionable trust in AI and its implications for scholarly rigor, critical thinking, and academic integrity in Ugandan universities. items.abstract_text: Human decision-making is often influenced by cognitive biases, especially under uncertainty and risk. Prior works have studied biases in single-step decision environments with immediate outcomes or in interaction with a single AI agent. However, less attention has been given to (1) cascaded settings with delayed outcomes, where decision at one step influences future system states and (2) to interaction with multiple AI agents. To study this, we designed a naval battle strategy game where participants interact with two AI advisors. We find asymmetric responses to positive and negative outcomes, with significant changes after negative outcomes. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and large language model (LLM)–based simulated patients are being evaluated for problem-based learning and case-based learning in undergraduate medical education, but delivery formats are often under-specified and outcome measurement is inconsistently reported. Feasibility outcomes (recruitment, encounter completion, survey completion, technical failures, and encounter duration) and acceptability outcomes (post-encounter engagement ratings, delivery-format preference, and open-ended comments) are reported descriptively. Of 72 students invited, 19 (26%) enrolled; all completed the encounter and paired pre/post surveys (100%), with no technical failures (no encounter was terminated and no participant was excluded), although learners reported intermittent technical problems that interrupted but did not end encounters; the group session lasted approximately 35 min and individual encounters a median of 31 min (range 17–83).
