The largest effect—a psychological-safety gain in the Individual cohort (Wilcoxon r = 0.62)—was significant before correction ( P =0.026) but not after (adjusted P =0.20). No between-cohort comparison reached significance. A single motivation item declined by one median point in both cohorts. The modal post-encounter preference was a hybrid “solo first, then group” model (7/12, 58%). On the feasibility and acceptability indicators examined, the encounter was delivered as planned in both formats and was rated favorably by learners; these data do not address educational effectiveness. items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a tool to support food risk assessment and broader food safety activities in response to the growing complexity of global food supply chains, emerging foodborne hazards, and evolving food fraud practices. Unlike previous reviews that have largely focused on individual AI technologies or specific applications, this review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), transformer-based models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), multimodal learning, and emerging AI paradigms within a unified framework relevant to food risk assessment and food safety decision-making. The review examines their applications in hazard identification, contamination detection, predictive microbiology, risk classification, food fraud detection, surveillance, traceability, and decision-support systems. Particular attention is given to the strengths, limitations, interpretability, validation requirements, and implementation challenges associated with different AI approaches. The integration of AI with multimodal data sources, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, spectroscopy, biosensors, and advanced analytical platforms is also discussed as a means to improve risk prediction, monitoring, and early-warning capabilities. Key challenges include data quality and availability, model generalizability, limited external validation, computational requirements, interpretability, and regulatory acceptance. Emerging developments, including foundation models, federated learning, blockchain, digital twins, edge AI, and multimodal frameworks, are highlighted as promising directions for future research. Overall, this review provides a critical comparative framework for understanding the evolving role of AI in food risk assessment and related food safety applications, while identifying key scientific, technical, and regulatory priorities for future development and implementation. publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Male infertility contributes to approximately half of all cases of couple infertility worldwide, yet its diagnostic cornerstone, conventional semen analysis anchored in World Health Organization (WHO) criteria, suffers from inter-observer variability that can reach 30–40% for morphological parameters even among trained andrologists. Computer-assisted sperm analysis (CASA) reduced some sources of error but failed to eliminate the subjectivity inherent in morphological classification, particularly for the acrosome, midpiece, and cytoplasmic droplet defect categories. Convolutional neural networks and ensemble deep learning architectures have since demonstrated high classification accuracy on selected benchmark datasets (detailed under Results), prompting fundamental questions about the clinical readiness and translational utility of AI-assisted andrology. Methods (Approach) This is a critical review that synthesises evidence from peer-reviewed studies identified through targeted searches of PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore (through May 2025), covering AI applications in sperm morphology classification, motility analysis, non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) outcome prediction, and sperm selection for intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), supplemented by hand-searching the reference lists of key articles. Search terms combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for “sperm morphology,” “deep learning,” “convolutional neural network,” “azoospermia,” “testicular sperm extraction,” and “ICSI,” restricted to English-language, peer-reviewed publications. Studies were selected for methodological relevance, recency, and clinical significance rather than through a pre-registered, reproducible systematic protocol; no formal risk-of-bias or quality-appraisal instrument (e.g., QUADAS-2 or PROBAST) was applied. This is a deliberate scope decision, declared here rather than implied: the review is a critical, evidence-synthesising appraisal of a fast-moving field, not a systematic or scoping review, and quantitative performance figures drawn from heterogeneous studies (summarised in Table 1) should be read as illustrative of the state of the field rather than as directly comparable, pooled estimates. Results Deep learning models, including ensemble and attention-augmented convolutional architectures, have reported accuracies of 94% to 96.77% and F1-scores of up to 98.2% for sperm morphology classification, principally on the HuSHeM benchmark dataset; the morphology-classification studies summarised in Table 1 report accuracy, precision, or F1-score rather than AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve). Machine learning models integrating hormonal, genetic, and histopathological features achieve AUC values of 0.807 to above 0.90 for predicting sperm retrieval success in microdissection testicular sperm extraction (m-TESE). For AI-assisted real-time sperm selection during ICSI, a prospective sibling-oocyte study of 646 metaphase II oocytes found only a non-significant trend towards improved fertilisation, whereas a separate, smaller sibling-oocyte comparison, reported to date only as a conference abstract, described a statistically significant improvement in fertilisation; live birth rate data remain scarce. However, the predominance of single-centre, algorithmically homogeneous training datasets, absence of prospective multicentre validation, and the opaque decision logic of most deployed models collectively constrain clinical adoption. Conclusions AI-assisted sperm morphology assessment has attained technical maturity but not clinical readiness. The transition from benchmark accuracy to actionable diagnostic utility requires prospective multicentre validation using clinically diverse and ethnically representative cohorts, live birth rate pre-specified as the primary endpoint, with fertilisation and blastulation rates as secondary endpoints, and the development of explainable AI frameworks compatible with regulatory standards including the EU AI Act. The Middle East and North Africa region, characterised by high rates of male-factor infertility, distinct genetic aetiologies, and constrained laboratory infrastructure, represents both a critical validation environment and an equity-relevant deployment target for these technologies.

Altmetric is placed in the study as an additional metric for tracking the scholarly and popular amplification of GenAI-integrity research.

items.venue: Journal of Language Teaching and Research
items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly transformed teacher professional learning in English as a foreign language (EFL) education. However, relatively limited research has examined how teachers strategically regulate and sustain their AI-related learning processes, particularly across different stages of professional experience. This study investigated AI self-regulated learning (AI-SRL) among novice and experienced Vietnamese in-service EFL teachers. An explanatory sequential mixed methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected from 1,108 Vietnamese in-service EFL teachers using the AI-SRL Scale, followed by semi-structured interviews with 10 teachers. The quantitative findings revealed that novice teachers demonstrated significantly higher levels of AI-SRL than experienced teachers, particularly in task planning, self-monitoring, and self-evaluation. Notably, no statistically significant differences were identified in help seeking and institutional support. Interestingly, the qualitative findings showed that teachers’ AI-SRL was shaped not only by technological factors, but also by professional identity, emotional responses toward AI learning, and contextual conditions surrounding AI integration. Novice teachers demonstrated remarkably stronger exploratory orientations toward AI learning, whereas experienced teachers expressed greater concerns regarding pedagogical stability and professional accountability. Overall, the study extends previous AI-related educational research by offering a more process-oriented and psychologically nuanced understanding of teacher professional learning in AI-mediated educational environments. The findings also provide valuable pedagogical implications for AI-related teacher professional development in EFL contexts.

items.title: Education After Cognitive Scarcity: A Capability–Experience–Institution Framework for Learning in the Age of Advanced AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Rapid improvements in generative and agentic artificial intelligence are changing a long-standing condition of education: access to high-level cognitive assistance is becoming less scarce. This shift does not make human knowledge obsolete. It changes the design problem. When external systems can explain, synthesize, calculate, generate, critique, plan, translate, code, and increasingly coordinate complex tasks, educators can no longer infer human capability from successful task completion alone. Nor is it sufficient to ask which abilities remain “uniquely human,” because that boundary is technologically unstable and normatively incomplete. This paper proposes a human-development framework for education under cognitive abundance. It introduces Human-Sovereign Capability as a criterion for deciding which capabilities people should remain meaningfully able to exercise even when AI can perform related tasks at higher average performance; Capability Residency as a way to distinguish capability residing in a person, an external system, or a governed human–AI arrangement; and a Learn–Augment–Supervise–Delegate allocation model for deciding the intended relationship between learners and AI. It then extends these decisions into learning design through Productive Friction, a Capability–Experience–Evidence Network, and a Learning Continuity Architecture. The framework culminates in a three-level derivation: Capability → Experience → Institution. The argument is intentionally not that every component concept is new. Cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, automation, scaffolding, tutoring, formative assessment, learner modelling, and lifelong learning have substantial prior literatures. The contribution is an integrated architecture that begins with the normative question of what humans should remain capable of doing, then derives educational experiences, evidence conditions, and institutional obligations from that choice. This paper is presented as an initial framework release from the LiA2036 Research Initiative, with the architecture intended to support inspectable and domain-specific extensions rather than a single universal implementation. The paper closes with research propositions and design questions that can make the framework empirically testable rather than merely rhetorical.

items.abstract_text: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) companions are increasingly used by post-secondary students for emotional support, stress management, and self-management, yet their potential implications for primary care in this population remain unclear. Students may engage with AI companions before encountering purpose-built therapeutic chatbots, which are more often accessed through intentional health-seeking or professional guidance. This distinction may position AI companions as an earlier influence on self-management and subsequent help-seeking. Objective: To examine how artificial intelligence (AI) companions may influence stress regulation, sleep quality, symptom interpretation, and healthcare-seeking behaviour among post-secondary students, and to identify the principal benefits, risks, and unresolved questions relevant to primary care. Methods: A conceptual narrative review was undertaken using literature identified through Harvard University’s Hollis Library and Google Scholar. Evidence related to AI companions, academic stress, sleep quality, emotional support, healthcare-seeking behaviour, primary care, and digital mental health was synthesized using Stress & Coping Theory and the stress-buffering hypothesis as theoretical foundations. Results: AI companions may support stress appraisal, cognitive reframing, emotional reflection, symptom articulation, and self-management before clinical encounters. However, they may also contribute to emotional overreliance, misinformation, reassurance seeking, sleep disruption, and altered help-seeking behaviour. This review proposes conceptual mechanisms linking AI companion engagement with stress regulation, sleep, and pathways into primary care while identifying relational intensity as a clinically meaningful dimension of engagement beyond frequency alone. Conclusion: AI companions should be understood as adjunctive rather than substitutive support. Their clinical relevance is based on how they can shape patients’ experiences before obtaining primary care. Longitudinal research is needed to determine how patterns of engagement influence stress, sleep, and healthcare utilization over time.

items.title: The Thirsty Machine: India's AI Data Centre Race, the Water Crisis, and the Choice Between Argentina's Libertarian Gamble and China's Governance Blueprint

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract India is building an artificial intelligence data centre network, which is expected to grow to 15 GW by 2031, almost entirely in severely water-stressed cities. This digital growth is coming at a time when we estimate that by 2025 water use has reached 150 billion litres per year, and by 2030 it will increase to 358 billion litres per year, while experiencing aquifer depletion, water scarcity in cities, and no requirement for environmental disclosure Significantly, under the Environment Impact Assessment Notification 2006, gigawatt-scale computing facilities are classified under building construction (Category B2) and hence do not require a public hearing, disclosure of water source, or mandatory Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) benchmarking.. There is no national data centre policy in force since it has been in draft since 2020. This study employs a most-different systems design model (Przeworski & Teune, 1970) to compare three distinct governance paradigms for AI infrastructure: India's democratic vacuum, Argentina's libertarian deregulation, and China's authoritarian spatial planning. This article examines the libertarian vision of the zero regulation, non-liability, AI corporation, governance-free zones for hyperscale infrastructure espoused by Argentina's Milei government as a model for Third World approaches to international law as neo-colonial resource extraction. China's "East Data, West Computing" initiative offers an alternative state-led roadmap and includes the commercial scale deployment of underwater cooling, the spatial movement of data centers to the interior, the imposition of PUE/WUE standards, and the implementation of water pricing. Based on the insights of recent sustainability science, of hydrology, and of governance scholarship, this article calls for a rejection of the race-to-the-bottom deregulatory impulse and of authoritarian centralisation in India, in favour of a sovereign, democratic path, based on mandatory environmental benchmarks, spatial planning, community consent, and institutional accountability. India's freshwater resources constitute a public commons requiring democratic governance, not an unregulated subsidy for expropriation of the global AI infrastructure expansion.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Incorporation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into academic writing instruction has made a huge difference in instruction for English as a Second Language (ESL) students who often struggle with grammar, vocabulary, coherence, and academic organization. The present study investigated the effectiveness of using AI assisted learning platforms to improve academic writing of ESL students in higher education. The convergent mixed methods research design was used and a purposive sampling method was used to select 120 undergraduate and postgraduate ESL learners. A twelve-week academic writing intervention was developed that uses AI Tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, and QuillBot. Pre-test and post-test writing evaluation, and structured questionnaires were used to gather quantitative data and semi-structured interviews were conducted to get qualitative data. Results indicated that after the intervention, there was a great improvement in all aspects of academic writing performance. The study concludes that AI-supported learning platforms have significant pedagogical potential in relation to the development of academic writing skills of ESL learners, provided they are used in relation to the academic writing process, considering responsible use in higher education settings.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Graph neural network (GNN) detectors of AI-generated text report state-of-the-art accuracy, and the architectural claim that graph topology captures signals invisible to sequential classifiers is now common in the literature. We report the complete lifecycle of one such detector, from construction to falsification. AEGIS, a graph attention network over k-nearest-neighbour text graphs with multi-signal edge weights, reaches 98.50% accuracy on scientific abstracts with only 73K trainable parameters, outperforming five established baselines. We then subject our own system to the evaluation its headline number deserves: generation-time length control, format normalization, leakage-free splits, a tuned frozen-embedding probe as the calibrated null, and a 10 × 10 cross-generator transfer study over three seeds. Under this protocol the graph's apparent contribution collapses from +0.240 AUROC over a surface baseline to −0.0004 AUROC against the tuned probe, inside the measured replication noise floor, and the two detectors' transfer geographies are near-identical (ρ = 0.986). A single untuned regularization default manufactured a +0.027 phantom advantage. The structural differences the graph encodes are real, but they are a re-encoding of information already present in the embeddings. We distil the audit into a practical checklist for evaluating architectural claims in text detection, and argue that accuracy numbers and mechanism claims must be validated separately.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence and extended reality (XR) offer unprecedented opportunities for adaptive educational entertainment, yet existing systems suffer from static content pipelines and weak integration between immersive interaction and intelligent adaptation. Here we introduce GenEdXR, a framework that unifies a transformer-based deep knowledge tracing (DKT) module, a large-language-model content synthesis pipeline, a proximal-policy-optimisation adaptive orchestration engine, and multi-modal XR rendering within a closed-loop architecture. These components are bound through a scaled dot-product cross-modal attention fusion mechanism that integrates semantic, cognitive and temporal representations. We evaluated GenEdXR through a large-scale simulation protocol involving 33,510 replayed learner trajectories from three complementary public datasets --- ASSISTments 2009--2010, the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, and KDD Cup 2010 Algebra 2005--2006 --- spanning question-level, session-level and step-level interaction granularities. Under five-fold cross-validation across four framework configurations, GenEdXR-Full attained the highest normalised learning gain (M = 0.523; Cohen's d = 2.71 versus baseline), highest engagement and flow-zone membership, and lowest cognitive-load proxy. items.abstract_text: Abstract Evaluating information generated by artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an everyday educational task. Families and classrooms offer different settings for learning this practice, yet their socioeconomic distribution is usually examined separately. This exploratory study analysed linked parent and student reports from the Programme for International Student Assessment 2025 across sixteen education systems. Among 94,262 paired respondents, the equal system mean proportion combining a lower or unfamiliar parental AI evaluation rating with never or almost never practising AI evaluation in lessons was 15.45%. This combination occurred among 24.69% of students in the lowest socioeconomic resource quintile and 8.27% in the highest, a difference of 16.42 percentage points (95% confidence interval 15.45 to 17.39). The contrast was positive in all sixteen systems. In 93,687 records, lower parental ratings were associated with a 3.87 percentage point lower probability of reporting practice at least sometimes after adjustment for school fixed effects, student backgrounds and the full parental rating of ordinary online information (95% confidence interval 3.02 to 4.73 points lower). Estimates changed little with science performance adjustment or response weighting. Allowing arbitrary missing focal responses widened the resource contrast to an identification interval of 0.69–30.40 points, with sampling uncertainty at the lower endpoint including zero. items.abstract_text: Abstract AI-enabled learning technologies are becoming routine in higher education. However, acceptance research tends to explain adoption through beliefs about technology while paying less attention to the capabilities that learners bring to AI interaction. Although AI literacy has recently been linked to acceptance, it is often modeled as a global score or as separate dimensions, leaving unresolved whether related competencies operate collectively within the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) mechanism. This study tests a higher-order extension of the TAM using survey data from 528 students across three Indonesian universities who had prior experience with AI for learning. AI literacy was specified through awareness, usage skills, critical understanding, and ethics awareness and estimated using a disjoint two-stage partial least squares structural equation modeling procedure. The results support a coherent higher-order representation and show that AI literacy is most strongly associated with perceived ease of use and is also positively related to perceived usefulness and attitude. Within TAM, attitude shows a stronger direct relationship with behavioral intention than usefulness. These findings position AI literacy as a learner capability layer that complements technology beliefs in explaining students’ evaluations of AI-enabled learning technologies. The study contributes a measurement-to-mechanism perspective that maintains practical, critical, and ethical competence in acceptance research and suggests that implementation should consider learner capability alongside access and usability. Because the evidence is cross-sectional, self-reported, and multi-tool, the relationships should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence can support legal case analysis, but perceived assistance, reported verification and confidence in evaluating reasoning represent different educational outcomes. This study examines their alignment in a Bangladesh questionnaire database containing 385 consenting, AI-aware adults. The primary analysis concerns the 237 respondents identifying as law students; the full database provides descriptive context and sensitivity analysis. Low internal consistency supported item-level analysis rather than a composite critical-reasoning scale. Endorsements, paired contrasts, joint response patterns and exploratory regression were used to distinguish reported practices from self-assessed capability. Among students, 66.7% reported checking AI-generated legal information against authoritative sources, 41.4% reported comparing alternative interpretations, 48.9% expressed confidence in detecting weak or unsupported reasoning and 52.3% reported retaining independent judgement. Verification endorsement exceeded detection confidence by 17.7 percentage points (bootstrap 95% interval 9.3–26.2; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Only 18.6% endorsed verification, detection confidence and independent judgement together. None of four focal predictors-comparison, legal-source verification, awareness of plausible inaccuracies and prompting capability-was retained after multiplicity correction in the adjusted student model. Ordinal, full-sample and secondary judgement-outcome analyses likewise retained no focal coefficient. Self-regulated learning supplies a process-oriented interpretation, while technology acceptance helps delimit perceptions of assistance. The findings identify uneven alignment among self-reports rather than an observed deficit in legal reasoning or a causal effect of AI. Educational implications concern evaluating source checks, argument comparison and independent revision through performance-based tasks, with explicit attention to jurisdiction and authority. The study supports more discriminating assessment of AI-assisted legal learning rather than inferring competence from use or confidence alone.

items.title: AI-Driven Reconstruction of Online Health Narratives Using Agent-Action-Outcome Modeling: Algorithm Development and Validation

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background People share health experiences online as stories, not isolated facts. Most computational systems reduce these narratives to keywords or claims, overlooking the agency, causality, and interpretation that determine whether health information is safe or potentially harmful to act on. Content can use medically accurate terminology while describing unsafe behavior, rendering it invisible to fact-checking and keyword approaches. This limitation, which we term narrative blindness , constrains the ability of computational systems to extract, represent, and reason over narratives as coherent wholes. Objective This study introduces the Narrative Builder, a computational framework that reconstructs unstructured online health stories into machine-readable agent-action-outcome (AAO) narrative graphs, preserving structural, causal, and interpretive dimensions. We formalize narrative blindness as a measurable property of natural language processing systems and evaluate whether theory-grounded reconstruction can address it. Methods We operationalized Labov and Waletzky’s sociolinguistic narrative theory within a computational AAO schema, enriched with interpretive dimensions from psychological and clinical communication frameworks. From 5386 Reddit health threads (spanning February 2019 to November 2024), 2 domain experts (a biomedical researcher and a physician) annotated a gold-standard dataset of 2000 segments from 704 threads, with interrater reliability (Krippendorff α) of 0.75 to 0.82 across all annotated tasks (0.78-0.81 for the 4 interpretive classification tasks). A dual-model architecture combining BioBERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations From Transformers for Biomedical Text Mining) with a conditional random field (CRF) layer for AAO extraction and multitask DistilBERT for interpretive classification was evaluated using 5-fold grouped cross-validation, grouped on the annotation-level key to prevent data leakage, with a separate held-out test set and a McNemar test against term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) and BioBERT-without-CRF baselines. Results The Narrative Builder achieved a span-level F 1 -score of 0.850 for AAO extraction on the held-out test set, with per-type F 1 of 0.90 (action), 0.83 (agent), and 0.77 (outcome), outperforming the TF-IDF baseline (0.781; P <.001). Labovian stage classification reached macro- F 1 of 0.501, and interpretive dimensions reached macro- F 1 values of 0.466 (emotion), 0.528 (stance), and 0.465 (tone). Clinical-value extraction achieved a precision of 0.90, and Unified Medical Language System concept normalization reached 100% coverage across 12,101 queries. A rule-based causal direction classifier identified 17.3% of segments as candidate outcome-to-action (inverted) patterns, though validation showed limited precision (0.277), and this distribution is reported as exploratory. Single-rater expert review of generated graphs indicated narrative coherence (mean 0.89, SD 0.08) and medical plausibility (mean 0.91, SD 0.07). Conclusions The Narrative Builder reads health stories as coherent wholes rather than isolated facts, producing AAO narrative graphs that retain the agents, actions, outcomes, and emotional framing that determine how individuals interpret and act on health information. By formalizing narrative blindness as a measurable property and reconstructing narrative structure with strong extraction performance, this work establishes narrative reconstruction as a feasible complement to fact-based health informatics, providing structured input for downstream credibility assessment.

items.abstract_text: Background Conversational AI systems are increasingly used for web-based mental health support, yet evidence on sustained engagement, therapeutic alliance, and longitudinal outcomes remains limited. Baseline data from 527 self-referred users of the large language model–enabled chatbot Clare indicated high psychological distress and early development of a subjective working alliance. Objective This exploratory study examined the feasibility and descriptive outcome patterns associated with the use of the multimodal conversational agent Clare over 4 and 8 weeks in a real-world setting, focusing on engagement, perceived working alliance, and mental health measures. Methods We conducted a naturalistic, single-arm, repeated-measures observational study of self-referred, English-speaking adults recruited online via social media and search advertisements. Participants interacted with Clare over 8 weeks. Two analytic samples were defined by engagement and assessment completion: a 4-week sample (active engagement plus completed 4-week assessment) and an 8-week sample (additionally requiring continued engagement and completed 8-week assessment). Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 4, and 8 weeks: engagement metrics (calls, messages, and call duration), alliance measures (Working Alliance Inventory–Short Revised and Mobile Agnew Relationship Measure), and mental health measures (Patient Health Questionnaire–4, Patient Health Questionnaire–Distress, Mini–Social Phobia Inventory, UCLA Loneliness Scale, and Satisfaction With Life Scale). Changes were evaluated using 2-tailed paired-samples t tests with effect sizes; given substantial attrition and reliance on complete-case analyses, linear mixed-effects models were run as sensitivity analyses, and findings warrant cautious interpretation. Results Of 527 baseline participants, 369 enrolled and 348 actively engaged with Clare; 53 out of 348 (15.2%) met the 4-week criteria and 21 out of 348 (6.0%) met the 8-week criteria. Engagement peaked in week 1 (calls: mean 1.77, SD 1.52; messages: mean 10.02, SD 16.68) and declined thereafter. Among T1-T2 complete pairs (n=52), mean Patient Health Questionnaire–Distress scores decreased by 1.13 (95% CI 0.25 to 2.02) points, Patient Health Questionnaire–4 scores decreased by 0.69 (95% CI −0.01 to 1.40) points, Mini–Social Phobia Inventory scores decreased by 1.73 (95% CI 0.88 to 2.58) points, Satisfaction With Life Scale scores increased by 6.23 (95% CI 4.70 to 7.76) points, and UCLA scores increased by 0.48 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.96) points. Among participants with Working Alliance Inventory–Short Revised data (n=53), total scores increased by 0.20 points from T1b to T2 (95% CI −0.01 to 0.42); among the 8-week retained subgroup (n=21), Mobile Agnew Relationship Measure scores increased by 0.22 points from T2 to T3 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.42). Conclusions Sustained engagement was limited, and outcome estimates were obtained from small, highly selected follow-up samples. The observed changes cannot be attributed to Clare because the study had no control group and substantial, nonrandom attrition.

items.title: Classroom Integration of AI-Simulated Patients and Automated Feedback in Doctoral Psychotherapy Training: Longitudinal Mixed Methods Study

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Psychotherapy education increasingly emphasizes technology-assisted methods that extend deliberate practice beyond human supervision. AI has enabled automated skill assessment and patient simulations, yet few studies have examined how students experience such tools in real-world settings alongside established practice modalities. Objective We aimed to evaluate students’ experiences with AI-augmented deliberate practice embedded in an existing psychotherapy course sequence. Secondary aims included identifying implementation barriers, ethical and pedagogical considerations, and factors influencing students’ acceptance of AI-assisted learning. Methods Participants were 29 first-year clinical psychology doctoral students in a 2-quarter psychotherapy sequence at an American Psychological Association–accredited program. In the fall course, students completed weekly peer role-plays and could optionally submit transcripts to CARE for AI feedback to supplement peer feedback. In the winter course, students completed required weekly deliberate practice through Skillsetter video vignettes and could optionally practice with CARE’s voice-based AI-simulated patients, receiving AI and instructor feedback afterward. Surveys with Likert-type and free-response items were voluntary in the fall and required in the winter; 9 and 25 students completed them, respectively. Analyses included descriptive statistics, matched-pairs testing, and thematic analysis. Results In the fall course (n=9), where privacy concerns and survey nonresponse limited data on AI feedback, students rated peer feedback higher than AI feedback on being constructive and helpful (median 3, IQR 3-3 vs median 2, IQR 2-2; P =.02) and recognizing areas to improve (mean 5.22, SD 0.83 vs mean 4.33, SD 0.87; P =.046), citing transcription errors and a narrow focus on empathy while valuing AI’s alternative phrasing. In the winter course (n=25), Skillsetter was rated higher than CARE only for learning from mistakes (mean 4.52, SD 2.00 vs mean 3.20, SD 2.04; P =.03); immersion, spontaneous responding, communication beyond words, and alliance building did not differ significantly. Students valued CARE for interactive practice not possible with vignettes but reported undetected vocal pauses (20/25, 80%), insufficient realism (14/25, 56%), and limited emotional expression (13/25, 52%), and raised concerns about AI replacing peer support (22/25, 88%) and peer interaction (20/25, 80%). Asked about AI broadly, students expressed mixed views, citing concerns about supplanted relational dynamics, nonconsensual data use, and generative AI’s environmental impacts. Conclusions Embedding AI-augmented deliberate practice into an existing course sequence was feasible, but students’ experiences favored established methods: they preferred human over AI feedback and described video vignettes as more realistic than voice-based AI interactions, while valuing AI-simulated patients for interactive practice other modalities could not provide. Implementation barriers included feedback quality, transcription accuracy, and instructor time required to supplement AI feedback. Perceptions of AI’s instructional utility appeared contingent on students’ trust in the technology, suggesting future deployments should weigh a sample’s attitudes toward AI and its value relative to existing training resources.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Natural language processing and AI models are increasingly used to extract emotional signals from textual data; however, systematic validation of different computational paradigms in emotionally complex relational contexts remains limited. Such approaches may contribute to digital health research, particularly in the fields of digital mental health and couples therapy, where understanding emotional expressions within romantic relationships is especially relevant. Objective This study aimed to compare a lexicon-based approach (NRC Emotion Lexicon) and a transformer-based model (Pysentimiento) in detecting affective patterns within spontaneous romantic relationship narratives and to evaluate their criterion-related associations with a theory-driven measure of relational well-being. Methods In this cross-sectional exploratory study, 112 Spanish adults completed the Couple Flourishing Measure (CFM) and provided an open-ended description of their romantic relationship. Narratives were analyzed using both computational approaches to generate emotion and sentiment indices. Pearson correlations were computed between model outputs and CFM scores. Steiger Z tests were conducted to compare dependent correlations across models. Results Both approaches showed significant associations with couple flourishing, although the transformer-based model yielded stronger correlations for several affective dimensions, particularly positive sentiment ( r =0.66, 95% CI 0.54-0.76) and negative sentiment ( r =−0.74, 95% CI −0.82 to −0.65). The lexicon-based approach showed smaller associations, primarily for negative emotions. Steiger Z tests identified significant between-model differences for disgust ( P =.04), joy ( P =.01), sadness ( P =.004), surprise ( P =.03), and positive and negative sentiment (both P <.001), but not for anger or fear. Conclusions In this sample, Pysentimiento showed stronger associations with couple flourishing than the NRC Emotion Lexicon across several affective dimensions, although differences were not consistent across all categories. These findings support the value of theory-driven external criteria for evaluating computational emotion detection in relational narratives and underscore the importance of context-sensitive interpretation when applying AI tools in psychologically sensitive domains. These findings also highlight the potential relevance of computational emotion analysis for digital health research, particularly in digital mental health and couples therapy research, although further validation in clinical settings is needed before clinical implementation.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background AI is increasingly embedded in health care and digital health applications, shaping clinical processes as well as how patients access information and participate in care. Research on bias in medical AI has largely focused on technical and performance-related disparities. Less attention has been paid to how such biases may affect patients’ access, understanding, trust, and opportunities for meaningful involvement in care. Objective This scoping review aimed to map how studies of bias in medical AI describe patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment and the digital divide and to identify gaps across technical, social, structural, and patient-centered perspectives. Methods This scoping review followed JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute) methodology and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE and EBSCOHost databases were searched in August 2025 and supplemented by Google Scholar searches. Peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 onward were included if they addressed bias in medical AI and described patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment or digital inequality. Data charting focused on AI application types, bias dimensions, patient empowerment domains, digital divide–related factors, intersectionality, and debiasing strategies. Findings were synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results The search identified 497 records, of which 22 studies met the inclusion criteria. Bias was represented as a multidimensional sociotechnical phenomenon, with social bias identified most frequently (21/22 studies), followed by algorithmic bias (16/22 studies), structural bias (14/22 studies), and design-related bias (12/22 studies). Patient empowerment was most frequently addressed through involvement in care (n=13), followed by health literacy (n=9) and trust and assurance (n=7), whereas broader psychosocial and everyday-life domains were addressed less frequently. Digital divide–related factors were identified in 19 of the 22 studies, with digital literacy and usability barriers reported most frequently. Seven studies considered 2 or more social or structural dimensions of disadvantage. Although many studies discussed approaches that could mitigate bias-related barriers, explicit empirical evaluation of debiasing strategies in relation to patient empowerment or digital equity was largely absent. Conclusions Patient-related consequences of bias in medical AI extend beyond algorithmic performance and are reflected in access, understanding, trust, and involvement in care. Broader empowerment dimensions, multidimensional disadvantage, and empirically evaluated mitigation strategies remain comparatively underexplored.

items.title: A Teacher's Concerns about AI in Primary School: Critical Thinking, Personal Data and the Fear of Cognitive Dependence

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of pupils' everyday lives and of school life. Written from the perspective of a primary school teacher and principal, this perspective paper examines three interrelated concerns of the author herself. These concerns arose from a wish to protect her pupils and led her to study the topic for her own professional development and to help her colleagues make teaching safer and better. They concern developing critical thinking towards AI-generated answers, protecting the personal data of minors, and the fear that excessive assistance from AI will weaken pupils' thinking. Drawing on a narrative, non-systematic review of recent research on cognitive offloading, the European and Greek regulatory framework, and illustrative examples from the author's own teaching practice and lesson scenarios for primary school, it argues that the fear of cognitive dependence is a plausible concern rather than an established finding for primary school pupils. The available evidence, which comes mainly from adolescents and adults, suggests that the form of AI support (whether it replaces the learner's effort or scaffolds it) may be an important factor. AI is regarded throughout as a valuable tool; the risk lies mainly in the way it is used. The classroom examples come from ordinary lessons whose only purpose was to teach pupils to question AI answers and to protect themselves when using AI. They were not planned as research, no research data were collected, and they are offered as the author's practitioner reflections, not as findings. The author's classroom experience illustrates that such activities can be implemented in ordinary primary school lessons, but their effects on pupils' critical thinking have not yet been evaluated. The paper relates the three concerns to long-standing educational principles, in particular Socratic questioning, Dewey's reflective thought and Vygotskian scaffolding. On this basis, it proposes a simple, as yet untested three-step classroom protocol (``think -- ask -- check''), age-appropriate data protection rules, and a role for school leadership, and outlines questions for future research.

items.abstract_text: The paper examines contemporary approaches to unmanned excavation using open-pit excavators, with a focus on reducing the human factor through data-driven and digital-model-based control. The objective is to develop and justify a methodological approach to algorithmic control of the digging and loading cycle. The method involves formalizing bucket path control as a multi-criteria optimization problem subject to constraints on the drive loads, face geometry, and safety requirements, combined with the system simulation based on the sensor data and a digital face model. It is shown that a closed-loop control system with feedback on loads and position of the working equipment stabilizes the cycle parameters, reduces the operating variability by 15–25%, and limits the peak loads by 10–18%. Methods are additionally considered for adapting the algorithms to changing face conditions, including the rock fragmentation analysis and telemetry data. It is established that introduction of a virtual loading zone and integration with the in-pit fleet management system improve safety and quality of loading. The results demonstrate that transition to the algorithmic control based on digital models creates prerequisites for conditionmonitored maintenance and further digital transformation of mining operations.

items.abstract_text: The determinants of the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-based virtual assistants in metaverse-enabled augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) training environments are the focus of this study, which is based on the need to improve the training experience of students who display anti-social behavior. An integrated approach based on the task-technology fit and the UTAUT2 models is adopted to investigate the factors that affect the training experience in AR and VR environments enabled by metaverse technologies. An online survey conducted in two languages—English and Arabic—yielded 310 participants. The data were then analyzed based on the hybrid approach of structural equation modeling and artificial neural networks. According to the study, the strongest predictor of the behavioral intention to use metaverse-based training systems is the performance expectancy factor, which is 94.1%, followed by the social influence factor, which is 67.5%, and the hedonic motivation factor, which is 66.6%. In addition, the effort expectancy and facilitating conditions factors did not affect the intention to use the training systems. In conclusion, the study revealed that the AI virtual assistant factors and the strategies adopted in the development of the training systems play an essential role in improving the training experience of students who display antisocial behavior in the classroom.

items.title: Minds Meet Machines: The Joint Role of Trust and Intellectual Humility in AI Persuasion

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Research shows that AI models have a remarkable ability to change people’s minds following a short conversation, a notoriously difficult task for human communicators. Such persuasive paradigms provide a unique opportunity to examine which psychological characteristics predict receptivity to counter-attitudinal information. We focus on two characteristics: intellectual humility (IH), reflecting openness to revising one’s beliefs following new information, and trust in the information source (AI). To establish the role of a-priori dispositions that determine acceptance of new information, we ran two online studies, sampling British participants with a negative attitude toward legal immigrants (N = 294). We replicated previous findings showing significant and lasting attitude change following a brief exchange with GPT, but crucially, this effect was not uniform. In Study 1, attitude change was greatest among participants with higher initial trust in AIs and higher intellectual humility. Study 2 extended this finding by measuring both dispositions a week before the conversation with GPT, revealing the same pattern: opinion change was greatest among those who were both open to new information and trusting of its source. These findings highlight the centrality of recipient dispositions, suggesting that the relationship between source trust and persuasion depends on recipients' intellectual humility. More broadly, source trust may function as more than a heuristic cue, and its relationship with attitude change may depend on recipients' willingness to recognize the fallibility of their beliefs. Together, these findings extend perspectives on persuasion by highlighting the joint role of source trust and recipients' epistemic dispositions in belief revision.

items.abstract_text: This paper reconsiders Bildung under the double condition of planetary crisis and AI-mediated life. It develops planetary Bildung as a renewal of the classical self–world relation beyond the autonomous subject, situating human formation within ecological interdependence, technological mediation, vulnerability, and responsibility. Bildung cannot be reduced to competencies, digital literacy, environmental knowledge, or ethical regulation but must cultivate embodied perception, situated judgement, and ethical responsiveness. Special attention is given to the algorithmic governance of attention, through which AI-mediated environments shape what appears relevant and desirable. Against this narrowing, planetary Bildung is presented as the formation of finite, embodied beings who transform knowledge into responsiveness, mediation into judgement, and limitation into attentiveness.

Transparent consent, responsible data practices, fairness audits, and human oversight remain essential. Emerging developments include generative AI, conversational systems, predictive personalisation, autonomous marketing agents, and privacy focused technologies. The paper emphasizes strategic integration and ethical governance. Ultimately, AI should complement human marketing judgment while enabling meaningful customer relationships, sustainable competitive advantage, and improved organizational performance.

items.abstract_text: Marketing theory and practice have changed a lot over the last seven decades. In the middle of the century, business strategies were mostly focused on the company, putting more emphasis on making a lot of products using the same messages and spreading them through one-way media channels like newspapers, radio, TV, and signs on the road. The internet arrived in the 1990s and started the move to digital. This brought interactive ways of talking, digital data, tracking performance, and grouping people by demographic attributes. Now, marketing is changing again because of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and big data analytics. AI marketing changes how businesses work from trying to keep customers to predicting what they might want, changing prices in real time, making suggestions that fit each person, and assisting via chatbots. This paper looks at the journey from old ways of pushing messages to today's smart AI systems. It examines theoretical concepts, how systems work, strategic benefits, implementation bottlenecks, and real examples from companies like Amazon, Flipkart, Zomato, Swiggy, Netflix, Spotify, and HDFC Bank.

items.abstract_text: Governance of agentic artificial intelligence has concentrated on the beginning and middle of a system’s operational life — how an agent is approved, what it may access, and how its behaviour is monitored while it runs — and has treated the end as a technical afterthought. This article argues that decommissioning an agentic system is not an endpoint but a transition, in which an accountable actor becomes a set of orphaned effects, access paths, and records that require an owner. Existing regimes govern much of an agent’s operating life and address fragments of retirement, but they do not specify an integrated governance approach to residuals that survive operational termination. The article distinguishes the retirement of an agent’s access, which identity and security practice addresses, from three residual problems it does not address: the plan interrupted mid-execution, the effect already propagating, and the decision record that must survive the actor. From this distinction it derives two governing principles — that the conditions for a clean death must be established during the agent’s life, and that the impacts of death must be provisioned for as soon as they are foreseeable while those incurred are remediated and owned. It specifies how these duties should scale with an agent’s discretion and reach, so that the architecture binds, as a condition of deployment, only above a materiality threshold; how they might be allocated across supplier, deployer, and custodian; and how the obligation to preserve an agent’s record can be made to survive (...)

items.title: CardioTwin-AI: development and internal validation of a digital twin-based adaptive risk-aware learning framework for heart disease prediction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Heart disease is one of the most common causes of death in the world and early identification of individuals at elevated cardiovascular risk requires reliable risk-assessment methods that can support clinical decision-making. Many conventional machine-learning models focus primarily on disease classification or risk prediction and do not explicitly provide patient-specific virtual representations. This study introduces CardioTwin-AI, a Digital Twin-based Adaptive Risk-Aware Learning Framework (ARLF) to predict the presence or absence of heart disease. We propose a data-driven, patient-specific Digital Twin representation based on clinical attributes, in which the patient state is mapped to a corresponding virtual state and evaluated using state-level synchronization measures, including Twin Simulation Error (TSE) and Twin Fidelity Score (TFS) to quantify representation consistency. The deep feature representations are generated by feature engineering process based on autoencoder, and then analysed by the ARLF prediction model to estimate the probability of the presence of heart disease. It achieved high patient-state representation consistency between the source clinical state and its virtual representation, with a Twin Fidelity Score of 99.76% and a Twin Simulation Error of 0.002402. The proposed ARLF model achieved accuracy of 90.21%, precision of 90.32%, recall of 94.11%, F1-score of 92.18%, and ROC-AUC of 95.13% in the fixed held-out evaluation. The results indicate the potential of CardioTwin-AI for predicting the presence or absence of heart disease and assessing patient-state representation consistency, subject to further external validation and prospective clinical evaluation.

items.title: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace has widened the gap between what universities teach and what employers expect of new hires. This study examines that gap through a mixed-methods research-to-practice design grounded in employer perspectives. Three objectives guided the work: (a) identify gaps between undergraduate AI preparation and workplace requirements, (b) develop a workforce-informed AI competency framework from documented industry needs, and (c) identify workforce-driven priorities for an AI literacy curriculum. Data were collected in four sequential phases: a structured narrative review ( n = 56), industry focus groups and interviews ( n = 13), survey instrument development, and a convenience sample of predominantly U.S. employers recruited through professional networks ( n = 110). Open-ended survey responses were analyzed through hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis. Findings indicated that employer-defined AI readiness is fundamentally socio-technical: task-specific prompting and tool fluency must be coupled with professional communication, collaboration, human oversight, and judgment, soft skills that employers rated as highly as technical AI competencies. Employers also perceived recent graduates as underprepared, particularly in AI output verification and AI ethics. Within this sample, stronger governance emphasis correlated with deeper AI integration and higher self-reported efficiency, but the results are descriptive and do not support causal inference. Employers recommended an undergraduate curriculum organized around five employer-informed AI competencies, with AI output verification and responsible AI use as core outcomes. The study contributes a socio-technical conception of workplace AI readiness in which technical and human-centered competencies are interdependent rather than parallel.

items.title: Interactive AI tools, personalized feedback, and EFL learners’ intention to use AI: an extended TAM study in Egyptian higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Introduction Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education, how interactive AI features and personalized learning feedback shape learners' acceptance remains insufficiently understood. This study examines their influence on Egyptian university students' behavioral intention to use AI tools through an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), focusing on the mediating roles of perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. Methods An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed. Survey data from 596 Egyptian university students were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM), followed by thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with eight purposively selected participants. Results Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use significantly predicted behavioral intention. Interactive AI features influenced intention indirectly through perceived usefulness, whereas personalized learning feedback influenced intention indirectly through perceived ease of use. Interviews revealed that interactivity supported engagement, clarification, and learner control, while personalized feedback facilitated error correction, reduced ambiguity, and alleviated anxiety. Participants viewed AI tools as flexible learning support rather than replacements for human instruction. Discussion The findings highlight the importance of pedagogically meaningful interaction and personalized feedback in shaping EFL learners' acceptance of AI tools. Responsible integration should emphasize learner agency, critical evaluation of AI-generated responses, and continued human pedagogical guidance.

items.title: AI-integrated programmatic assessment: a proposed framework for safeguarding cognitive development in AI-augmented learning environments

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence has unsettled a quiet assumption on which assessment in higher education has long relied: that the work a student submits is a reasonable proxy for what that student can do. When a fluent essay or a plausible solution can be produced with little independent effort, the inference from product to competence weakens. Institutional responses have concentrated on integrity, detection, and compliance, and less on what sustained reliance on these tools may do to learning. Emerging evidence shows that performance with AI and learning without it can come apart, and we argue that the more important risk is therefore developmental: that some forms of reliance may bypass or, over time, erode the effortful thinking through which durable understanding and professional judgement are built. We treat this as a testable possibility rather than an established general effect. Building on programmatic assessment, we propose AI-Integrated Programmatic Assessment (AIPA). The model samples three streams of evidence on the same construct: unaided cognition, AI-mediated performance, and the quality with which learners orchestrate AI. It treats orchestration as a professional competence to be taught and assessed rather than a behaviour to be policed, and it specifies explicit rules for interpreting differences between what a learner can do with and without AI, including band thresholds, recurrence and corroboration requirements, and a distinction between coherent and discrepant profiles. A confirmed discrepancy is read as a hypothesis about a current competence gap that prompts further sampling and a proportionate response; the term erosion is reserved for documented decline from a comparable earlier level. We position AIPA against adjacent approaches, including programme-level secure and open assessment, process-focused and interaction-trace assessment, and linked assessment designs, illustrate it through four worked cases, and set out a research agenda to test its claims.

items.title: Editorial: Harnessing AI to support self-regulated learning in educational and workplace settings

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The Research Topic begins with Achuthan's Artificial intelligence and learner autonomy: a meta-analysis of self-regulated and self-directed learning, which provides a broad empirical examination of the relationship between AI and learner autonomy. Synthesizing 32 empirical studies, 92 effect sizes, and 3,029 participants, the study examines the effects of AI-based interventions on SRL, self-directed learning (SDL), different dimensions and phases of SRL, and learning outcomes. The findings indicate positive effects of AI interventions on overall SRL and SDL, with particularly notable effects during the forethought phase, including goal setting and planning. At the same time, less consistent effects for behavioral regulation point to an important design challenge: supporting learners in knowing what to do and why to do it does not necessarily ensure that they will translate those intentions into effective action. The findings therefore provide encouraging evidence for AI as a scaffold for self-regulation while highlighting the importance of designing support across the full SRL cycle.Building on this macro-level evidence, Agustin's AI as a co-regulator: relational design for strengthening self-regulated learning addresses the theoretical mechanics of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in Winne and Hadwin's COPES architecture, this conceptual paper tackles a core dilemma in educational technology: how can AI assist learners without eroding the cognitive agency and productive struggle essential to self-regulation? Agustin introduces "productive metacognitive friction" -the deliberate structuring of challenge and discrepancy within AI interaction -as a design mechanism to prevent passive reliance. The article presents five relational design principles alongside an evaluation framework prioritizing learner autonomy, interpretability, process integrity, and long-term developmental growth across both formal education and workplace reskilling environments.Moving from meta-analytic synthesis and conceptual frameworks to empirical classroom research, Gu et al.'s Fostering feedback literacy by scaffolding self-regulated feedback: a comparative study of GenAI and human peers examines the operational mechanisms through which GenAI fosters feedback literacya key component of self-regulated learning. In a comparative mixed-methods study of first-year undergraduates in Hong Kong, the authors compare the developmental impact of GenAI-generated feedback against traditional human peer review. Their findings demonstrate that GenAI yields a statistically significant improvement in feedback literacy over human peer feedback alone. Qualitative evidence reveals that this advantage stems from GenAI's ability to scaffold distinct self-regulatory behaviors: providing immediate, non-judgmental spaces for goal setting, structured planning, critical evaluation, and real-time self-reflection. By removing the interpersonal friction and psychological safety concerns common in peer review, GenAI emerges as an effective tool for cultivating student feedback literacy.Finally, Chang et al.'s "Should I tell my teacher?" Student AI disclosure practices, stigma, and selfregulated learning in higher education examines the affective, social, and institutional factors that influence how learners adopt these tools in practice. Focusing on undergraduate students at a Canadian university, the authors explore the intersection of student AI disclosure practices, social stigma, and SRL processes. Their findings illuminate a key tension: while transparent disclosure to instructors correlates with proactive self-regulated learning behaviors (a "transparent-disclosure pattern"), fear of academic judgment and social stigmatization often triggers an "anxious-concealment pattern." Highly anxious students who use AI heavily are more likely to conceal their usage or restrict sharing to peer networks. This study highlights that technical scaffolds cannot succeed in a vacuum; institutional policies and pedagogical environments must account for emotional and social dynamics to prevent secrecy from undermining reflective SRL practices.Considered together, the four articles in this Research Topic illustrate that AI's role in self-regulated learning extends far beyond simple automation or content delivery. Achuthan's meta-analysis provides evidence of AI's potential to strengthen SRL and SDL, while also identifying limitations in behavioral regulation. Agustin's framework addresses this challenge conceptually by positioning AI as a co-regulator that supports learners without displacing their agency. Gu et al. demonstrate how such support can be enacted in feedback processes, whereas Chang et al. show how emotions, stigma, and institutional expectations shape learners' decisions about AI use. This collection highlights that realizing the promise of AI-supported self-regulated learning requires more than personalization or automation. Research and design must examine how AI can scaffold regulatory processes, support learner autonomy and human agency, and safeguard against cognitive over-reliance.

items.title: The human in the loop: a conceptual framework for understanding humanness in AI-integrated higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: As AI becomes more embedded in higher education, critical questions are being asked about whether components of academic work are still human. This conceptual article offers a theoretical framework and an eight-proposition process model to explain how university educators might perceive, negotiate, and maintain their humanness within the context of AI use. Based on Haslam’s dual-dimension model of humanness, sociomateriality, and professional identity theory, we propose that AI pressures compel educators to renegotiate their professional roles across four interrelated dynamics: articulating an indispensable human core, managing identity disruptions, restoring humanness through increased relationality, and cultivating a constructive ambivalence. Our specific theoretical contributions are a “humanness-in-the-mirror” reframing of dehumanization theory, a precisely specified construct of productive ambivalence as a persistent (rather than transitional) professional posture, and an AI-Humanness Inversion argument distinguishing professional and institutional claims about AI from ontological ones. We extend humanness theory by arguing that educators, in response to AI influence, emphasize features of human nature (e.g., warmth, presence, authentic connection) while reconceptualizing human distinctiveness as cognition that is situated, vulnerable, and relational rather than simply abstract problem solving. The paper offers these propositions and the conceptual model as a basis for future empirical research, not as established findings.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Watershed environmental governance increasingly combines dense sensing infrastructure with institutions whose attention, authority, and coordination capacity remain limited. We develop the cognitive orchestration layer as a theory-building concept for examining how large language model (LLM)-based agents may connect sensing, assessment, decision advice, institutional response, and feedback without displacing domain models or public authority. Methods The Agentic Framework for Watershed Governance (AFWG) specifies three enabling pathways, three institutional interfaces, and four propositions. A purposively selected set of eight publicly documented cases is used to illustrate functional configurations, source limitations, and research gaps; it is not a systematic review or empirical evaluation. Results The cases document sensing, assessment, and decision-support functions, but do not establish improved decision quality, sustained institutional use, environmental outcomes, or agent-executed response closure. MAESTRO is retained as an adjacent-domain design illustration, not an existence proof of full-loop closure: human authorization remains necessary, and its reported performance has not been independently replicated. Discussion Transfer to watershed governance is plausible only where domain models remain authoritative, outputs carry provenance and uncertainty, named officials retain authority to authorize consequential actions, and institutional audit and failure handling are built into deployment. AFWG therefore offers a bounded conceptual framework and a falsifiable research agenda, rather than a claim that agents have already closed the watershed response loop.

items.title: The relationship between AI-assisted learning and academic performance through learning engagement

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Introduction The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has raised an important question regarding whether AI-assisted learning is associated with students' academic performance. Although prior studies have highlighted the potential benefits of AI in education, the psychological processes underlying this relationship remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the association between AI-assisted learning and academic performance, with a particular focus on the mediating role of learning engagement as an educational psychological mechanism. Methods Data were collected through an online survey of university students in Shanxi Province, China. Using a convenience and snowball sampling strategy, 438 valid responses were obtained and analyzed. The study employed multi-item scales to measure AI-assisted learning, learning engagement, and academic performance, including a literature-informed self-developed scale for AI-assisted learning and adapted scales for learning engagement and academic performance. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS 27.0 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY, USA) and AMOS 24.0 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY, USA), including descriptive statistics, reliability and validity tests, correlation analysis, structural equation modeling (SEM), and bootstrapped mediation analysis. Results and discussion The results indicate that AI-assisted learning is positively associated with both learning engagement and academic performance. Learning engagement also has a significant positive effect on academic performance. More importantly, the findings show that learning engagement partially mediates the relationship between AI-assisted learning and academic performance, highlighting the role of students' psychological involvement in the learning process. These findings suggest that the educational value of AI-assisted learning is associated not only with technological support but also with students' psychological engagement in learning activities. This study contributes to the literature on AI in education by providing a psychologically grounded explanation of the relationship between AI-assisted learning and academic outcomes. It also offers practical implications for educators and institutions seeking to integrate AI into higher education in ways that foster meaningful engagement and enhance effective learning.

items.title: Production cues and conditional reliance in AI-mediated news: a three-study investigation of audience judgment under information asymmetry

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into digital news presentation, understanding how audiences interpret AI-related production cues is critical to explaining evaluations of journalistic authority and reliance. Yet existing research has largely focused on transparency and generalized trust, leaving the relationships among production cues, perceived journalistic attributes, cognitive authority, and context-dependent reliance insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we propose a Signal–Attribute–Authority–Conditional Reliance (SAAC) framework and evaluate it across three complementary studies involving Chinese digital-news users: a 2 × 2 randomized experiment manipulating AI-disclosure and human editorial-review cues while holding the underlying AI-produced news stimulus constant ( n = 473); a cross-sectional survey integrating structural modeling, predictive analysis, and necessary condition analysis ( n = 522); and explanatory semi-structured interviews ( n = 29). The experiment showed that production cues influenced several post-exposure evaluations despite identical news content. Survey findings revealed associations linking perceived disclosure quality and human editorial oversight to perceived news quality and accountability, with further associations involving journalistic cognitive authority, conditional reliance, and acceptance intention, although explanatory and predictive performance remained modest. Interviews indicated that participants distinguished technological presentation capability from journalistic source qualification and evaluated reliance in relation to news topics, perceived stakes, editorial involvement, and institutional safeguards. Together, the findings suggest that,within the present study settings, AI-mediated news acceptance is better understood as an I nstitutionally situated and conditionally bounded judgment than as a simple function of transparency or generalized trust.

items.abstract_text: With the widespread adoption of online educational technologies, instructional videos have become a pivotal tool for flexible and efficient learning. The integration of visual aids, such as animations and dynamic elements, aims to enhance the learning experience; however, their effectiveness remains debated. This study examined learning performance and subjective experience when instructional videos presented static AI-generated images or manually animated versions of those images. A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 40 undergraduate participants ( n = 10 per cell), comparing static versus motion-enhanced presentation conditions across male and female participant groups. Stable Diffusion XL generated the base images, and CapCut was used to add motion; the motion itself was not AI-generated. Participants viewed a 140-s mobile video on mortise-and-tenon structures, completed a 10-item accuracy test, and rated willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and mental effort. The ANOVA results provided no statistically significant evidence of a main effect of motion on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several subjective outcomes. For acceptability, the gender × motion interaction was statistically significant, but Bonferroni-adjusted simple-effect tests supported a gender-group difference only in the static condition. For mental effort, the interaction was also statistically significant; adjusted simple-effect tests indicated higher mental effort among female than male participants in the dynamic condition and higher mental effort in the static than dynamic condition among male participants. Given the small sample and multiple outcomes, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping labor market structures and transforming how college students perceive their future career development. Understanding the psychological processes associated with the relationships between perceptions of AI and career-related outcomes has therefore become increasingly important. Drawing on Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), this study examined the relationships between perceived career impacts of AI and career decision-making self-efficacy among college students, with particular attention to the indirect roles of career planning and career anxiety. A questionnaire survey was conducted with 415 Chinese college students, and the proposed hypotheses were tested using structural equation modeling. The results showed that positive perceived career impacts of AI were positively associated with career decision-making self-efficacy, with career planning representing an indirect pathway in this relationship. In contrast, negative perceived career impacts of AI were not directly associated with career decision-making self-efficacy but were indirectly associated with lower self-efficacy through an indirect association involving career anxiety. These findings indicate that college students' perceptions of AI are associated with career decision-making self-efficacy through distinct cognitive and affective processes. The study provides empirical support for the applicability of SCCT in understanding career development in the context of AI and enriches the literature on the relationships between AI-related career perceptions and students' career decision-making processes.
