items.abstract_text: Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Adolescents increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots for schoolwork, yet evidence on whether this use supports or undermines learning is mixed. Drawing on research on cognitive offloading and self-regulated learning, we examined whether GenAI use for schoolwork is related to scientific literacy directly and through two components of self-regulated learning, academic help-seeking and metacognitive strategy use, and whether the purpose of use matters. Methods We analyzed the Program for International Student Assessment 2025 (PISA 2025) data from 12,191 15-year-old students in 374 schools in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China. Weighted two-level mediation models compared students within the same school, used all ten plausible values, and evaluated indirect effects with Monte Carlo confidence intervals. Results were checked against a design-based model with school fixed effects and balanced repeated replication weights. Results Students who used GenAI more often than their schoolmates reported more help-seeking ( β = 0.17) and more metacognitive strategy use ( β = 0.30). Help-seeking was positively associated with scientific literacy, yielding a positive indirect effect ( β = 0.013, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]); the indirect effect through metacognitive strategies was smaller ( β = 0.007) and was fully accounted for by science self-efficacy. The direct association between GenAI use and scientific literacy was negative ( β = −0.048, about 4 PISA points), and the positive indirect effects offset about 40% of it, leaving a small negative total association ( β = −0.028). Purpose mattered: among users, using GenAI “to help me learn” was associated with higher scientific literacy (+5.8 points per response category), whereas using it to summarize texts, research new topics, or draft assignments was associated with lower scores (−6.6 points). The results did not differ by gender or socioeconomic status and were identical under the design-based model. Discussion GenAI use for schoolwork is associated with scientific literacy through opposing pathways: a positive one through academic help-seeking and a negative direct one, and the direction of the association differs by purpose of use. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations may partly reflect which students use GenAI rather than the effects of its use.

items.title: From disclosure to epistemic accountability: preserving meaningful human control across the AI-assisted research lifecycle

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics
items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded across the scientific research lifecycle, while prevailing governance remains centered on disclosure of tool use and the assignment of responsibility to human authors. We argue that disclosure is necessary but insufficient because it does not establish that researchers understood, verified, challenged, and authorized the AI-assisted processes that shaped scientific claims. We define this disconnect as the epistemic accountability gap and develop the Lifecycle Epistemic Accountability Framework (LEAF) as a testable theory of how meaningful human control can be preserved across AI-assisted knowledge production. Drawing on a structured integrative review and critical interpretive synthesis, LEAF links four human-control capacities—competence, contestability, intervention authority, and traceable ownership—supported by evaluability by design, to five lifecycle checkpoints spanning evidence identification, study design and ethics, data processing and analysis, interpretation, and reporting or knowledge translation. The framework proposes that accountability improves when oversight is exercised prospectively at epistemically consequential decision points, documented through an audit trail, and calibrated to epistemic materiality: the extent to which AI assistance can alter the validity, interpretation, or consequences of a scientific claim. Six propositions specify testable relationships among disclosure, epistemic materiality, meaningful human control, lifecycle checkpoints, auditability, and defensibility of scientific claims. LEAF therefore shifts AI research governance from retrospective visibility to prospective, risk-proportionate control. We identify boundary conditions, implementation pathways, and an empirical research agenda for testing the framework across disciplines and resource settings. LEAF's distinctive explanatory mechanism is conditional: epistemic materiality escalates oversight, evaluability enables four human capacities, lifecycle checkpoints interrupt error propagation, and retained audit evidence makes consequential decisions answerable.

items.abstract_text: Digital transformation is reshaping academic work through remote and hybrid arrangements, intensified digital connectivity and the expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI). These developments can support flexibility, autonomy and efficiency, but may also intensify workload, erode work–life boundaries and generate demands associated with continuous adaptation, academic integrity and professional responsibility. Existing evidence is fragmented across technostress, remote and hybrid work, digital readiness and AI-enabled academic work, leaving insufficiently explained how technological change becomes embedded in the organisation and experience of academic work and, through this process, relates to wellbeing. This conceptual paper addresses this gap by developing the Digital Academic Work Reconfiguration and Wellbeing (DAWR-W) Framework. The framework was developed through theory synthesis informed by a structured literature foundation of 40 empirical studies and complementary theoretical research. The synthesis distinguishes the characteristics through which digital transformation reconfigures the organisation, boundaries, demands, relationships and professional content of academic work from the psychosocial mechanisms through which academics experience these changes. The resulting framework identifies seven characteristics of digitally transformed academic work and six psychosocial mechanisms involving resource depletion and replenishment, recovery and psychological detachment, perceived control and autonomy, competence and adaptive capacity, relational connection and psychological safety, and professional meaning and identity. Organisational and institutional conditions shape how digital transformation becomes embedded in academic work, while boundary conditions and feedback processes recognise contextual variation and adaptation over time. The central contribution of the DAWR-W Framework is to position work reconfiguration, rather than technology exposure alone, as the occupational process connecting digital transformation with academic employee wellbeing. In doing so, the framework integrates previously fragmented digital-work phenomena within a common explanatory architecture and locates responsibility for sustainable digital academic work across both individual and institutional levels. It provides an occupation-specific foundation for empirical testing, work-design interventions, and digital and AI governance in higher education.

items.title: Access, not ability: gender disparities in access to smartphone-based AI advisory tools for banana disease management among smallholder farmers in Rwanda

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered decision support tools can strengthen crop disease management, but their benefits reach farmers only when access is equitable. This study investigated how gender shapes access to smartphone-based AI advisory tools for banana disease management among smallholder farmers in Rwanda, using Tumaini, an AI-powered banana disease detection app, as a case. Using a mixed-method design, we combined a survey of 357 smallholder farmers across three districts, 12 focus groups, interviews with 61 farmers, and 12-month WhatsApp monitoring of 40 smartphone owners. Men had significantly greater smartphone ownership than women, and gender remained a significant predictor after controlling for education, income, and electricity access. However, among smartphone users, no significant gender differences were observed in digital literacy. Decision-making power was significantly lower among married women than married men. Despite high willingness to adopt, post-training use remained limited, with women significantly less likely to use the app than men. Men interacted with the app on significantly more days than women, though engagement per active day was comparable. Gender disparities in AI-tool use are associated with unequal access to devices and enabling conditions rather than with differences in technical capability. Addressing them requires gender-responsive interventions prioritizing equitable access, localized design (local-language and voice-guided interfaces), and structured group-based support. Such gender-responsive efforts are essential for women farmers to benefit equally from improved banana disease management and sustainable banana production, and for inclusive digital transformation in agriculture.

items.title: BACE: Bloom’s Asymmetric Hybrid Cognitive-Level Classification Educational Large Language Model

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used in intelligent teaching and cognitive-level classification. However, mainstream Transformer architectures incur redundant attention computation, and a single feed-forward network struggles to perform the fine-grained routing of features for Bloom’s cognitive features. This study proposes BACE, an educational LLM for cognitive-level text classification based on an asymmetric hybrid architecture guided by Bloom’s taxonomy. Built on the pretrained ChatGLM3-6B, BACE replaces the MLP in the first 4 layers with a shallow Top-2 sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing module to achieve token-level dispatching of cognitive features while retaining the self-attention mechanism. The middle 20 layers retain the native self-attention and MLP structures to maintain semantic transition. In the last 4 layers, attention is replaced with a deep, selective state-space modeling strategy, combined with chain-of-thought fine-tuning based on Bloom’s taxonomy, to integrate the global instructional context. Experiments on a public computer science course question dataset across multiple random seeds show that BACE achieves an average accuracy of 73.56% and a weighted F1 score of 0.6915, improving on ChatGLM3-6B (65.78%/0.6011) by 7.78 percentage points and 0.0904, respectively. Although its accuracy and weighted F1 are slightly lower than those of Qwen1.5-7B, BACE attains a BLEU-4 of 0.3426 and a ROUGE-L of 0.4601 on the generated chain-of-thought reasoning, both outperforming open-source models including Qwen1.5-7B, Mistral-7B, and Llama-3-8B. Through its asymmetric hybrid architecture, the model enables the classification of Bloom’s cognitive levels and provides a scalable technical pathway for question-answering-based cognitive-level assessment in intelligent education scenarios.

items.title: Structured ChatGPT-Assisted Writing Instruction and Academic Writing Performance Among Jordanian EFL University Students: Experimental Findings and Associations with Critical Thinking, Self-Regulated Learning, and Academic Motivation

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence in teaching English as a foreign language (EFL) writing is becoming prevalent, though there is still a gap between writing performance and cognitive and motivational variables. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study, incorporating an individually randomized pre-test/post-test controlled comparison, explored the impact of an eight-week intervention program based on ChatGPT for EFL writing on 300 Jordanian university EFL learners. The subjects were randomly assigned to experimental (n = 150) and control (n = 150) groups following purposive sampling. Writing performance was tested using independent-samples t-tests and ANCOVA, and the relationships between ChatGPT-based learning, critical thinking, self-regulated learning, academic motivation, and writing performance were measured using PLS-SEM. The experimental group demonstrated significantly better post-test performance compared to the control group. There were positive correlations between ChatGPT-based learning and writing performance (β = 0.237), critical thinking (β = 0.456), self-regulated learning (β = 0.341), and academic motivation (β = 0.270) (p < 0.001). The qualitative results emphasized better feedback utilization, revision, autonomy, motivation, and responsible AI usage.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Drug-Safety and Toxicity Assessment: Molecular Determinants and Bridging Preclinical Signals to Patient Safety

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The accurate prediction of drug-safety risks remains a major challenge in drug development, particularly for biologics and advanced therapeutic modalities, for which complex molecular and cellular interactions can contribute to immune and toxicological responses. Preclinical approaches have limitations in predicting human safety outcomes because of species-specific differences, incomplete characterization of molecular mechanisms, and limited integration of heterogeneous data. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) provide computational approaches for analyzing molecular, preclinical, bioanalytical, clinical, and real-world safety data. This review critically examines AI/ML applications across the drug-safety continuum, with particular emphasis on immunogenicity as a molecularly driven safety consideration for biologic therapeutics. Applications in peptide–HLA-binding and antigen-presentation modeling, anti-drug antibody-risk assessment, hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, systems toxicology, and pharmacovigilance are evaluated with attention to biological endpoint, validation strategy, and translational relevance. We further examine sources of failure in translating molecular and preclinical predictions to human outcomes, the role of multimodal and hybrid mechanistic–AI approaches, and the evidentiary requirements for increasingly consequential applications. Finally, we discuss regulatory considerations and emerging patient-specific frameworks, including digital safety twins, while distinguishing currently feasible supportive applications from approaches that remain preliminary or conceptual. Collectively, the evidence indicates that progress toward clinically useful AI-enabled safety assessment will depend not only on predictive performance but also on mechanistic relevance, independent and prospective validation, uncertainty characterization, and clearly defined contexts of use.

items.title: Automation Bias in AI-Assisted Simulated Radiotherapy Decision-Making Among Undergraduate Radiological Sciences Students: A Controlled Experimental Study

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) may support clinical decision-making but introduce automation bias when incorrect recommendations influence users. This study aimed to determine the occurrence of harmful automation bias among undergraduate radiological sciences students during AI-assisted radiotherapy decision-making and to examine the influence of time pressure. Methods: In a controlled experiment, 54 final-year undergraduate radiological sciences students with no prior clinical radiotherapy placement experience completed 20 simulated radiotherapy decision-making scenarios with 13 correct and seven deliberately incorrect AI recommendations (1080 trials). Initial and final responses, AI advice acceptance, confidence, perceived workload, and attitudes toward AI verification were assessed. Students were assigned to time-pressure (n = 26) or no-time-pressure (n = 28) conditions. Harmful automation bias was operationally defined as switching from an initially correct response to an incorrect response matching AI advice. Results: Harmful automation bias occurred in 20/220 eligible trials (9.1%), affecting 15/54 students (27.8%). Incorrect AI advice was followed in 137/378 trials (36.2%). Overall accuracy remained similar before and after AI exposure (75.65% vs. 74.91%; p = 0.289). Time pressure increased workload, but no statistically significant association with harmful automation bias was observed (OR = 0.78; p = 0.654). Lower post-decision confidence was associated with harmful automation bias (OR = 0.599; p = 0.028). No statistically significant difference in harmful automation bias was observed between participants who supported AI verification and those who did not. Conclusions: Harmful automation bias can occur despite stable overall accuracy, suggesting that greater emphasis on critical appraisal, active verification, and independent judgement may be valuable in radiotherapy education.

items.title: AI Adoption in Language Education: Learner–Instructor Differences and the Affordance–Accountability Asymmetry

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: This study examines whether artificial intelligence (AI) adoption operates similarly across learner and instructor roles in language education. Grounded in Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovations Theory, it used an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. The quantitative phase included 415 participants—276 international learners of Turkish and 139 instructors—while the qualitative phase comprised eight focus groups with 22 learners and 22 instructors. Multi-group structural equation modeling, measurement invariance, ordinal logistic regression, and the Framework Method were used. Relative advantage, compatibility, trialability, and observability showed positive bivariate associations with attitudes toward AI in both groups, although predictor overlap limited interpretation of unique simultaneous effects. No significant between-group differences were detected in the structural paths. Role differences instead emerged in construct organization: complexity components were closely related among learners but more differentiated among instructors, whereas attitude and intention were distinguishable among learners but largely overlapped among instructors. Although both attitude and intention were positively associated with self-reported AI use, intention added little explanatory value beyond attitude when modeled jointly. Qualitative findings showed that similar AI affordances were evaluated through responsibility frameworks. Conceptualized as affordance–accountability asymmetry, this pattern suggests that responsible and sustainable AI integration requires alignment between technological opportunities and role-specific pedagogical responsibilities.

items.title: Generative AI in Tourism and Hospitality: A Systematic Review

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming tourism and hospitality, yet reviews have largely focused on bibliometric mapping, conceptual discussions, or specific applications, leaving limited integration of research methods, theories, benefits, risks, and tourism experience personalization. This study systematically reviews GenAI research in tourism and hospitality to identify its methodological and theoretical foundations, major applications and constraints, personalization mechanisms, and future research directions. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the Web of Science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026, yielding 125 eligible peer-reviewed journal articles. Through qualitative content analysis and systematic coding, the studies were classified by methodology, theoretical foundation, application context, benefits, constraints, and personalization mechanisms. The findings show that quantitative approaches, particularly SEM/PLS-SEM and scenario-based experiments, dominate the field, while S-O-R, TAM, trust-related theories, social exchange theory, and UTAUT/UTAUT2 are the most frequently adopted theoretical foundations. Four major benefit categories and four constraint categories are identified, while personalization occurs mainly through situational adaptation, role-based interaction, and cognitive activation. The study contributes an integrated analysis of the field and proposes a Technology–Psychology–Organization framework linking GenAI characteristics, tourist responses, and organizational implementation. Practically, it highlights the need for transparent, risk-sensitive, and human-centered GenAI deployment.

items.title: Exploring Education Sciences Students’ Intentions to Use Artificial Intelligence for Academic Use

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: This study advances the understanding of Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption in higher education by introducing an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) that integrates Social Influence, Trustworthiness, and Ethics. Partial Least Squares and SEM (PLS-SEM) analysis was conducted. Based on data collected from 131 Greek Education Sciences students at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, the model demonstrates substantial explanatory power, accounting for 64% of the variance in behavioral intention. While the core TAM constructs (Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, and Attitude) remain fundamental, the research highlights a notable “Ethics-Intention Gap,” as ethical considerations were found to have no significant direct effect on behavioral intention. Instead, users appear to prioritize functional reliability, while social influence contributes to adoption through its effects on core TAM constructs. Furthermore, the results indicate that social circles play a significant role in shaping perceived ease of use of AI tools, functioning as informal support structures that facilitate engagement with emerging technologies. These findings offer important insights for stakeholders and developers, suggesting that fostering trust and leveraging social influence may represent more influential drivers of AI integration than an exclusive focus on ethical frameworks. By identifying these nuanced behavioral drivers, this research provides a robust empirical foundation for future strategies in AI-enhanced educational environments.

items.title: Artificial Co-Regulation: AI Tutors That Never Fade Capture Learners’ Regulation Instead of Transferring It

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Conversational AI tutors operate at national scale in some school systems and are used by most university students, while field experiments show assisted performance rising as unassisted performance falls. This paper argues that such agents produce artificial co-regulation: they recruit the learner’s attachment system while lacking the feature that made human scaffolding developmental, contingent fading. The argument draws on scaffolding theory, attachment theory, self-regulated learning research, and recent evidence on attachment and dependence in chatbot use. Because a scaffold that never fades does not transfer regulation, performance improves while the agent is present but unassisted competence, calibration, and epistemic independence lag, most consequentially at reading transitions, with multilingual and first-generation university students as the central case. So “permanent partner” models of human–AI scaffolding describe a developmental end state, not a starting point: shared epistemic agency requires a learner capable of partnership, and five design and measurement standards would protect that precondition.Preprint of a manuscript submitted to Educational Psychology (Taylor &amp; Francis), special issue “AI in Educational Psychology,” 31 October 2026; version 1, under review.

items.title: Bridging textile design and AI: An innovative methodological approach for the Ghanaian Textile Designer

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose: The study aimed to investigate the feasibility of employing selected artificial intelligence (AI) software to generate contemporary textile designs. Focusing on bridging textile design and AI, with a methodological approach for the Ghanaian Textile Designer. With AI emerging as a transformative force in multiple industries, including textiles, the research sought to assess its capacity to enhance design processes and meet consumer preferences. Methodology/Design: Three AI software programs, including Playground, Leonardo, and Lexcia, were selected for the study. Each was provided with identical prompts to generate contemporary textile designs. The outputs were then systematically analysed to identify similarities, differences, and overall design quality. Findings: The results showed that while the software received identical prompts, the generated designs displayed notable variations, alongside some shared visual features. The AI-driven process proved significantly faster and more efficient than traditional methods and yielded designs consistent with consumer specifications. Practical and Social Implications: The findings suggest that AI tools can substantially improve productivity, creativity, and responsiveness in textile design. Introducing AI-based design tools to textile designers in Ghana could enhance competitiveness, foster innovation, and better align production with evolving market demands. Originality: This study offers an early exploration of the comparative application of multiple AI software tools for contemporary textile design, contributing novel insights into their feasibility, efficiency, and adaptability within the Ghanaian textile industry context.

items.title: Realizing personalized prediction for the reversal of chronic hepatitis B-associated liver fibrosis through machine learning

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Although long-term antiviral therapy can reverse liver fibrosis in a considerable proportion of patients with chronic hepatitis B, treatment response differs markedly among individuals, and reliable methods for predicting who will benefit remain lacking. Conventional clinical tools such as liver stiffness measurement and the aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index were originally dewsigned for cross-sectional staging rather than longitudinal prediction, and their ability to capture the dynamic process of fibrosis reversal is limited. In this opinion review, we discuss how machine learning (ML) may help address this unmet need. We focus on three areas where ML has shown early but encouraging results: Quantitative analysis of images using ML, integration of pathological and clinical data through multimodal models, and dynamic prediction of treatment response based on serial measurements during antiviral therapy. In our view, the greatest value of ML lies not in replacing existing assessment tools but in complementing them, particularly through the early identification of patients who are unlikely to achieve fibrosis reversal with antiviral therapy alone. However, we also caution that most current models have been developed from small, single-center retrospective cohorts, and their clinical adoption will require prospective multi-center validation, improved model interpretability, and adherence to standardized reporting frameworks.

items.title: Human Agency under Conditions of Algorithmic Mediation by Artificial Intelligence

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Galactica Media: Journal of Media Studies
items.abstract_text: The widespread integration of artificial intelligence systems into everyday and professional practices challenges classical philosophical conceptions of agency, autonomy, and responsibility. Under conditions of algorithmic mediation, human action is increasingly shaped within hybrid sociotechnical systems in which cognitive, epistemic, and normative functions are distributed between humans and AI. This situation calls for a reexamination of which properties of agency remain distinctively human and how they manifest within this new configuration of human–AI interaction. The aim of this article is to provide a philosophical analysis of the specific properties of human agency in hybrid human–artificial intelligence systems and to identify how intentionality and control are transformed under algorithmic mediation. The article demonstrates that human agency in AI-mediated sociotechnical systems is characterized by weakened epistemic autonomy, contextually distributed control, and a hybrid form of intentionality that incorporates algorithmically generated elements. The article identifies several distinctive features, including vulnerability to algorithmic framing and cognitive codependence on AI systems, that distinguish hybrid agency from classical instrumental models of human action. The article concludes that, despite these transformations, humans retain a unique role in normative reflection and meaning-making. This role enables them to critically evaluate and reconfigure the architectures that structure interaction with AI. The article is intended for philosophers, media scholars, digital technology researchers, specialists in AI ethics, and others engaged in analyzing sociotechnical systems and questions of responsibility in algorithmically mediated social realities.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Driven Forecasting of Value Added Tax: A Case Study of the Tanzania Revenue Authority

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: This study set out to assess the applicability of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models in forecasting Value Added Tax revenue, with a focus on the Tanzania Revenue Authority. In assessing the applicability, the historical trends and performance of VAT collection were used to develop AI models to forecast monthly VAT revenue, thereafter providing recommendations for improving VAT forecasting through the adoption of AI technologies. The study utilised time series for the period of January 2021 to December 2024, constructing a dataset covering 48 months. The variables under the data set are: VAT revenue statistics, which provide detailed transactional records of VAT collections across three main categories: imports, purchases, and sales. The granular daily entries are aggregated to obtain monthly totals, creating a coherent time series that is suitable for statistical modelling and forecasting purposes. Other variables include the Consumer Price Index (CPI), GDP and inflation rate. Five forecasting models, SARIMAX, Elastic-Net, XGBoost, CNN-LSTM, and SNaive, were basically applied in predicting VAT revenue. All models under testing performed at different levels, with XGBoost performing better with the lowest MAE TZS 150 billion, RMSE TZS 205 billion and MAPE 275%, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing non-linear patterns and handling outliers in VAT revenue data. The Elastic-Net had an MAE of TZS 159 billion, a MAPE of 933% and a moderate RMSE of TZS 2.49 billion, pinpointing its limitations in relative accuracy and large error management. SARIMAX and SNaive slightly underperform with MAE of TZS 8.42 billion and TZS 904, respectively, and MAPE of 344% and 322%. The CNN-LSTM underperforms with an MAE of TZS 787 billion, an RMSE of TZS 2.54 and a MAPE of 873%, suggesting challenges in overfitting or pattern complexity. By combining methodological rigour, domain-specific feature engineering, and robust validation, these models offer a credible pathway toward more accurate, timely, and actionable fiscal forecasts. Therefore, the study results revealed that AI-based methods, particularly ensemble modelling, can be substantially applied in VAT revenue forecasting for TRA.

items.title: Content Validity of a Framework for Problem-Solving Competence in Programming Among Information Technology Students: A Two-Round Delphi Study in Vietnam

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal Of Education And Teaching Learning (JETL)
items.abstract_text: Competence-based education requires that learning outcomes for information technology (IT) programs rest on a competence framework whose content has been validated by experts, yet Vietnam has no framework for problem-solving competence in programming validated through a quantitative, criterion-based procedure. This study validated the content of such a framework, comprising five competence components, twenty-one criteria, and behavioural indicators across four developmental levels, using a two-round Delphi procedure with a purposively heterogeneous, Vietnam-based panel of 23 experts drawn from programming instruction, the software industry, and educational measurement. Round 1 (21 respondents; 91.3%) elicited structured qualitative judgements that generated six documented revisions. Round 2, sent to the same fixed panel (n = 20; 87.0%; 19 also responding in Round 1), rated 169 items against three consensus criteria set in advance: an item-level content validity index (I-CVI) of at least 0.78, a median of at least 4, and an interquartile range of at most 1. Every one of the 169 items satisfied all three criteria simultaneously, the scale-level index (S-CVI/Ave) reached 0.98, and the predefined stopping rule was therefore met after two rounds; a sensitivity analysis restricted to respondents who passed an embedded attention check left this conclusion unchanged. The validated core comprises twenty-one criteria and eighty-four indicators. Two content areas that experts raised without prompting, collaboration with generative artificial intelligence and exception handling, were integrated as twelve extended indicators at the indicator layer rather than as new criteria, preserving the validated criterion structure; these twelve await separate validation. The framework supplies an evidence-based foundation for writing learning outcomes, constructing analytic rubrics, and designing project-based instruction in IT programmes.

items.title: AI Driven Talent Management and the Performance of Agri Based Enterprises in Central Region Cameroon

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of Economics, Management, Entrepreneurship, and Business (JEMEB)
items.abstract_text: Purpose: This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) driven talent management practices and the performance of agri based enterprises in the Central Region of Cameroon, focusing on the mediating roles of workforce productivity and employee resilience. Research Methodology: A quantitative cross sectional survey design was employed, targeting 250 managers and human resource professionals. Data were collected with a structured questionnaire and analyzed with SPSS and AMOS through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and mediation analysis with 5.000 bootstrap resamples. Results: AI driven talent management was positively and significantly related to enterprise performance (r=0.523, p<0.01). Workforce productivity (β=0.18) and employee resilience (β=0.14) significantly mediated this relationship. Both the total indirect effect (β=0.32, p<0.01) and the direct effect (β=0.29, p<0.01) were significant, indicating partial mediation, with about 52 percent of the total effect transmitted through the two mediators. Conclusions: AI driven talent management enhances the performance of agri based enterprises both directly and indirectly through improved workforce productivity and stronger employee resilience. Enterprises should integrate AI strategically into talent management and support employees through change management. Limitations: The cross sectional design, self reported data, purposive sampling, and focus on a single region limit causal inference and generalizability. items.abstract_text: All participatory projects seek to create change, yet their intended impact is rarely planned and evaluated systematically. In this article, we reflect on the instruments we used to plan and evaluate the impact of How to Explain AI, a twelve-month participatory process that developed an art-based science communication intervention to foster artificial intelligence (AI) literacy among non-experts. We focus specifically on its effects on the 20 participating co-researchers from diverse backgrounds (citizen scientists, artists, AI experts). We combined a Theory of Change approach with the map and instruments of the Open Innovation in Science (OIS) Impact Model to guide initial conceptualization, continuous reflection, and systematic impact evaluation. Central goals were to create a shared vision, to activate co-researchers as multipliers, and foster engagement with and critical reflection on the research topic beyond the project activities. Ongoing contact in a series of workshops allowed us to support and evaluate impact directly. Drawing on the instruments applied, we examine how continuous, formative evaluation supported impact planning, assessment, and project management in a process-oriented, open-ended participatory project. Our findings indicate that impact can be planned and evaluated even when outcomes are not predetermined at the outset. Ongoing formative evaluation guided iterative adaptations and also contributed to impact itself, for example, by strengthening the shared vision it was designed to assess. The project further increased co-researchers’ confidence and agency and motivated independent engagement with AI. We derive practical guidance for evaluating impact on co-researchers in art-based, co-creative, and other intensely collaborative participatory projects.

items.abstract_text: As digital technology becomes more deeply embedded in education, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly present in junior high school students' daily learning. This paper explores the "scaffolding" role of GenAI in students' self-regulated learning (SRL) and its possible influence on enhancing academic self-efficacy. Based on Zimmerman's cyclical phase model of SRL and learning scaffolding theory, the study systematically deduces the human-AI interaction process. The analysis suggests that GenAI acts as planning, monitoring, and reflective feedback scaffolds across the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases, effectively addressing the lack of personalized support in traditional autonomous learning. Furthermore, GenAI assistance contributes to the internalization of academic self-efficacy by accumulating direct mastery experiences and alleviating trial-and-error anxiety. Acknowledging the potential risks of cognitive offloading and academic misconduct associated with GenAI dependency, the paper proposes coping strategies such as cultivating students' critical GenAI literacy and implementing dynamic scaffold fading. This research provides theoretical support and practical guidance for educators to optimize GenAI-assisted self-regulated learning environments.

items.abstract_text: Against the backdrop of generative AI emerging as a core strategic asset for major powers, the rhetorical tropes of national security and industrial competitiveness are subject to strategic manipulation by divergent domestic actors. The deregulatory camp within the White House invokes industrial competitiveness to roll back security-focused executive orders; the security faction in Congress expands chip export controls in the name of national defense; state-level authorities counter federal overreach through consumer protection mandates; and Silicon Valley deploys a two-pronged lobbying strategy. Taking the 2023-2026 policy pendulum and BIS chip regulations as its analytical case, this paper demonstrates that domestic contestation spills over globally through transmission channels. This has produced a global AI governance landscape defined by fragmentation, hollowed-out soft law processes, and a three-bloc divide across the U.S., the EU, and China, while the shortening commitment half-life of U.S. policy positions has inflated the costs of multilateral cooperation. The study also identifies limited positive spillover effects. In response, the paper puts forward targeted strategies. The conclusion argues that U.S. internal regulatory divisions constitute a mechanism that externalizes domestic political costs as global governance uncertainty. Understanding this mechanism is a prerequisite for reshaping the multilateral AI order.

items.abstract_text: With AI agents increasingly involved in teamwork, whether AI can substitute human collaboration has become a heated topic in academia. Large-model-driven agents are now capable of participating in team brainstorming, task coordination, and collaborative problem-solving, and knowledge-intensive industries are beginning to form a large number of human-machine hybrid teams. Existing research mostly relies on theoretical reasoning and lacks empirical perceptual data from front-line practitioners. Drawing on a questionnaire survey of 158 employees with cross-industry teamwork experience, this paper explores practitioners' perceptions regarding the substitution of human collaborative behaviors by AI. The results show that AI can only partially substitute procedural and rule-oriented collaborative tasks, whereas social-emotional communication, conflict mediation and value judgment remain irreplaceable human strengths. Position, work experience and AI familiarity jointly shape individual perceptions of the substitution boundary. Most practitioners regard AI as an auxiliary tool rather than a leader of team collaboration. This study provides a practical reference for enterprises applying AI collaboration tools.

items.abstract_text: This study set out to examine how artificial intelligence is currently being employed in Jordanian government academic libraries, and to look closely at the ethical questions that come with that employment, particularly around three areas: the contribution of artificial intelligence to developing library services, the extent of commitment to information ethics and privacy, and the institutional and technical obstacles standing in the way of wider adoption. The descriptive-analytical approach was adopted for this purpose. A questionnaire covering these three areas was built and distributed to a random sample of (137) employees drawn from a total population of (258) employees across Jordanian government academic libraries, a sample that made up (53.1%) of the population. Results indicated that the role artificial intelligence currently plays in improving library services is still moderate (mean=3.154), and that commitment to information ethics and privacy likewise falls at a moderate level (mean=3.318), with legal accountability and intellectual-property protection drawing somewhat more attention than transparency and algorithmic neutrality. The challenges axis came out highest of the three (mean=3.638), driven mainly by staff resistance to new technologies and unease over a shrinking human role in decision-making. None of the differences across gender, age group, educational level, or years of experience reached statistical significance, suggesting these perceptions are broadly shared across staff regardless of their personal or professional background. In light of these results, the study recommends that library administrations put in place a clear code of ethics for artificial-intelligence use, invest in dedicated staff training, and move forward through small pilot projects before any large-scale rollout, while urging the Ministry of Higher Education to issue a unified national framework for artificial-intelligence ethics across academic institutions.

items.title: A transformer-based explainable machine learning framework for heterogeneous ESG risk and return prediction using text intelligence

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Corporate ESG disclosure has shifted toward narrative form, yet vendor ESG ratings that most empirical work depends on show substantial disagreement across providers, and encoders dominant in financial text analysis inherit a 512-token ceiling that discards most of a typical 10-K. HET-ESGFormer combines hierarchical long-document encoding, heterogeneity-aware sparse expert routing conditioned on industry sector and firm size, and a dual-channel explanation layer subject to faithfulness verification. The framework is evaluated on 3,182 U.S.-listed firms over 2015 to 2024 using 10-K filings, sustainability reports, earnings call transcripts, and ESG-tagged news. Against nine baselines spanning econometric, dictionary-based, contextual encoder, sparse-attention, and time-series approaches, HET-ESGFormer reduces return RMSE from 0.0417 to 0.0389 and QLIKE from 0.148 to 0.128, with Diebold-Mariano tests rejecting equal predictive accuracy against every baseline after correction for multiple comparisons. The text channel's marginal contribution to downside risk prediction is materially larger than its contribution to return prediction, widening at longer forecast horizons, indicating that ESG narratives carry more information about risk than about expected return. Ablations reveal a decoupling between predictive skill and explanation faithfulness: removing the consistency regularizer barely affects accuracy but sharply degrades explanation quality. The dual-channel explanation improves ERASER comprehensiveness by 50% over SHAP applied to XGBoost, and human raters significantly prefer the framework's rationales over SHAP-based rationales on trustworthiness. Decile-sorted long-short portfolios deliver a post-cost Sharpe ratio of 1.31 against 0.74 and 0.62 for portfolios built on Refinitiv and MSCI ratings, and pass VaR backtests at 95% coverage. The results support text-based ESG modeling as an alternative to vendor-rating-based approaches, particularly where downside risk management and traceable explanation are jointly required.

items.abstract_text: Autonomous systems pose liability issues when automated decisions contribute to harm, failure, or non-compliance with regulations. Current legal AI studies primarily focus on classification, retrieval, question answering, and judicial prediction, and little has been done to translate legal and regulatory texts into structured signals that convey liability-relevant information. This research paper proposes a decision-support model for categorizing liability cues under European Union and Indian law. The source datasets were MultiEURLEX and IndicLegalQA, and a rule-based proxy mapping was developed to assign five labels: damage, defect, liability, regulation, and risk. This model is based on word-level and character-level TF-IDF, jurisdiction encoding, and a One-vs-Rest Linear Support Vector Machine classifier for multi-label classification. The final best configuration had an overall 91.33% subset accuracy, 96.08% Micro-F1, 87.81% Macro-F1, and 0.0201 Hamming Loss, compared to the best configurations of Logistic regression, Linear SVM, and Rand Forest. The framework aids initial legal and regulatory analysis and does not decide liability on doctrinal grounds or substitute for proficient legal analysis.

Using a case study methodology, the research combined a GenAI use survey of 74 students with an educational experiment involving 12 teams in November 2023. items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming manufacturing supply chains by enabling intelligent decision-making, adaptive operations, and more efficient resource utilization. Its potential to advance sustainable operations management, however, extends beyond technological adoption to the organizational integration of AI capabilities into operational processes and sustainability-oriented strategies. Despite growing scholarly attention, research in this field remains fragmented across technological applications, manufacturing functions, organizational conditions, and sustainability dimensions. In particular, limited conceptual integration exists regarding how AI capabilities are translated into operational transformation and under what organizational and technological conditions such transformation generates sustainable value. To address these limitations, this study conducts a systematic literature review and structured research gap analysis of peer-reviewed studies published between 2016 and 1 June 2026. The review examines the intellectual evolution of the field, synthesizes dominant research themes, evaluates AI applications across manufacturing and supply chain operations, and critically assesses their implications for operational, environmental, economic, and social sustainability. The synthesis highlights an emerging shift from isolated, function-specific AI applications towards interconnected and increasingly autonomous operational ecosystems, supported by the convergence of AI with the Internet of Things (IoT), digital twins, cyber-physical systems, and advanced analytics. These developments create opportunities for predictive and prescriptive decision-making, intelligent production planning, predictive maintenance, quality optimization, resource efficiency, supply chain visibility, and disruption management. Nevertheless, the realization of these benefits remains contingent upon organizational readiness, digital infrastructure maturity, data quality, workforce capabilities, effective governance, and the alignment of technological investments with sustainability priorities. The review further identifies persistent theoretical, methodological, technological, organizational, and empirical gaps, particularly concerning human–AI collaboration, implementation scalability, algorithmic accountability, sustainability trade-offs, and the assessment of long-term performance outcomes. Building on these insights, the study develops an AI-Driven Sustainable Operations Management Strategic Framework that integrates AI technological capabilities, organizational and digital enablers, AI-enabled operational transformation mechanisms, sustainability-oriented governance, and multidimensional performance outcomes. By connecting technological potential with organizational transformation and sustainability performance, the proposed framework provides an integrative conceptual foundation for understanding AI-enabled sustainable value creation across manufacturing supply chains. It also establishes a structured agenda for future research and offers strategic implications for manufacturing organizations and policymakers seeking to advance responsible AI adoption, strengthen operational resilience, and achieve sustainable long-term competitiveness.

items.abstract_text: Background and Aim: Evidence on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in secondary science education remains limited. This systematic review examined students’ conceptual understanding and engagement, teachers’ pedagogical strategies and challenges, and students’ critical thinking and scientific inquiry. Materials and Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, ERIC, Scopus, and Lens.org were searched for peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2022 and 2026. Two authors independently screened 187 unique records (Cohen’s κ = .78), identifying 20 eligible studies. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Framework synthesis integrated findings, informed by Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK). Results: Seven studies assessed AI capabilities rather than classroom implementation. Only two compared learning outcomes across conditions; none employed a randomized controlled design. Student perceptions and engagement were generally positive, whereas learning outcomes were mixed. A chatbot supporting self-regulated learning outperformed a rule-based chatbot, but ChatGPT-4o yielded smaller gains than peer collaboration. Teachers reported concerns regarding content accuracy, assessment reliability, and instructional readiness. Generative AI matched or exceeded student performance on structured examinations but demonstrated lower grading reliability than human assessors. Evidence concerning critical thinking was particularly limited. Richer reasoning was reported with dialogue-oriented tools or teacher guidance, whereas answer-seeking use of general-purpose tools was associated with weaker reasoning. items.venue: Frontiers in Emerging Computer Science and Information Technology
items.abstract_text: Prior authorization is a critical function in health insurance; however, traditional processes regularly cause operational delays, member dissatisfaction, inconsistent denials, provider frustration, delayed access to care, and increased regulatory scrutiny. Current authorization workflows are often overloaded by manual reviews, unclear policies, fragmented clinical documentation, limited decision transparency, and insufficient visibility into denial reasons. As health insurers adopt AI-enabled automation, these challenges become more complex if decisions are not explainable, evidence-based, auditable, and supported by human oversight. This study introduces a secure AI-driven decision-support framework for prior authorization that integrates explainable decision logic, policy-rule traceability, clinical-evidence mapping, bias monitoring, human review checkpoints, and appeal-ready explanations within a single governance model. Unlike automation focused mainly on speed and cost, the proposed framework prioritizes fair, transparent, and accountable decision-making across the authorization lifecycle. Each AI recommendation explains why it was made and links the decision to medical guidelines, policy rules, supporting evidence, prior reviewer actions, and member-specific details. The framework is expected to reduce authorization turnaround time, decrease avoidable denials, reduce appeal overturns, improve provider and member satisfaction, and make decisions more consistent and fairer across clinical and demographic groups.

items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as an important driver of workplace transformation, influencing how organisations organise work, make decisions, monitor employees, develop skills and deliver services. Unlike earlier forms of workplace automation that primarily focused on replacing manual or repetitive tasks, contemporary AI systems can analyse large volumes of data, support managerial decisions, predict operational outcomes, monitor performance and interact with employees and customers. The study examines the relationships between Artificial Intelligence-Driven Workplace Transformation and Employee Voice in the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry. The study adopted a cross-sectional survey in its investigation of the variables. The primary source of data was generated through a structured questionnaire. The population of the study was 4,700 employees from 17 selected Oil and Gas companies in Rivers State, Nigeria. The sample size was determined using the Taro Yamane formula at a 5% precision, and the result was 369. Therefore, the study respondents were made up of 369 employees from the oil and gas industry. Artificial Intelligence-Driven workplace Transformation was used as a predictor variable, while Employee Voice was measured with employee participation in decision-making, Upward Communication and expression of Concerns. The validity was confirmed by academic experts, and reliability was confirmed using Cronbach’s Alpha coefficients above 0.70. The hypotheses were tested using Spearman’s Rank Order Correlation Statistics. The tests were carried out at a 0.05 significance level. Findings from the study revealed that there is a significant relationship between Artificial Intelligence-Driven Workplace Transformation and Employee Voice in the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry. The study concludes that Artificial Intelligence-Driven Workplace Transformation significantly influence Employee Voice in the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry. The study recommends that oil and gas companies should establish structured mechanisms that allow employees to participate meaningfully in decisions concerning the introduction and implementation of artificial intelligence technologies.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) writing companions are changing how second-language (L2) writers plan, formulate, and revise texts. Yet improved textual fluency does not necessarily indicate deeper learning or stronger independent writing ability. This conceptual article develops a framework for interpreting AI-assisted L2 writing through the Cognitive Process Model of Writing, Cognitive Load Theory, and the Output Hypothesis. It argues that AI assistance may redistribute rather than simply reduce cognitive effort: linguistic suggestions can ease some local formulation demands, while evaluating, adapting, and verifying generated language creates additional monitoring demands. Whether this redistribution supports learning depends on the learner’s agency, the transparency of the task, and the instructional design. The article proposes a three-phase pedagogical model: supported conceptual ideation, autonomous drafting, and collaborative critical revision. Across these phases, AI support is deliberately varied so that learners can benefit from assistance without surrendering authorship, monitoring, or opportunities for linguistic retrieval. The paper is conceptual and does not report an empirical experiment. It therefore offers propositions and a research agenda rather than claims of measured effects. The framework can guide future classroom research, instrument development, and responsible integration of generative AI into L2 writing curricula.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping science education by expanding access to information, supporting adaptive instruction, enabling simulations, and providing timely feedback. This article examines the opportunities, challenges, and implications of AI integration for students’ critical thinking in the digital era. Using a narrative literature review, the study synthesizes foundational scholarship on AI in education, science learning, AI literacy, and critical thinking, alongside recent reviews and international guidance. The synthesis indicates that AI can support critical thinking when it is embedded in inquiry-oriented activities that require students to formulate questions, interpret scientific evidence, compare explanations, identify limitations, and justify conclusions. AI-supported simulations, conversational systems, and feedback tools may make abstract concepts more accessible and provide opportunities for iterative reasoning. However, these benefits are not automatic. Hallucinated information, algorithmic bias, privacy risks, unequal access, academic integrity concerns, and cognitive over-reliance may weaken learning if AI outputs are accepted without verification. The article argues that AI should function as a cognitive partner rather than a substitute for students’ intellectual work. Effective integration therefore requires scientific and AI literacy, teacher mediation, transparent assessment, ethical safeguards, and learning tasks that make reasoning visible. A human-centred approach can help science education use AI to strengthen, rather than displace, independent and evidence-based thinking.

items.title: Do AI Symptom Checkers Help or Hinder Timely Care-Seeking for Early Heart Disease? A Narrative Review of the Evidence by Insurance Status

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Cardiovascular disease killed 919,032 people in the United States in 2023, and how long people wait before getting help shapes much of that toll. The wait is not the same for everyone. In a 24-hospital U.S. registry, 48.6% of uninsured heart attack patients waited more than six hours, compared with 44.6% of insured patients who worried about costs and 39.3% of insured patients who did not. AI symptom checkers now show up at exactly the moment people decide whether to get care. Yet I found no study that measures whether using one changes how fast people seek care for heart symptoms, or whether the answer depends on insurance. This narrative review, organized with guidance from PRISMA 2020, pulls together evidence on four things: how accurate symptom checkers are, how they change people's plans for care, who uses them, and how insurance shapes the decision to seek cardiac care. I searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar between June and September 2026, along with publisher, journal, and government websites, and checked the reference lists of key studies. Twenty-two sources form the core evidence base: 20 peer-reviewed studies and 2 survey reports that were not peer-reviewed. Because the studies ranged from simulated-case audits to national registries, I appraised each one with four questions (real patients or simulated cases, observed behavior or stated intention, independence from the tool's developer, and how representative the sample was) and synthesized the findings narratively. Following the Commonwealth Fund, I treated insurance as three levels: adequately insured, underinsured, and uninsured. The evidence cuts both ways. Symptom checkers reduce uncertainty and usually catch emergencies. But in the largest real-world dataset, users lowered the urgency of their care plans eight times as often as they raised it. Most tools triage no better than an average layperson, and in studies with real patients, 2-9% of cases were under-triaged. In a randomized trial, people using AI chatbots made no better care decisions than people using other sources. The typical user is insured, college-educated, and female, so little is known about the groups most likely to delay. I argue that insurance likely decides whether a symptom checker speeds care up or slows it down. Insured users can act on advice, or double-check it, at little cost. Uninsured and underinsured users are the least able to catch a falsely reassuring answer. Three hypotheses follow. Among adequately insured adults, prior symptom checker use will shorten the time to professional consultation for early cardiac symptoms. Among uninsured adults, it will not shorten that time and may lengthen it. Underinsured adults will fall in between, and pairing advice with navigation to low-cost care should narrow the gaps among the three groups. I outline an equity-focused design with measurable safety thresholds, such as sensitivity for emergencies of 95% or higher and harmful under-triage in 2% or fewer encounters, along with community health worker review and community governance. I also propose four studies to test the hypotheses: an audit of standardized cardiac cases, a prospective cohort stratified by insurance tier, a stepped-wedge trial of community health worker navigation, and qualitative interviews.

items.title: Neural Mechanisms of Willed Attention Control

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Cueing paradigms are commonly used to study the neural mechanisms of visual spatial attention control. In these paradigms, each trial starts with an external cue, which instructs the subject to pay covert attention to a spatial location in anticipation of an impending stimulus (instructed attention). Recent work has introduced a new type of cue which prompts the subject to spontaneously decide which spatial location to attend (willed attention). We studied the neural mechanisms of willed attention control by analyzing fMRI and EEG data recorded at two institutions (UF and UC Davis) using the same willed attention paradigm. The findings include: (1) both instructional cues and the choice cue activated the DAN, (2) the choice cue additionally activated a frontoparietal decision network consisting of dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), anterior insula (AI), anterior prefrontal cortex (APFC), dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), and inferior parietal lobule (IPL), (3) the decision about where to attend can be decoded in frontoparietal decision network in choice trials but not in instructional trials, and (4) EEG alpha oscillation patterns immediately preceding the choice cue, but not the instructional cues, predicted the postcue direction of attention and the frontoparietal decision network activity. Based on these findings we proposed a model of willed attention control suggesting how the direction of visual spatial attention was decided upon in the absence of external instructions.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in language education, yet evidence from secondary-school settings remains fragmented. This integrative review examines empirical research on GenAI in formal secondary language education published from January 2023 to September 2026, with attention to pedagogical applications, language skills and activities, learning outcomes, teacher mediation, implementation challenges, and gaps in the evidence. Guided by Whittemore and Knafl’s integrative-review methodology and a PICo framework, the review drew on Google Scholar, ERIC, publisher and journal websites, and citation chasing. Twenty-two empirical studies were examined against the review criteria and available original publication records. Narrative and thematic synthesis were used to compare study contexts, methods, reported outcomes, and limitations. The studies describe uses of GenAI for writing support, feedback, conversation, tutoring, learning companionship, teacher support, and AI-literacy activities. Writing is the most represented language focus. Reported outcomes are mixed, ranging from gains in selected skills and learner perceptions to null or qualified findings. Overall, the evidence indicates that the educational contribution of GenAI depends on task design, teacher mediation, verification, AI literacy, and the conditions in which the technology is used.

quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction Adolescents increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots for schoolwork, yet evidence on whether this use supports or undermines learning is mixed. Drawing on research on cognitive offloading and self-regulated learning, we examined whether GenAI use for schoolwork is related to scientific literacy directly and through two components of self-regulated learning, academic help-seeking and metacognitive strategy use, and whether the purpose of use matters. quarantine.abstract_text: Purpose This paper extends Luhmann's concept of programmes – decision premises specifying the conditions under which a system's binary code is operatively assigned – into the domain of algorithmically mediated communication. It conceptualises recommendation systems, ranking algorithms and feedback architectures as ambient cognitive programmes: recursive, probabilistic selectors that perturb the structural coupling between social and psychic systems, and examines the constitutional implications of their opacity and transfunctional reach. Design/methodology/approach The study develops a systemic–cybernetic model grounded in Luhmann's social systems theory and the epistemology of autopoietic cognition, integrating Teubner's theory of societal constitutionalism to address the normative dimensions of algorithmic mediation. Analytical illustrations from Facebook and TikTok contrast two recommendation architectures – affinity-based cascading and behavioural-similarity propagation – to demonstrate how the model applies across distinct platform logics. Findings Algorithmic cognitive programmes operate as meta-programmes that reconfigure multiple forms of social differentiation simultaneously, enacting a binary operational distinction of visibility/invisibility through engagement metrics. Their colonisation of communicative environments – by economic imperatives and, as the analysis argues, by the autonomous logic of technical mediation – becomes a constitutional pathology where its effects cannot be contested or corrected, requiring internal self-limiting mechanisms that render operative selection criteria observable to affected systems. Originality/value The paper advances a novel theoretical category – ambient cognitive programmes – that extends Luhmann's organisational typology by identifying a configuration it does not explicitly address: a purpose programme without a terminal goal state that continuously revises the conditional programmes it governs. It connects this analytical framework to Teubner's societal constitutionalism, proposing constitutional observability as a structural condition for the compatibility between algorithmic regimes and communicative pluralism.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affective regulation, transfer, stable self-efficacy, persistence, and learning habits was much thinner. Ethical evaluation likewise remained uneven, emphasizing feedback quality, pedagogical validity, well-being, autonomy, motivation, inclusivity, and agency, while transparency, data minimization, scaffold fading, developmental suitability, manipulation risk, and ethical nudging were addressed far less often. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

Conclusion The findings provide exploratory evidence of differences in critical thinking and learning outcomes between the structured AI feedback and conventional instructor feedback classes. quarantine.abstract_text: Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

quarantine.abstract_text: This study examined the influence of AI-assisted problem solving on decision quality and the moderating role of cognitive reflection among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed, with a target sample of 335 undergraduate and postgraduate students from selected public and private universities, including the University of the Punjab, Bahauddin Zakariya University, Government College University Faisalabad, University of Karachi, University of Sindh, University of Peshawar, University of Malakand, and International Islamic University Islamabad. Primary data were planned to be collected through a structured, self-administered questionnaire distributed using Google Forms, while convenience sampling was adopted as the proposed sampling technique. The statistical analysis framework included Pearson correlation, simple linear regression, and moderation analysis using Hayes’ PROCESS Macro Model 1 in IBM SPSS Statistics. The preliminary analysis tables indicated a positive relationship between AI-assisted problem solving and decision quality (r = .582, p < .01), while regression analysis indicated that AI-assisted problem solving positively predicted decision quality (β = .582, R² = .339, p < .001). The moderation analysis further indicated a positive interaction between AI-assisted problem solving and cognitive reflection (B = .156, p = .001), suggesting that cognitive reflection may strengthen the relationship between AI-assisted problem solving and decision quality. These findings highlight the potential importance of combining AI-based support with analytical reasoning and reflective judgment in academic decision-making. The study addresses an important issue in higher education because the growing use of generative AI requires students to evaluate AI-generated information carefully rather than rely on automated recommendations without independent assessment. The research may contribute to understanding how individual cognitive characteristics influence the usefulness of AI tools and may help educators design learning activities that integrate AI literacy, critical thinking, and responsible technology use. The findings may also inform university policies and teaching practices aimed at encouraging effective AI adoption while preserving students’ independent reasoning and decision-making abilities. Future research using experimental or longitudinal designs may provide stronger evidence about the direction of these relationships and clarify how cognitive reflection influences decision quality across different academic contexts.
