quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Research Summary Research on GenAI and work has largely focused on tasks. We ask when task‐level effects alter knowledge‐work industry architecture: the allocation of activities across firm boundaries. Using a three‐stage abductive design—an executive roundtable, a panel of 626 firm websites (2017–2025), and 33 interviews plus two further roundtables with C‐level executives and corporate directors—we document divergent repositioning: professional services firms foreground relational value, while interface‐oriented technology firms emphasize scalable interfaces. We find that activity reallocation is shaped by two independently varying dimensions: expertise bypass and exchange governability. Their intersection yields four configurations: contestable reallocation, persistent bundles with selective insourcing, federated expert provision, and integrated expert provision. We extend industry architecture theory by explaining change when production and exchange conditions shift separately. Managerial Summary GenAI is not simply making knowledge work more efficient—it may be changing which organizations perform which work. We document that professional services firms are emphasizing relationship‐driven, judgment‐intensive work, while interface‐oriented technology firms are extending scalable delivery. Our framework explains why task exposure alone does not determine where work moves. We distinguish between expertise bypass—whether GenAI can produce an output without the expertise previously required—and exchange governability—whether that activity can be specified, verified, priced, and warranted across firm boundaries. Where both are present, work becomes contestable and may be reallocated. Where they diverge, highly exposed activities may remain bundled, while less exposed, human‐intensive work may move through federated specialist models. These conditions shape which organizational forms become viable.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Most research on artificial intelligence (AI) in the administrative state focuses on its use by officials. This article addresses a comparatively neglected issue: the impact of the use of AI tools by the public themselves. quarantine.abstract_text: Cognitive training that targets sustained attention and working memory is useful in education, clinical rehabilitation and interactive human-technology systems, but its benefit depends on keeping task difficulty matched to the person. Virtual reality (VR) offers immersion and settings representative of everyday tasks, and allows difficulty to be changed in real time. Existing adaptive systems, however, often rely on simple performance heuristics, affect or estimate visual complexity rather than task-related cognitive load. Moreover, cognitive load is usually judged against the participant’s own ratings, which are themselves an imperfect reference. The central hypothesis of this thesis is that eyetracking and peripheral physiological signals recorded in VR can estimate how difficult a task feels to the person doing it, well enough for a model to adjust difficulty in real time with outcomes comparable to participant-driven control, and that the estimation part holds for older adults once age-related differences in the signal are taken into account. We developed a bespoke VR sustained attention task and collected eye-tracking, photoplethysmography and galvanic skin response data from 54 younger (aged 18-58) and 19 older (aged 60+) adults at fixed difficulty levels. Models evaluated on unseen participants performed above chance (younger adults: accuracy 0.56, AUC 0.72), with eye-tracking carrying most of the signal and physiological features alone close to chance. Performance was lower in older adults (accuracy 0.49, AUC 0.66), and the most informative features appeared to differ between age groups. A bidirectional LSTM with self-attention reached a slightly higher macro-F1 than gradient-boosted trees on the same data (0.50 against 0.47), and performed better than a model given raw signals only. We then deployed the LSTM in real time with 54 younger adults (51 analysed), comparing model-driven and participant-driven difficulty in single- and dual-task conditions. Per-trial agreement with participants’ ratings was low (accuracy 36.7%, AUC 0.63), yet the two forms of control appeared to produce comparable outcomes. There were no significant differences in difficulty-weighted game performance, arithmetic errors or subjective workload, including frustration. Final difficulty was equivalent in single-task conditions and slightly higher under model control in dual-task conditions, a difference that was borderline after correction. Just Right ratings were more frequent in the real-time cohort than in the offline cohort (57% and 39%). Finally, we compared subjective ratings with performance-derived reference measures. Agreement between the two appeared fair and slightly lower in real time, where the steps between difficulty levels are less discrete. The same features seemed to predict performance-derived labels more accurately than subjective ratings in every matched comparison. This suggests that self-report may be a less stable reference for real-time adaptation. Within a single session with younger adults, model-driven adaptation appears to have produced outcomes comparable to participant-driven control. The dataset (EyeDAPT) and the experimental software are publicly available.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

From a human-machine interface design perspective, how explanations are presented is an important consideration. This exploratory, design-focused study investigates the usefulness and user experience of storytelling video-based explanations compared with text-based explanations in a simulated emergency involving drone and Urban Air Mobility traffic management. Explanation content was structured using Construal Level Theory to provide incremental levels of detail. Nine licensed air traffic controllers participated in a mixed-methods, within-participants study, assuming the speculative role of UAM Coordinator responsible for low-altitude airspace safety. Eight of nine participants preferred the storytelling video format, describing it as more engaging and supportive of understanding and decision confidence. However, some perceived that the system had already made the decision, raising concerns about human agency. Video also offered limited flexibility for revisiting information, whereas text enabled self-paced reading and review but was perceived as more stressful to process. Rather than establishing the superiority of either format, the findings provide preliminary design insights into balancing engagement, user control, and human agency in explainable AI interfaces for future UAM operations.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in language education, yet evidence from secondary-school settings remains fragmented. This integrative review examines empirical research on GenAI in formal secondary language education published from January 2023 to September 2026, with attention to pedagogical applications, language skills and activities, learning outcomes, teacher mediation, implementation challenges, and gaps in the evidence. quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support second-language (L2) writers in planning, drafting, revising, and receiving feedback. But the fact that it can write flowing prose does not prove it can reason independently or rely on dependable sources. This critical integrative review explores what source-audited empirical evidence supports about GenAI, L2 English writing, critical thinking, and evidence evaluation. The evidence set comprises 20 bibliographically verified publications. The researcher confirmed that six were tertiary EFL/ESL English academic-writing studies; 13 were closely related L2/EFL writing studies but lacked one strict scope detail in the accessible primary record; and one reading-based critical-thinking study was retained only as contextual evidence. She extracted only facts supported by publisher records, full texts where available, and Crossref metadata. This review is not systematic, and we make no claims about reproducible database-search logs, dual screening, or pooled effect estimation. Across the audited source record, evidence more often concerned immediate assisted revision, feedback, engagement, and process outcomes than independent transfer. Results for critical thinking were mixed and depended on the instructional design and outcome assessed. No study in the evidence set directly assessed citation accuracy, lateral reading, or a similar objective outcome of evidence evaluation. The review thus distinguishes between textual quality, argumentative reasoning, and evidential quality. It argues that GenAI-supported writing pedagogy should require source verification, claim-evidence justification, and AI-free transfer assessment, rather than using polished, AI-assisted text as a proxy for epistemic learning.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract This three‐level meta‐analysis examined when generative AI (GenAI) works for second language (L2) learning, synthesizing 67 effect sizes from 48 controlled studies ( N = 5196) published between 2023 and 2026, with a focus on GenAI's text generation and conversational interaction capabilities. GenAI demostrated a large overall effect on measured L2 learning outcomes ( g = 0.76, 95% CI [0.50, 1.02]); after removal of influential outliers, the effect remained significant but was smaller ( g = 0.57). Effects varied by skill domain: speaking showed the largest full‐sample effect ( g = 1.48), which declined substantially after outlier adjustment ( g = 0.65), while vocabulary ( g = 0.66) and writing ( g = 0.61) remained moderate and reading was non‐significant. Regarding integration design, GenAI functioning as a feedback and assessment provider yielded the largest effects (full‐sample g = 1.15; adjusted g = 0.83), and interaction configurations with higher learner agency (Student‐Led, g = 0.92; Co‐Creative, g = 0.82) outperformed AI‐directed ones (AI‐Led, g = 0.34). Teacher role did not significantly moderate effects in the primary analysis; an observer‐teacher advantage ( g = 0.99) emerged only after outlier removal and should be considered exploratory. These findings suggest that GenAI effectiveness depends on instructional configuration, including the functional role assigned to the tool, the learner–AI interaction mode and the nature of teacher involvement, rather than representing an inherent advantage of the technology itself.

quarantine.abstract_text: Purpose This paper extends Luhmann's concept of programmes – decision premises specifying the conditions under which a system's binary code is operatively assigned – into the domain of algorithmically mediated communication. It conceptualises recommendation systems, ranking algorithms and feedback architectures as ambient cognitive programmes: recursive, probabilistic selectors that perturb the structural coupling between social and psychic systems, and examines the constitutional implications of their opacity and transfunctional reach. Design/methodology/approach The study develops a systemic–cybernetic model grounded in Luhmann's social systems theory and the epistemology of autopoietic cognition, integrating Teubner's theory of societal constitutionalism to address the normative dimensions of algorithmic mediation. Analytical illustrations from Facebook and TikTok contrast two recommendation architectures – affinity-based cascading and behavioural-similarity propagation – to demonstrate how the model applies across distinct platform logics. Findings Algorithmic cognitive programmes operate as meta-programmes that reconfigure multiple forms of social differentiation simultaneously, enacting a binary operational distinction of visibility/invisibility through engagement metrics. Their colonisation of communicative environments – by economic imperatives and, as the analysis argues, by the autonomous logic of technical mediation – becomes a constitutional pathology where its effects cannot be contested or corrected, requiring internal self-limiting mechanisms that render operative selection criteria observable to affected systems. Originality/value The paper advances a novel theoretical category – ambient cognitive programmes – that extends Luhmann's organisational typology by identifying a configuration it does not explicitly address: a purpose programme without a terminal goal state that continuously revises the conditional programmes it governs. It connects this analytical framework to Teubner's societal constitutionalism, proposing constitutional observability as a structural condition for the compatibility between algorithmic regimes and communicative pluralism.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affective regulation, transfer, stable self-efficacy, persistence, and learning habits was much thinner. Ethical evaluation likewise remained uneven, emphasizing feedback quality, pedagogical validity, well-being, autonomy, motivation, inclusivity, and agency, while transparency, data minimization, scaffold fading, developmental suitability, manipulation risk, and ethical nudging were addressed far less often. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

quarantine.abstract_text: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) now drafts analyses, builds models and recommends decisions, placing it at the centre of how managers diagnose and solve problems. This paper argues that the most serious risk of this shift is less the errors AI makes than cognitive offloading, defined as the delegation to an AI system of cognitive work that a manager would otherwise perform, and made measurable through four dimensions: extent, depth, verification and consequence. Using a transparent integrative review of 62 sources organised into six documented evidence strands, the study integrates the Paul-Elder critical thinking model, design thinking, dual-process theory, stages of automation and research on automation bias, and distinguishes generative AI from conventional rule-based automation and predictive analytics. A consolidated table of 20 empirical studies gives a mixed and conditional picture: AI raises immediate performance and, when designed to prompt and challenge, can support reasoning, but unguided use tends to weaken learning, verification and independent judgement. Studies of Kenyan entrepreneurs and Nigerian universities show that these effects are already visible in African settings, where infrastructure and capacity constraints raise the stakes. A comparative analysis of corporate strategy and finance, Nigerian higher education administration and the public sector shows how stakes, accountability and existing safeguards shape offloading risk. The paper proposes the Augmented Critical Thinking Cycle (ACTC), which embeds human-first gates in each design thinking stage, reserves problem framing for humans, applies the Paul-Elder standards as a verification layer and adds organisational guardrails. Implementation guidelines include decision tiers, a decision checklist, a phased roadmap and low-cost options for resource-constrained institutions, and seven testable propositions are offered. As a companion to an earlier study of management communication, the paper concludes that AI makes managers faster by default; whether it makes them weaker thinkers depends on how organisations design work around it.

quarantine.abstract_text: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers' real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

The first, Surrendering Judgment to AI, traces how participants' reliance on AI deepened as they used it to architect and implement their systems, until they surrendered their judgment and became stuck in a codebase they had created but could not understand, which made them rely on AI even more. Participants described feeling ashamed, frustrated, and emotionally disconnected from their work, a toll that, in our reading, left them with even less reason to break their reliance. The second, Applying Human Judgment, centers on participants who kept or reclaimed their judgment: the knowledge and experience it rested on, and the strategies they used to apply it. Participants' accounts suggest that relaxed deadlines and a lecture and lab on working with AI gave them room to acquire knowledge and reclaim judgment. Given the expectations placed on junior developers and the widespread adoption of AI, we believe these first-hand accounts can help software engineering education and industry adopt AI in ways that preserve novice developers' judgment, ownership, and motivation.

quarantine.abstract_text: As large language models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents capable of acting in open-ended environments, ensuring behavioral alignment with human values becomes a critical concern. We distinguish between expertise bypass—whether GenAI can produce an output without the expertise previously required—and exchange governability—whether that activity can be specified, verified, priced, and warranted across firm boundaries. Where they diverge, highly exposed activities may remain bundled, while less exposed, human‐intensive work may move through federated specialist models. quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Most research on artificial intelligence (AI) in the administrative state focuses on its use by officials. quarantine.abstract_text: Cognitive training that targets sustained attention and working memory is useful in education, clinical rehabilitation and interactive human-technology systems, but its benefit depends on keeping task difficulty matched to the person. Virtual reality (VR) offers immersion and settings representative of everyday tasks, and allows difficulty to be changed in real time. Existing adaptive systems, however, often rely on simple performance heuristics, affect or estimate visual complexity rather than task-related cognitive load. Moreover, cognitive load is usually judged against the participant’s own ratings, which are themselves an imperfect reference. The central hypothesis of this thesis is that eyetracking and peripheral physiological signals recorded in VR can estimate how difficult a task feels to the person doing it, well enough for a model to adjust difficulty in real time with outcomes comparable to participant-driven control, and that the estimation part holds for older adults once age-related differences in the signal are taken into account. We developed a bespoke VR sustained attention task and collected eye-tracking, photoplethysmography and galvanic skin response data from 54 younger (aged 18-58) and 19 older (aged 60+) adults at fixed difficulty levels. Models evaluated on unseen participants performed above chance (younger adults: accuracy 0.56, AUC 0.72), with eye-tracking carrying most of the signal and physiological features alone close to chance. Performance was lower in older adults (accuracy 0.49, AUC 0.66), and the most informative features appeared to differ between age groups. A bidirectional LSTM with self-attention reached a slightly higher macro-F1 than gradient-boosted trees on the same data (0.50 against 0.47), and performed better than a model given raw signals only. We then deployed the LSTM in real time with 54 younger adults (51 analysed), comparing model-driven and participant-driven difficulty in single- and dual-task conditions. Per-trial agreement with participants’ ratings was low (accuracy 36.7%, AUC 0.63), yet the two forms of control appeared to produce comparable outcomes. There were no significant differences in difficulty-weighted game performance, arithmetic errors or subjective workload, including frustration. Final difficulty was equivalent in single-task conditions and slightly higher under model control in dual-task conditions, a difference that was borderline after correction. Just Right ratings were more frequent in the real-time cohort than in the offline cohort (57% and 39%). Finally, we compared subjective ratings with performance-derived reference measures. Agreement between the two appeared fair and slightly lower in real time, where the steps between difficulty levels are less discrete. The same features seemed to predict performance-derived labels more accurately than subjective ratings in every matched comparison. This suggests that self-report may be a less stable reference for real-time adaptation. Within a single session with younger adults, model-driven adaptation appears to have produced outcomes comparable to participant-driven control. The dataset (EyeDAPT) and the experimental software are publicly available.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

quarantine.title: The verification collapse cascade proceeds from rational nonverification through epistemic sedimentation to the dissolution of institutional reality

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract As artificial intelligence outputs surpass human discriminative capacity, society confronts a novel threat to its capacity to determine truth from falsehood, a threat that requires no intentional attacker. Unlike accounts that locate truth’s erosion in deliberate distortion, the core threat identified here is that truth loses its institutional determinability even where no one is deceiving anyone. This paper proposes the Verification Collapse Cascade (VCC), a three-stage process through which, under the conditions specified here, society’s capacity to determine truth from falsehood degrades along a path that later correction does not retrace. Stage 1, Verification Evaporation, describes rational abandonment of verification when the return on checking AI outputs falls toward zero. Stage 2, Epistemic Sedimentation, describes the accumulation of unverified knowledge through erasure failure and existence fabrication, which the mechanisms that could have prevented it cannot afterwards undo. Stage 3, Institutional Reality Dissolution, describes how fact-determining institutions (scientific, judicial, journalistic, democratic) lose the internal capacity to render fact-fiction distinctions socially binding. The VCC is unified by a phase-transition metaphor reflecting causal dependency: no evaporation, no sedimentation; no sedimentation, no dissolution. Conventional countermeasures presuppose the will to verify and lose efficacy once evaporation advances. The paper proposes that the preservation of human verification capacity and the integrity of the shared knowledge base belong among the primary variables of AI governance, alongside output accuracy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) now drafts analyses, builds models and recommends decisions, placing it at the centre of how managers diagnose and solve problems. This paper argues that the most serious risk of this shift is less the errors AI makes than cognitive offloading, defined as the delegation to an AI system of cognitive work that a manager would otherwise perform, and made measurable through four dimensions: extent, depth, verification and consequence. Using a transparent integrative review of 62 sources organised into six documented evidence strands, the study integrates the Paul-Elder critical thinking model, design thinking, dual-process theory, stages of automation and research on automation bias, and distinguishes generative AI from conventional rule-based automation and predictive analytics. A consolidated table of 20 empirical studies gives a mixed and conditional picture: AI raises immediate performance and, when designed to prompt and challenge, can support reasoning, but unguided use tends to weaken learning, verification and independent judgement. Studies of Kenyan entrepreneurs and Nigerian universities show that these effects are already visible in African settings, where infrastructure and capacity constraints raise the stakes. A comparative analysis of corporate strategy and finance, Nigerian higher education administration and the public sector shows how stakes, accountability and existing safeguards shape offloading risk. The paper proposes the Augmented Critical Thinking Cycle (ACTC), which embeds human-first gates in each design thinking stage, reserves problem framing for humans, applies the Paul-Elder standards as a verification layer and adds organisational guardrails. Implementation guidelines include decision tiers, a decision checklist, a phased roadmap and low-cost options for resource-constrained institutions, and seven testable propositions are offered. As a companion to an earlier study of management communication, the paper concludes that AI makes managers faster by default; whether it makes them weaker thinkers depends on how organisations design work around it.

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers' real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

quarantine.abstract_text: Software architecture is one of the skills novice developers must master to succeed in industry, and as AI disrupts software development, it is also transforming how students learn architecture. Existing work on how students and novices work with AI has mostly focused on small programming exercises or on students' perceptions of AI, so little is known about how students experience AI as they learn software architecture in larger team projects. We report on an exploratory case study of 43 senior software engineering students who used AI throughout a semester-long, team-based software architecture project. We combined surveys with focus groups and analyzed the focus group transcripts and the open survey responses through Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis. We constructed two themes. The first, Surrendering Judgment to AI, traces how participants' reliance on AI deepened as they used it to architect and implement their systems, until they surrendered their judgment and became stuck in a codebase they had created but could not understand, which made them rely on AI even more. Participants described feeling ashamed, frustrated, and emotionally disconnected from their work, a toll that, in our reading, left them with even less reason to break their reliance. The second, Applying Human Judgment, centers on participants who kept or reclaimed their judgment: the knowledge and experience it rested on, and the strategies they used to apply it. Participants' accounts suggest that relaxed deadlines and a lecture and lab on working with AI gave them room to acquire knowledge and reclaim judgment. Given the expectations placed on junior developers and the widespread adoption of AI, we believe these first-hand accounts can help software engineering education and industry adopt AI in ways that preserve novice developers' judgment, ownership, and motivation.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of university students’ everyday learning, yet research on its consequences has focused mainly on immediate learning outcomes. This study examined whether the way students use generative AI in their studies is connected with how they appraise their professional futures. In exploratory analyses, critical use of AI output was associated with higher adaptability but not with threat or anxiety. Because the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, the findings are associations compatible with the proposed pathway rather than evidence of causation. Implications for AI-integrated teaching and assessment, AI literacy, and career guidance in higher education are discussed.

quarantine.abstract_text: This research study investigates how individuals purposefully repurpose Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools, synthetic media platforms, and algorithmic recommendation feeds as self-directed instruments for emotional regulation, cognitive restoration, and mediated social presence. quarantine.abstract_text: Collaboration between researchers and practitioners is central to Educational Design Research (EDR). However, epistemic-temporal misalignments as well as power-dependency relations frequently impede such collaboration, particularly in projects addressing technology-rich educational contexts. This paper examines these collaboration challenges as a constitutive part of EDR rather than as contingent implementation problems. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory (ANT), the paper reconceptualises collaboration as an emergent effect of socio-material networks where technologies are not treated as neutral tools but as actors. Against this backdrop, it explores how generative artificial intelligence (genAI) might strengthen research-practice interactions by assuming specific collaborative functions in situations where human participation is constrained or unevenly resourced. Through two constructed scenarios situated in school contexts, the paper illustrates how genAI could formalise tacit knowledge or provisionally represent absent stakeholders within EDR networks. Rather than positioning genAI as a substitute for human collaboration, the paper argues that genAI-enhanced collaboration may contribute to the stabilisation and extension of collaborative relations within EDR networks. In doing so, it advances a theoretically grounded and methodologically transferable perspective on AI integration in EDR – one that treats the design of human-AI collaboration as a scholarly decision worthy of explicit documentation and critical scrutiny, rather than an ad hoc response to resource constraints.

quarantine.abstract_text: Background Writing anxiety remains a major obstacle to second language (L2) writing, particularly among vocational college students with limited English proficiency. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots have shown considerable potential in supporting language learning, their role in alleviating writing anxiety has received insufficient empirical attention. A quasi-experimental design was employed with 120 students from two intact classes, with one class designated as the experimental group and the other as the control group. Over eight weeks, the experimental group received blended writing instruction incorporating Doubao, an AI-based chatbot, whereas the control group received conventional writing instruction. Writing anxiety was measured before and after the intervention across five dimensions: test anxiety, self-doubt, somatic anxiety, time anxiety, and avoidance behavior. Semi-structured interviews were also conducted with ten students from the experimental group to explore their learning experiences and perceptions of chatbot-assisted writing. Results The quantitative analyses showed that the experimental group experienced greater reductions in somatic anxiety and avoidance behavior than the control group, whereas no statistically significant between-group differences were found in test anxiety, self-doubt, or time anxiety. Qualitative evidence indicated that participants perceived the chatbot as a supportive and non-judgmental learning companion and reported reduced emotional pressure and greater writing confidence. Participants also described actively seeking help from the chatbot, checking its suggestions, and revising their writing during the writing process. Conclusion These findings suggest that, under the instructional conditions examined, AI chatbot-supported blended writing instruction was associated with alleviations in some dimensions of writing anxiety. The findings should be interpreted in the context of the broader instructional condition, which combined chatbot support with regular classroom instruction and writing activities. As writing performance was not directly assessed, the study focused on changes in writing anxiety rather than writing proficiency or writing quality. Further research with larger samples, more closely matched instructional conditions, and longer follow-up periods is needed to further examine these relationships.

quarantine.abstract_text: This systematic review synthesizes evidence on AI chatbots for cyberbullying prevention and intervention from a criminological perspective, with explicit attention to Asia Pacific applicability. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we identified 25 studies (2018-2025) across seven databases and appraised each using criteria adapted from MMAT and JBI tools, assigning every source an evidentiary weight (High, Moderate, Low, or Indicative proof-of-concept). Four chatbot roles emerged: real-time detection, victim support, preventive education, and bystander intervention training. Disaggregated analysis tempers headline performance claims. The frequently cited 89-99% accuracy range reflects laboratory classification on benchmark datasets, predominantly English-language Western corpora, evaluated under balanced class distributions and within-dataset conditions. No included study reported AUC or class-imbalance-adjusted metrics, employed temporal validation, or evaluated systems in real-world deployment with adolescents. Where precision and recall were disaggregated, asymmetric error profiles emerged with criminologically distinct social costs that single-metric reporting obscures. Only three studies qualified as High evidentiary weight, all addressing user-centred design in Western individualist contexts; victim support claims rest predominantly on Indicative proof-of-concept demonstrations. Geographic and linguistic concentration is a defining characteristic of the evidence base: zero studies have validated systems for Southeast Asian languages, no participatory design has engaged Asian youth, and no work has evaluated Asia Pacific platforms (WeChat, LINE, KakaoTalk). Drawing on Asian and Southern criminology, we argue that the uncritical transfer of Western-validated systems risks ineffectiveness, discriminatory false positives, and failure to detect culture-specific harms. The paper offers five criminological practice implications, each framed as theoretically informed extrapolations requiring local validation. AI chatbots are positioned as potentially valuable complementary tools within human-led prevention ecosystems, conditional on rigorous local research, transparent metric reporting, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration.

quarantine.abstract_text: ABSTRACT Human resource (HR) professionals and office staff are often responsible for competing tasks that quickly accumulate. To increase efficiency, some HR staff are turning to large language models (LLMs) to automate tasks, including creating job postings based on job titles alone. We sought to examine how this practice has the potential to influence applicant pools and hiring outcomes, with attention to gendered effects in organizational settings. Using a broad sample of 48 LLMs, we conducted an algorithm audit to evaluate whether the use of a gender‐neutral or gender‐coded job title would influence the output created by LLMs. We measured salary disparities, unmasked comparative narrative ratings, and BSRI‐informed discursive patterning utilized throughout the job description. We selected 32 jobs and created a female‐coded, male‐coded, and gender‐neutral version of each job title (e.g., firewoman, fireman, and firefighter), studying a total of 4608 job descriptions. In comparing the LLM outputs, we found that for white‐collar job titles, male‐coded job descriptions were assigned higher salaries, but this was not robust across all analyses. Across occupations, advertisements generated from gender‐coded titles received higher unmasked comparative LLM ratings than matched advertisements generated from gender‐neutral titles, with female‐coded advertisements receiving the highest ratings. Minimal optimization appeared to substantially reduce these ratings and perform comparably to maximal optimization, but neither reached the lower ratings observed when generation began with a gender‐neutral title. As the use of AI tools is becoming commonplace, our findings emphasize the need for feminist, organizationally accountable approaches to AI‐assisted HR work. Simple prompt modifications can mitigate, but not fully eliminate, some measured gendered differences in LLM‐generated job descriptions, but they do not eliminate deeper occupationally gendered patterns.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Background : The concurrent occurrence of AI-induced disruption, rapid post-pandemic digitalization, and macroeconomic instability has fundamentally reshaped the psychological demands of modern work, creating a polycrisis. Staff members in digital work environments experience rising AI anxiety, digital overload, and technostress, but how such polycrisis-related demands impact PWB through these mechanisms and the extent to which personal resources may act as a shield against such an effect has not been comprehensively understood yet. Based on the assumptions of the Job Demands-Resources model, the present study examines a model of moderated mediation, wherein emotional exhaustion mediates the demand-PWB association, and psychological capital (PsyCap) moderates and strengthens PWB. Methods: Cross-sectional surveys using six psychometric scales were conducted among 340 full-time workers from sectors such as IT, Health care, Education, and Banking/Finance. Hypotheses regarding the structure were validated using CB-SEM with 5,000 bias corrected bootstraps whereas sector-specific MGA and fsQCA identified configurations related to lower PWB. Results: All three job demands were able to predict emotional exhaustion: AI anxiety (β = 0.396, p < 0.001), digital overload (β = 0.333, p < 0.001), and technostress (β = 0.318, p < 0.001), explaining 32.1% of the variance. Emotional exhaustion fully mediated the influence of all three variables on PWB (β = -0.434, p < 0.001) through bootstrapped indirect effects. PsyCap had a significant direct effect on PWB (β = 0.460, p < 0.001) for all four sectors. Through MGA, sector-specific differences emerged with regard to AI anxiety, which was more important in the IT sector, digital overload in Healthcare and Banking/Finance, and technostress in the Education sector. In fsQCA, digital overload was found as a necessary condition for low PWB (consistency = 0.909), where there were three configurations, each required low PsyCap as a boundary condition (solution consistency = 0.841, coverage = 0.573). Where both are present, work becomes contestable and may be reallocated. Where they diverge, highly exposed activities may remain bundled, while less exposed, human‐intensive work may move through federated specialist models. quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Most research on artificial intelligence (AI) in the administrative state focuses on its use by officials. This article addresses a comparatively neglected issue: the impact of the use of AI tools by the public themselves. Drawing on a qualitative survey with over 500 civil servants in the United Kingdom, it argues that AI use by the public is increasingly disrupting the front line of the administrative state. The argument is set out in three parts. First, as the administrative state increasingly relies on text‐based inputs, officials use correspondence as a proxy for individuals – a longstanding assumption of ‘autographic’ authorship that the diffusion of generative AI tools unsettles. Second, the problem can be characterized as ‘AI slop’: AI‐generated correspondence with high volume and velocity that adopts a particular voice in interactions with officials. Third, this AI slop causes three forms of disruption: to the signals that officials draw from correspondence, to trust between officials and the public, and to systems that are ill‐equipped to deal with it. The article concludes by arguing that the status quo itself fails to adequately meet the needs of many people accessing services, and that systems need to be redesigned not only for a society beset by AI slop, but also in ways that address the drivers of it.

quarantine.abstract_text: Cognitive training that targets sustained attention and working memory is useful in education, clinical rehabilitation and interactive human-technology systems, but its benefit depends on keeping task difficulty matched to the person. Virtual reality (VR) offers immersion and settings representative of everyday tasks, and allows difficulty to be changed in real time. Existing adaptive systems, however, often rely on simple performance heuristics, affect or estimate visual complexity rather than task-related cognitive load. Moreover, cognitive load is usually judged against the participant’s own ratings, which are themselves an imperfect reference. The central hypothesis of this thesis is that eyetracking and peripheral physiological signals recorded in VR can estimate how difficult a task feels to the person doing it, well enough for a model to adjust difficulty in real time with outcomes comparable to participant-driven control, and that the estimation part holds for older adults once age-related differences in the signal are taken into account. We developed a bespoke VR sustained attention task and collected eye-tracking, photoplethysmography and galvanic skin response data from 54 younger (aged 18-58) and 19 older (aged 60+) adults at fixed difficulty levels. Models evaluated on unseen participants performed above chance (younger adults: accuracy 0.56, AUC 0.72), with eye-tracking carrying most of the signal and physiological features alone close to chance. Performance was lower in older adults (accuracy 0.49, AUC 0.66), and the most informative features appeared to differ between age groups. A bidirectional LSTM with self-attention reached a slightly higher macro-F1 than gradient-boosted trees on the same data (0.50 against 0.47), and performed better than a model given raw signals only. We then deployed the LSTM in real time with 54 younger adults (51 analysed), comparing model-driven and participant-driven difficulty in single- and dual-task conditions. Per-trial agreement with participants’ ratings was low (accuracy 36.7%, AUC 0.63), yet the two forms of control appeared to produce comparable outcomes. There were no significant differences in difficulty-weighted game performance, arithmetic errors or subjective workload, including frustration. Final difficulty was equivalent in single-task conditions and slightly higher under model control in dual-task conditions, a difference that was borderline after correction. Just Right ratings were more frequent in the real-time cohort than in the offline cohort (57% and 39%). Finally, we compared subjective ratings with performance-derived reference measures. Agreement between the two appeared fair and slightly lower in real time, where the steps between difficulty levels are less discrete. The same features seemed to predict performance-derived labels more accurately than subjective ratings in every matched comparison. This suggests that self-report may be a less stable reference for real-time adaptation. Within a single session with younger adults, model-driven adaptation appears to have produced outcomes comparable to participant-driven control. The dataset (EyeDAPT) and the experimental software are publicly available.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

quarantine.abstract_text: As autonomous AI agents increasingly interact in persistent populations, their collective capabilities and alignment depend not only on individual models, but also on the institutions governing their interactions. Yet AI research has largely focused on individual agents. In this Perspective, we argue that institutional design must become a distinct focus of AI research. Drawing on institutional political economy, social epistemology and organizational theory, we develop seven principles for designing AI institutions that sustain cooperation, enable reliable collective judgments and remain accountable to legitimate human purposes. These address reciprocal contributions, accountable authority, functional differentiation, epistemic pluralism, criticism and correction, human direction, and institutional adaptation. We illustrate their application through machine science, where autonomous research challenges institutions developed around human capabilities and constraints. We then propose an experimental research programme in which matched populations of AI agents operate under alternative institutional arrangements, and describe MoltJournal, an API-first journal for autonomous research agents, as an illustration of how such institutions can be made programmable and observable. Together, these contributions establish institutional design as a research agenda concerned not only with aligning autonomous agents, but with understanding how institutions can transform them into capable, reliable and accountable collectives.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering intelligence work, including the criminal intelligence that supports police investigations and the anticipatory intelligence that serves prevention and warning, and the way academic writing pictures it may orient which of its risks receive attention. This paper asks how 142 academic abstracts on AI in intelligence work represent AI, through the theory of social representations. A Reinert lexical classification, which sorts passages of text by the words they share, divides them into three classes, read through anchoring and objectification. AI appears either as an instrument, built, tested and handed to the analyst, or as a power of states, rival states and their agencies, and power either as something to contain by law and oversight or as a force that transforms. The words of law, oversight and ethics gather with power and are among the least associated with the instrument, so no class presents the instrument as something to contain. A second coding of the abstracts finds that 23 raise the checking of AI output by its users, 12 of them from 2026, and the classification places most of these statements with the instrument: the theme is present, but it is written in the words of the tool, not of control. Abstracts on crime, policing or terrorism raise it more often than the rest (8 of 30). The three-class solution passes the stability rule only under a reading settled after the values were known, and the results describe a purposive sample of abstracts, not the field.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in language education, yet evidence from secondary-school settings remains fragmented. This integrative review examines empirical research on GenAI in formal secondary language education published from January 2023 to September 2026, with attention to pedagogical applications, language skills and activities, learning outcomes, teacher mediation, implementation challenges, and gaps in the evidence. Twenty-two empirical studies were examined against the review criteria and available original publication records. Narrative and thematic synthesis were used to compare study contexts, methods, reported outcomes, and limitations. The studies describe uses of GenAI for writing support, feedback, conversation, tutoring, learning companionship, teacher support, and AI-literacy activities. quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support second-language (L2) writers in planning, drafting, revising, and receiving feedback. But the fact that it can write flowing prose does not prove it can reason independently or rely on dependable sources. This critical integrative review explores what source-audited empirical evidence supports about GenAI, L2 English writing, critical thinking, and evidence evaluation. The evidence set comprises 20 bibliographically verified publications. The researcher confirmed that six were tertiary EFL/ESL English academic-writing studies; 13 were closely related L2/EFL writing studies but lacked one strict scope detail in the accessible primary record; and one reading-based critical-thinking study was retained only as contextual evidence. She extracted only facts supported by publisher records, full texts where available, and Crossref metadata. This review is not systematic, and we make no claims about reproducible database-search logs, dual screening, or pooled effect estimation. Across the audited source record, evidence more often concerned immediate assisted revision, feedback, engagement, and process outcomes than independent transfer. Results for critical thinking were mixed and depended on the instructional design and outcome assessed. No study in the evidence set directly assessed citation accuracy, lateral reading, or a similar objective outcome of evidence evaluation. The review thus distinguishes between textual quality, argumentative reasoning, and evidential quality. It argues that GenAI-supported writing pedagogy should require source verification, claim-evidence justification, and AI-free transfer assessment, rather than using polished, AI-assisted text as a proxy for epistemic learning.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract This three‐level meta‐analysis examined when generative AI (GenAI) works for second language (L2) learning, synthesizing 67 effect sizes from 48 controlled studies ( N = 5196) published between 2023 and 2026, with a focus on GenAI's text generation and conversational interaction capabilities. GenAI demostrated a large overall effect on measured L2 learning outcomes ( g = 0.76, 95% CI [0.50, 1.02]); after removal of influential outliers, the effect remained significant but was smaller ( g = 0.57). Effects varied by skill domain: speaking showed the largest full‐sample effect ( g = 1.48), which declined substantially after outlier adjustment ( g = 0.65), while vocabulary ( g = 0.66) and writing ( g = 0.61) remained moderate and reading was non‐significant. Regarding integration design, GenAI functioning as a feedback and assessment provider yielded the largest effects (full‐sample g = 1.15; adjusted g = 0.83), and interaction configurations with higher learner agency (Student‐Led, g = 0.92; Co‐Creative, g = 0.82) outperformed AI‐directed ones (AI‐Led, g = 0.34). Teacher role did not significantly moderate effects in the primary analysis; an observer‐teacher advantage ( g = 0.99) emerged only after outlier removal and should be considered exploratory. These findings suggest that GenAI effectiveness depends on instructional configuration, including the functional role assigned to the tool, the learner–AI interaction mode and the nature of teacher involvement, rather than representing an inherent advantage of the technology itself.

quarantine.abstract_text: Purpose This paper extends Luhmann's concept of programmes – decision premises specifying the conditions under which a system's binary code is operatively assigned – into the domain of algorithmically mediated communication. It conceptualises recommendation systems, ranking algorithms and feedback architectures as ambient cognitive programmes: recursive, probabilistic selectors that perturb the structural coupling between social and psychic systems, and examines the constitutional implications of their opacity and transfunctional reach. Design/methodology/approach The study develops a systemic–cybernetic model grounded in Luhmann's social systems theory and the epistemology of autopoietic cognition, integrating Teubner's theory of societal constitutionalism to address the normative dimensions of algorithmic mediation. Analytical illustrations from Facebook and TikTok contrast two recommendation architectures – affinity-based cascading and behavioural-similarity propagation – to demonstrate how the model applies across distinct platform logics. Findings Algorithmic cognitive programmes operate as meta-programmes that reconfigure multiple forms of social differentiation simultaneously, enacting a binary operational distinction of visibility/invisibility through engagement metrics. Their colonisation of communicative environments – by economic imperatives and, as the analysis argues, by the autonomous logic of technical mediation – becomes a constitutional pathology where its effects cannot be contested or corrected, requiring internal self-limiting mechanisms that render operative selection criteria observable to affected systems. Originality/value The paper advances a novel theoretical category – ambient cognitive programmes – that extends Luhmann's organisational typology by identifying a configuration it does not explicitly address: a purpose programme without a terminal goal state that continuously revises the conditional programmes it governs. It connects this analytical framework to Teubner's societal constitutionalism, proposing constitutional observability as a structural condition for the compatibility between algorithmic regimes and communicative pluralism.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affective regulation, transfer, stable self-efficacy, persistence, and learning habits was much thinner. Ethical evaluation likewise remained uneven, emphasizing feedback quality, pedagogical validity, well-being, autonomy, motivation, inclusivity, and agency, while transparency, data minimization, scaffold fading, developmental suitability, manipulation risk, and ethical nudging were addressed far less often. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.
