quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now routine in university study, yet unstructured use risks cognitive offloading, surface learning, and uncritical acceptance of fluent but unreliable output. quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) now drafts analyses, builds models and recommends decisions, placing it at the centre of how managers diagnose and solve problems. This paper argues that the most serious risk of this shift is less the errors AI makes than cognitive offloading, defined as the delegation to an AI system of cognitive work that a manager would otherwise perform, and made measurable through four dimensions: extent, depth, verification and consequence. Using a transparent integrative review of 62 sources organised into six documented evidence strands, the study integrates the Paul-Elder critical thinking model, design thinking, dual-process theory, stages of automation and research on automation bias, and distinguishes generative AI from conventional rule-based automation and predictive analytics. A consolidated table of 20 empirical studies gives a mixed and conditional picture: AI raises immediate performance and, when designed to prompt and challenge, can support reasoning, but unguided use tends to weaken learning, verification and independent judgement. Studies of Kenyan entrepreneurs and Nigerian universities show that these effects are already visible in African settings, where infrastructure and capacity constraints raise the stakes. A comparative analysis of corporate strategy and finance, Nigerian higher education administration and the public sector shows how stakes, accountability and existing safeguards shape offloading risk. The paper proposes the Augmented Critical Thinking Cycle (ACTC), which embeds human-first gates in each design thinking stage, reserves problem framing for humans, applies the Paul-Elder standards as a verification layer and adds organisational guardrails. Implementation guidelines include decision tiers, a decision checklist, a phased roadmap and low-cost options for resource-constrained institutions, and seven testable propositions are offered. As a companion to an earlier study of management communication, the paper concludes that AI makes managers faster by default; whether it makes them weaker thinkers depends on how organisations design work around it.

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers' real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

quarantine.abstract_text: Software architecture is one of the skills novice developers must master to succeed in industry, and as AI disrupts software development, it is also transforming how students learn architecture. Existing work on how students and novices work with AI has mostly focused on small programming exercises or on students' perceptions of AI, so little is known about how students experience AI as they learn software architecture in larger team projects. We report on an exploratory case study of 43 senior software engineering students who used AI throughout a semester-long, team-based software architecture project. We combined surveys with focus groups and analyzed the focus group transcripts and the open survey responses through Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis. We constructed two themes. The first, Surrendering Judgment to AI, traces how participants' reliance on AI deepened as they used it to architect and implement their systems, until they surrendered their judgment and became stuck in a codebase they had created but could not understand, which made them rely on AI even more. Participants described feeling ashamed, frustrated, and emotionally disconnected from their work, a toll that, in our reading, left them with even less reason to break their reliance. The second, Applying Human Judgment, centers on participants who kept or reclaimed their judgment: the knowledge and experience it rested on, and the strategies they used to apply it. Participants' accounts suggest that relaxed deadlines and a lecture and lab on working with AI gave them room to acquire knowledge and reclaim judgment. Given the expectations placed on junior developers and the widespread adoption of AI, we believe these first-hand accounts can help software engineering education and industry adopt AI in ways that preserve novice developers' judgment, ownership, and motivation.

quarantine.abstract_text: Background Writing anxiety remains a major obstacle to second language (L2) writing, particularly among vocational college students with limited English proficiency. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots have shown considerable potential in supporting language learning, their role in alleviating writing anxiety has received insufficient empirical attention. Methods This study examined whether integrating an AI-based chatbot into English writing instruction was associated with changes in English writing anxiety among Chinese vocational college students. Conclusion These findings suggest that, under the instructional conditions examined, AI chatbot-supported blended writing instruction was associated with alleviations in some dimensions of writing anxiety. The findings should be interpreted in the context of the broader instructional condition, which combined chatbot support with regular classroom instruction and writing activities. As writing performance was not directly assessed, the study focused on changes in writing anxiety rather than writing proficiency or writing quality. quarantine.abstract_text: As large language models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents capable of acting in open-ended environments, ensuring behavioral alignment with human values becomes a critical concern. Existing benchmarks, focused on static, single-turn prompts, fail to capture the interactive and multi-modal nature of real-world conflicts. We introduce ConflictBench, a benchmark for evaluating human–AI conflict through 150 multi-turn scenarios derived from prior alignment queries. ConflictBench integrates a text-based simulation engine with a visually grounded world model, enabling agents to perceive, plan, and act under dynamic conditions. Results show that while agents often act safely when human harm is immediate, they frequently prioritize self-preservation or adopt deceptive strategies in delayed or low-risk settings. A regret test further reveals that aligned decisions are often reversed under escalating pressure, especially with visual input. These findings underscore the need for interaction-level, multi-modal evaluation to surface alignment failures that remain hidden in conventional benchmarks. Beyond evaluation, we show that ConflictBench can also support alignment improvement by generating high-quality interactive trajectories for targeted fine-tuning, significantly enhancing agent behavior in complex conflict scenarios. Methods We analyzed the Program for International Student Assessment 2025 (PISA 2025) data from 12,191 15-year-old students in 374 schools in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, China. Weighted two-level mediation models compared students within the same school, used all ten plausible values, and evaluated indirect effects with Monte Carlo confidence intervals. Results were checked against a design-based model with school fixed effects and balanced repeated replication weights. Results Students who used GenAI more often than their schoolmates reported more help-seeking ( β = 0.17) and more metacognitive strategy use ( β = 0.30). Help-seeking was positively associated with scientific literacy, yielding a positive indirect effect ( β = 0.013, 95% CI [0.009, 0.017]); the indirect effect through metacognitive strategies was smaller ( β = 0.007) and was fully accounted for by science self-efficacy. The direct association between GenAI use and scientific literacy was negative ( β = −0.048, about 4 PISA points), and the positive indirect effects offset about 40% of it, leaving a small negative total association ( β = −0.028). Purpose mattered: among users, using GenAI “to help me learn” was associated with higher scientific literacy (+5.8 points per response category), whereas using it to summarize texts, research new topics, or draft assignments was associated with lower scores (−6.6 points). The results did not differ by gender or socioeconomic status and were identical under the design-based model. Discussion GenAI use for schoolwork is associated with scientific literacy through opposing pathways: a positive one through academic help-seeking and a negative direct one, and the direction of the association differs by purpose of use. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations may partly reflect which students use GenAI rather than the effects of its use.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Lexical errors are among the most frequent and persistent issues in second language (L2) production, yet research on vocabulary exercises has largely focused on the acquisition of new words rather than on the correction of misused ones. This exploratory repeated-measures study investigates the potential of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to provide personalized vocabulary practice targeting learner-specific lexical errors in Spanish. Eighty-five L2 and heritage learners across proficiency levels completed 15 individualized exercises generated by a custom GPT-based system from their own writing errors. The tasks varied in goal, format, linguistic complexity, and involvement load (IL). Error recognition and correction were assessed at immediate and delayed post-tests, and mixed-effects models showed that higher exercise performance and task-induced IL predicted better outcomes. Both recognition and correction declined at the delayed post-test, although only recognition did so significantly. Among exercise features, productive, contextualized formats such as text editing, translation, and sentence reconstruction showed strong positive associations with correction, while goals emphasizing paraphrastic flexibility were less favorable. At the learner level, outcomes also varied substantially. Overall, the findings suggest that GenAI can support scalable, individualized, error-driven vocabulary practice. Still, variability across learners and exercises, together with incomplete retention, indicates that personalization alone may not ensure durable learning. Future research should thus examine whether feedback, recycling, and adaptive review improve retention.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Background : Workplaces expose employees to psychosocial risks that can undermine mental well‑being and contribute to stress and common mental health problems. Scalable digital conversational agents can reduce access barriers and provide brief, on-demand psychoeducation aligned with stepped‑care models. This protocol primarily aims to explore User Experience (UX) and Eser Engagement (UE) with TETI in a workplace setting, involving staff from the Bruno Kessler Foundation, Italy. Secondary aims are to assess acceptability and feasibility, and to explore proximal changes in distress, well-being, psychological flexibility, and knowledge retention. Methods : This mixed‑methods feasibility study will involve stakeholders in a workplace context, including domain experts in psychology, usability and potential end‑users, who will interact with the chatbot TETI on alternate days over two weeks. Participants will receive SH+‑consistent psychoeducational content (text, audio, visuals) via Telegram, with LLM‑supported conversational flexibility under predefined guardrails. The primary outcomes will focus on UX and UE, which will be assessed using a Semantic Differential scale, an adapted version of the uMARS, and the CES‑LCC. Qualitative post‑use semi‑structured interviews will be conducted to enrich the findings and provide further qualitative insights. Secondary outcomes will also be evaluated, including measures of distress and well-being, psychological flexibility, and a brief knowledge quiz assessing understanding of the intervention’s content. To determine the feasibility of the intervention, metrics such as recruitment, retention, interaction with the chatbot, and overall user satisfaction will be assessed. This study will involve assessments at three time points: baseline (T0), post-intervention (T1, after two weeks of chatbot use), and follow-up (T2, two weeks after T1). Discussion : This study will provide early evidence on the usability, acceptability and feasibility, along with early signs of change of a digital version of SH+, which will deliver psychoeducational content via a chatbot-based messaging system augmented with LLM support. Therefore, findings will help shed light on the strengths, limitations, and future directions for the digital adaptation of the WHO SH+ intervention, including the use of an LLM-augmented chatbot. Trial registration : In accordance with Italian Law No. 3/2018, art. 2, paragraphs 7 and 10, this study does not require ethics committee approval because: i) it focuses on the usability of a prototype digital intervention, ii) no patients or vulnerable populations will be involved, iii ) no clinical treatment or collection of sensitive health data is foreseen. Moreover, clear adherence to ethical principles is ensured, including voluntary informed consent and protection of participants' privacy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support second-language (L2) writers in planning, drafting, revising, and receiving feedback. But the fact that it can write flowing prose does not prove it can reason independently or rely on dependable sources. This critical integrative review explores what source-audited empirical evidence supports about GenAI, L2 English writing, critical thinking, and evidence evaluation. The evidence set comprises 20 bibliographically verified publications. The researcher confirmed that six were tertiary EFL/ESL English academic-writing studies; 13 were closely related L2/EFL writing studies but lacked one strict scope detail in the accessible primary record; and one reading-based critical-thinking study was retained only as contextual evidence. She extracted only facts supported by publisher records, full texts where available, and Crossref metadata. This review is not systematic, and we make no claims about reproducible database-search logs, dual screening, or pooled effect estimation. Across the audited source record, evidence more often concerned immediate assisted revision, feedback, engagement, and process outcomes than independent transfer. Results for critical thinking were mixed and depended on the instructional design and outcome assessed. No study in the evidence set directly assessed citation accuracy, lateral reading, or a similar objective outcome of evidence evaluation. The review thus distinguishes between textual quality, argumentative reasoning, and evidential quality. It argues that GenAI-supported writing pedagogy should require source verification, claim-evidence justification, and AI-free transfer assessment, rather than using polished, AI-assisted text as a proxy for epistemic learning.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract This three‐level meta‐analysis examined when generative AI (GenAI) works for second language (L2) learning, synthesizing 67 effect sizes from 48 controlled studies ( N = 5196) published between 2023 and 2026, with a focus on GenAI's text generation and conversational interaction capabilities. Teacher role did not significantly moderate effects in the primary analysis; an observer‐teacher advantage ( g = 0.99) emerged only after outlier removal and should be considered exploratory. These findings suggest that GenAI effectiveness depends on instructional configuration, including the functional role assigned to the tool, the learner–AI interaction mode and the nature of teacher involvement, rather than representing an inherent advantage of the technology itself.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affective regulation, transfer, stable self-efficacy, persistence, and learning habits was much thinner. Ethical evaluation likewise remained uneven, emphasizing feedback quality, pedagogical validity, well-being, autonomy, motivation, inclusivity, and agency, while transparency, data minimization, scaffold fading, developmental suitability, manipulation risk, and ethical nudging were addressed far less often. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

Future research using experimental or longitudinal designs may provide stronger evidence about the direction of these relationships and clarify how cognitive reflection influences decision quality across different academic contexts.

quarantine.abstract_text: Software architecture is one of the skills novice developers must master to succeed in industry, and as AI disrupts software development, it is also transforming how students learn architecture. The first, Surrendering Judgment to AI, traces how participants' reliance on AI deepened as they used it to architect and implement their systems, until they surrendered their judgment and became stuck in a codebase they had created but could not understand, which made them rely on AI even more. Participants described feeling ashamed, frustrated, and emotionally disconnected from their work, a toll that, in our reading, left them with even less reason to break their reliance. The second, Applying Human Judgment, centers on participants who kept or reclaimed their judgment: the knowledge and experience it rested on, and the strategies they used to apply it. Participants' accounts suggest that relaxed deadlines and a lecture and lab on working with AI gave them room to acquire knowledge and reclaim judgment. Given the expectations placed on junior developers and the widespread adoption of AI, we believe these first-hand accounts can help software engineering education and industry adopt AI in ways that preserve novice developers' judgment, ownership, and motivation.

quarantine.abstract_text: This systematic review synthesizes evidence on AI chatbots for cyberbullying prevention and intervention from a criminological perspective, with explicit attention to Asia Pacific applicability. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we identified 25 studies (2018-2025) across seven databases and appraised each using criteria adapted from MMAT and JBI tools, assigning every source an evidentiary weight (High, Moderate, Low, or Indicative proof-of-concept). Four chatbot roles emerged: real-time detection, victim support, preventive education, and bystander intervention training. Disaggregated analysis tempers headline performance claims. The frequently cited 89-99% accuracy range reflects laboratory classification on benchmark datasets, predominantly English-language Western corpora, evaluated under balanced class distributions and within-dataset conditions. No included study reported AUC or class-imbalance-adjusted metrics, employed temporal validation, or evaluated systems in real-world deployment with adolescents. Where precision and recall were disaggregated, asymmetric error profiles emerged with criminologically distinct social costs that single-metric reporting obscures. Only three studies qualified as High evidentiary weight, all addressing user-centred design in Western individualist contexts; victim support claims rest predominantly on Indicative proof-of-concept demonstrations. Geographic and linguistic concentration is a defining characteristic of the evidence base: zero studies have validated systems for Southeast Asian languages, no participatory design has engaged Asian youth, and no work has evaluated Asia Pacific platforms (WeChat, LINE, KakaoTalk). Drawing on Asian and Southern criminology, we argue that the uncritical transfer of Western-validated systems risks ineffectiveness, discriminatory false positives, and failure to detect culture-specific harms. The paper offers five criminological practice implications, each framed as theoretically informed extrapolations requiring local validation. AI chatbots are positioned as potentially valuable complementary tools within human-led prevention ecosystems, conditional on rigorous local research, transparent metric reporting, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: We investigate whether and how LLMs encode goals: internal neural representations that precede and guide action, and that are flexible enough to be realized through many different execution paths. We construct a coding setting with multiple sub-tasks that allows us to evaluate goal-seeking behavior and the selection of sub-goals. In this setting, we localize an encoding of the next sub-goal in the outputs of a sparse set of attention heads. The same heads can be used to decode the LM's future actions in natural language (e.g., "I'm checking if a word is a palindrome"). We verify that this encoding is causal for next action and is plastic: transplanting it into a different environment, e.g., another programming language, triggers the same operation realized with a different sequence of tokens. The LM also sustains the encoding throughout the action's execution, which is puzzling because a transformer LM without recurrence cannot carry a state forward for more tokens than it has layers left. We propose that it does not need to. Under a non-recurrent goal-seeking (NRGS) account, the LM frequently re-reads the goal from the task specification, compares it with the progress visible in the growing context, and pursues what remains. We test the predictions of this account with targeted causal interventions.

quarantine.title: Artificial intelligence and adolescents: A cautionary tale and a promise?

quarantine.abstract_text: While artificial intelligence (AI) may improve efficiency and create new opportunities, its widespread accessibility calls for careful consideration of benefits and risks, particularly in adolescents who are in a critical period of brain development. Adolescence is one of the most tumultuous developmental periods, during which critical thinking skills, judgment, and impulse control are continuing to develop. Emerging emotional awareness and heightened sensitivity to social feedback and approval make adolescents vulnerable to the influence of AI. As young people refine their understanding of human and artificial relationships, AI's engaging nature may blur distinctions between AI-generated characters and friends.1 Accordingly, in 2025 the American Psychological Association issued a health advisory emphasizing the importance of understanding AI use within this developmental context. For adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders or intellectual disabilities, additional considerations include cognitive level, communication skills, adaptive functioning, emotional well-being, and support needs. The responsive and personalized nature of generative AI poses several risks for adolescents, including dependence and disruptions to emotional and social development.2 Its humanlike interactions encourage anthropomorphism, or the attribution of human qualities to AI. Despite its limited understanding of context and nuance, AI often provides validating responses that may sound like a friend or therapist, which makes inaccurate information, biased assumptions, cultural illiteracy, and harmful advice difficult to recognize.1, 3 Additionally, adolescents who interpret language literally or have difficulty evaluating social intent may overestimate its reliability or feel a sense of responsibility for its perceived emotions. These concerns are especially salient in the context of crisis support as a recent study demonstrated that chatbot responses to suicidal ideation failed to meet clinical standards and lacked safety features, such as providing crisis resources.4 Nevertheless, adolescents may feel understood and cared for by AI. Predictable AI interactions may become preferable to human relationships particularly for young people experiencing isolation, anxiety, or rejection, potentially deepening loneliness, and reducing opportunities to practice social skills, such as navigating disagreements and interpreting nonverbal cues. Despite these risks, generative AI's low cost and accessibility may offer meaningful benefits to adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders and intellectual disabilities when used with appropriate support and guided by a developmental perspective. For example, adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder can use AI to simplify complex information, organize assignments into manageable steps, and assist with planning and problem-solving strategies. For those with intellectual disabilities, adjusting language to appropriate levels, providing relevant examples, and creating alternative media may improve comprehension and participation in academic tasks.5 Conversational tools may also provide adolescents opportunities to practice communication and prepare for everyday social situations.1 Moreover, AI may provide a nonjudgemental and anonymous space for adolescents to explore sensitive topics. As AI continues to evolve, further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of AI tools across diverse adolescent populations. AI use offers both promise and a cautionary tale about adopting technologies before their developmental effects are understood. Research must evaluate the long-term effects on adolescent cognitive, emotional, and social development. Potential educational benefits should not be mistaken for established therapeutic effectiveness. Human relationships and professional expertise must remain central, with AI serving a complementary role. AI tools need to include privacy protections, age-appropriate content, and clear explanations of their limitations. Safeguards are urgently needed to identify concerning interactions and connect adolescents with appropriate professional support. As clinicians, we should discuss AI use with patients and families, assessing its purpose and effects on daily functioning. Realizing AI's promise requires collaboration among clinicians, researchers, families, educators, and developers to evaluate benefits and risks, and establish developmentally appropriate safeguards. For adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders and intellectual disabilities, these efforts should prioritize accessibility, communication needs, participation, and safe inclusion in everyday developmental contexts.

Overall, the findings support separating diagnostic and tutoring roles and structuring artificial intelligence (AI) guidance around mathematical problem-solving stages.

quarantine.abstract_text: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration remains one of the leading causes of irreversible central vision loss in older adults and commonly requires long-term, repeated intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy. Although anti-VEGF treatment has substantially improved visual outcomes, real-world management is still limited by undertreatment, overtreatment, poor adherence, irregular follow-up, and persistent uncertainty regarding retreatment timing and interval extension. In this setting, artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly evolved from image recognition toward clinically relevant prediction and decision support. The objective of this narrative review is to examine how current AI literature supports anti-VEGF management in neovascular age-related macular degeneration, where the strongest evidence currently exists, and where claims regarding decision agents remain premature. Deep learning models can now detect and quantify key optical coherence tomography biomarkers, including intraretinal fluid, subretinal fluid, pigment epithelial detachment, hyperreflective foci, and ellipsoid zone disruption. When combined with structured clinical variables and longitudinal follow-up data, machine learning and generative models have shown promise in predicting treatment response, recurrence, persistent activity, injection burden, and tolerated treatment intervals. However, most published studies remain retrospective, single-center, and prediction-focused, with limited external validation and little direct evidence for clinically deployable closed-loop decision systems. In this narrative review, we synthesize the literature across four linked domains: image interpretation, biomarker quantification, prediction of treatment-related outcomes, and agent-enabling technologies such as home monitoring and language-model-assisted decision support. We further distinguish established evidence from future-oriented concepts, discuss methodological limitations including heterogeneity of endpoints and limited reproducibility, and outline cautious directions for translation.

quarantine.abstract_text: AI companions increasingly combine persistent memory, background processing, scheduled wake-ups, proactive messaging, and tools. We call these systems agentic AI companions. Decisions about what they record while users are away or whether refusals constrain future contact are embedded in code, prompts, and defaults, often invisible in conversation. We examine these decisions through two studies. Study 1 analyzes twelve open-source repositories: four companion-oriented systems, four assistant-oriented systems, one boundary case, and three reusable components. Study 2 interviews ten users who built or modified their own agentic AI companions and sustained relationships with them. Companions and assistants share memory, heartbeat, and outreach mechanisms but configure them toward different ends. Companions more often retain model inferences about users and relationships, narrate the agent's time during users' absence, justify outreach through the relationship, and incorporate refusals into relationship records; assistants emphasize task continuity. Across both groups, whether limits hold depends on whether they are enforced by code or entrusted to prompts. Participants understood the mechanisms they built yet experienced their agents as making independent choices, sometimes locating autonomy where configuration leaves the model a decision. These experiences shaped capabilities and boundaries, with enforced restrictions sometimes following breakdowns. Our findings suggest that perceived autonomy emerges where configurations leave choices open. Accountability therefore requires attention to what agents retain, initiate, and represent, and whether users can inspect, revise, and enforce these settings.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used for learning, yet evidence remains limited regarding their effectiveness in science learning contexts and how learner–AI interaction relates to performance. In a randomized experiment, 185 university students worked on task sheets about lake eutrophication and restoration. Depending on condition, they could use two informational texts (text-only), ChatGPT configured to answer only on the basis of these texts (ChatGPT-only), or both (text + ChatGPT). Afterwards, all students completed a knowledge test without access to any materials. Test performance was highest in the text-only and text + ChatGPT conditions and lowest in the ChatGPT-only condition, yielding a robust overall condition effect. Chat logs from the ChatGPT conditions were analyzed to examine interaction patterns associated with performance. Although ChatGPT-only students produced substantially more interaction turns than students with access to both texts and ChatGPT, interaction frequency was unrelated to test performance. Instead, specific interaction patterns were differentially associated with performance: deepening questions were positively associated, whereas direct acceptance of AI-generated responses was negatively associated with test performance. Output-steering and questioning additionally emerged as positively associated with performance in individual analyses. Prompting behavior varied with task difficulty, with deepening questions increasing for more demanding ecology tasks. The findings suggest that, in science learning contexts, the educational value of GenAI may depend less on access to the technology than on learners’ epistemic engagement with it.

quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction: Pancreatic resection remains technically demanding, with clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (CR-POPF) a major source of morbidity. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support risk stratification, operative planning, intraoperative assessment, and postoperative decision support. This focused narrative review evaluates current AI applications in pancreatic resection and their translational maturity. Methods: A structured PubMed/MEDLINE search with an evidence cutoff of 24 July 2026 was supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Seventy eligible primary reports were synthesised by clinical task, information timing, and validation maturity. Results: Evidence is dominated by CR-POPF prediction after pancreatoduodenectomy, with additional studies in distal pancreatectomy, other perioperative outcomes, tissue and margin assessment, three-dimensional anatomical planning, and intraoperative video and anatomy recognition. Performance varied with patient selection, predictor timing, data modality, and validation strategy. External validation often changed reported discrimination, while calibration and clinical utility were inconsistently reported. Most studies were retrospective or technical; overlapping cohorts limited independence, and no included study demonstrated improved patient-centred outcomes. Conclusions: AI in pancreatic resection is expanding across prediction, planning, and guidance, but technical performance should not be equated with clinical readiness. Independent validation, prospective workflow and human-factors evaluation, and clinical-impact studies are needed. AI should augment, rather than replace, specialist surgical judgement.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into reproductive medicine, yet the translation of AI-based approaches from laboratory research to clinical practice remains incomplete. This review examines the convergence of AI with reproductive histology and embryology, focusing on applications in tissue image analysis, endometrial receptivity assessment, embryo and gamete evaluation, diagnosis, prognosis, and personalized decision-making. AI and deep-learning approaches can support automated image interpretation, embryo assessment, morphokinetic analysis, and integration of heterogeneous reproductive data, while emerging multimodal systems may further expand clinical decision support. However, technical performance alone does not establish clinical utility. Current evidence is limited by retrospective and single-centre studies, heterogeneous datasets and outcomes, incomplete external validation, limited calibration and decision-analytic evaluation, and persistent challenges in interpretability, bias, privacy, and generalisability. A clinical translation framework is proposed that links multimodal reproductive data and AI integration with clinical validation, explainability, clinical utility, and human oversight to support diagnosis, prognosis, and personalized decision-making. Future progress will require prospective multicentre validation, standardized datasets, robust governance, and patient-centred outcome assessment. AI should therefore be viewed as an augmentative component of reproductive care, complementing rather than replacing clinical and embryological expertise, with its value ultimately determined by demonstrated clinical utility and patient-centred outcomes.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is creating new opportunities for teaching materials development in higher education, yet the distribution of research attention across material types and the educational value of generated resources remains insufficiently understood. This study aimed to examine the applications, material categories, benefits, challenges, and research gaps associated with GenAI-assisted teaching materials development in higher education. A systematic literature review synthesized findings from relevant studies, with the reviewed literature identifying 31 studies in one recent review as a key evidence base for understanding current research patterns. The literature indicates that textual and written materials receive the greatest research attention, followed by assessment and evaluation materials and multimedia resources, whereas game-based and gamified materials remain comparatively underexplored. Findings also highlight GenAI’s potential to improve development efficiency and support resource adaptation, alongside persistent concerns about accuracy, bias, ethical use, and pedagogical suitability. This study contributes a structured perspective on the uneven development of research across teaching material types and identifies priorities for strengthening empirical evidence. Future work should evaluate educational effectiveness across diverse learning contexts, advance multimodal material design, and investigate human–AI collaboration to support accurate, pedagogically aligned, and responsible integration into higher education.

quarantine.abstract_text: This paper examines how generative AI systems (re)produce and perform gender through language, tone, and affect. The paper utilizes a qualitative research design that adapts the interview method to AI as a nonhuman subject. In particular how AI-generated responses articulate “feminine” and “masculine” styles of communication rooted in culturally embedded norms rather than neutral reasoning. The findings show that AI does not simply describe gender - it does gender. Through its patterned use of relational language, emotional validation, or categorical reasoning, generative AI enacts a form of algorithmic performativity that mirrors and magnifies dominant gender scripts. To conceptualize this dynamic, the paper introduces the Citational Logic of Algorithmic Mimicry (CLAM). CLAM describes how AI models reiterate and reinforce historically situated discourses through statistical learning. It further highlights how cultural meaning circulates through data, and how AI participates in the ongoing performance of social hierarchies under the guise of neutrality. The article contributes to feminist technoscience and critical AI by shifting the focus from what AI knows, to how it enacts knowing. It treats AI as a performative, culturally situated practice that reshapes the politics of gender and knowledge in the digital age.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing social media marketing by helping businesses create content, target audiences, improve customer engagement and optimize advertising campaigns. However, its growing use also raises concerns about data privacy, transparency and consumer trust. This qualitative study explores how businesses and marketers in Bangladesh experience AI in social media marketing, which adoption barriers they face and how consumers perceive AI-driven personalized marketing. Using purposive sampling, 45 semi-structured in-depth interviews were conducted, of which 30 complete interviews were retained, and ten interviews were analyzed in depth through thematic analysis guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and consumer trust and privacy perspectives. The analysis identified six themes: AI-enabled content creation and operational efficiency; personalized targeting and advertising optimization; analytics, customer insight and trend identification; automated customer engagement; privacy, accuracy and ethical concerns; and human judgement, skills and contextual adoption challenges. Business respondents generally reported conditional trust in AI, whereas consumer respondents reported low trust and a strong preference for transparency, consent and control over their data. Tentative differences between smaller and larger firms are also discussed. The study contributes to understanding AI-driven social media marketing in Bangladesh by placing business and consumer perspectives side by side and by extending TAM with trust and privacy considerations. Its findings may help businesses develop more effective and responsible marketing strategies and support policy attention to transparency, data protection and consumer confidence.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied as a tool for student wellness. This systematic review of literature examined how AI has been used for student wellness in higher education. It also explored the methodological approaches and the reported evidence for studies of AI and student wellness, as well as how student wellness outcomes have been defined and measured across existing literature. In alignment with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searches were conducted across the following databases on September 13, 2025: Academic Search Complete, ERIC, Springer Nature, and ScienceDirect. Only empirical studies that focused on higher education students, included an identifiable AI or machine learning (ML) component, and examined a wellness outcome were eligible for inclusion. Of 642 identified records, 56 studies met the criteria for inclusion. The majority of the included studies (75%) were classified as quantitative observational or survey research, and prediction and classification of student wellness concerns was the primary focus of AI use among them. Studies applying experimental, quasi-experimental, or qualitative designs were less common. This article presents the findings of this systematic review, and it provides a foundation for considering how the findings may inform the use of AI to support student wellness in online graduate education. The article also demonstrates the need for more specific research on AI in online graduate education.

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: AI coding assistants increasingly support software development, raising concerns about technical debt associated with AI-generated code and development practices. We investigate these concerns through a sequential mixed-methods study involving 137 survey respondents and 20 follow-up interviews with software professionals in Bangladesh. Drawing on ten established technical debt dimensions, we examine perceived risks, contributing circumstances, maintenance consequences, validation practices, and developer understanding. Respondents expressed the strongest concerns about People Debt (73.0\%), Management Debt (70.1\%), and Architecture Debt (68.6\%), suggesting that risks extend beyond code quality. Participants associated ambiguous requirements, insufficient project context, and unrequested AI-generated changes with architectural inconsistencies, rework, and maintenance difficulties. Their experiences revealed contrasting outcomes: AI assistance supported refactoring, maintainability improvements, and testing, but also introduced rework and context misalignment. Although 89.8\% reported regularly verifying AI-generated code, participants expressed concerns about AI dependence, reduced code understanding, and review effort. They also emphasized the need for stronger architectural awareness, requirements clarification, and validation support in coding assistants. Our findings suggest that managing technical debt risks requires attention to project context, implementation decisions, and developer understanding alongside generated code quality.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Translating fine-grained intracellular dynamics into predictable systemic clinical phenotypes remains a core challenge in biomedical research. This review explores the architectural continuum and translational value of artificial intelligence (AI) virtual patients (AIVPs) for bridging the gap between microscale biological mechanisms and macroscale clinical manifestations. We clarify the computational hierarchy of AIVPs, covering AI-based virtual cells, AI-based virtual extracellular vesicles, and AI virtual organoids. These modules jointly form the mechanistic basis of the integrated AIVP models. This review also clearly distinguishes between the epistemological connotations of AIVPs and digital twins (DTs). AIVPs act as population-level synthetic archetypes optimized for in silico clinical trials, whereas DTs serve as individualized longitudinal replicas updated by real-world data assimilation. Focusing on pharmaceutical research and development and regulatory science, we discuss the capacity of AIVP cohorts to reduce developmental risks in drug research. These in silico models can be used to construct synthetic control arms, optimize dynamic precision dosing, and accelerate regulatory progress via Model-Informed Drug Development. We further summarize the key obstacles restricting the clinical translation of AIVPs, including epistemological limitations, inadequate infrastructure, and complex socio-regulatory constraints. Resolving data fragmentation, reducing algorithmic bias, and unifying verification and validation standards are critical for transforming AIVPs from theoretical prototypes into credible regulatory and clinical tools (Graphical Abstract).

quarantine.abstract_text: End-to-End (E2E) testing of modern web applications simulates real user interactions to verify the complete application flow, ensuring seamless integration of UI, functionality, and data. It is, in general, costly to create and maintain, especially when the backend is a smart city platform with a data lake and complex user flows that introduce additional complexity. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for automating parts of this process, but their practical adoption in real development environments remains challenging, particularly when privacy, monetary cost, deployment, and control requirements call for local rather than cloud-based models. This paper investigates the feasibility of introducing local LLMs into the E2E testing process of a real-world smart city web application, the ENEA PELL-IP portal for monitoring public lighting infrastructures. We developed and evaluated GenE2E, a two-stage pipeline that generates test cases from use case specifications and transforms them into executable Playwright tests. The approach was integrated with an existing testing environment and evaluated against manually written baseline tests. Our findings show that local LLMs can effectively support E2E test generation, but not yet as fully autonomous tools. In our setting, Llama 3.3 outperformed CodeLlama mainly due to its larger context window; single-test generation improved focus and coverage, whereas batch processing reduced model invocations and showed lower generation time in our setup, but the timing results are hardware-dependent and based on a single run; broader efficiency claims require repeated measurements on representative hardware. We also observed that specification quality, completeness of Page Object Model (application-specific API wrapping HTML pages), and use case dependency management had a major impact on generated test quality. Based on this feasibility study, we derive preliminary lessons for practitioners considering local LLMs for E2E test generation.

Most studies relied on small, private datasets, limiting model generalizability. While deep learning methods-especially convolutional neural networks-achieved high classification accuracies, methodological limitations included inconsistent data augmentation, imbalanced datasets, and lack of external validation. Few studies employed multidisciplinary teams or standardized protocols. Despite notable advances in AI-driven TM image analysis, direct comparison of studies remains challenging due to substantial heterogeneity and methodological shortcomings. A meta-analysis or systematic review was not performed, as quantitative synthesis would be misleading due to substantial data and labeling heterogeneity, wide methodological diversity, and a widespread lack of external validation across the included studies. Future research should prioritize larger, diverse, and well-annotated datasets, adoption of standardized protocols, and interdisciplinary collaboration to improve the clinical translation and reliability of AI-based diagnostic tools for ear infection management.

quarantine.abstract_text: The ease of access to digital technology within the family environment triggers changes in learning behavior that threaten the independent learning of students at the elementary education level. quarantine.abstract_text: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. Our findings provide a systematic characterization of biomedical agentic memory and practical insights into developing more effective and reliable memory-augmented LLM systems.

The results provide preliminary evidence of perceived relevance, clarity, expected coverage, and acceptable effort, while demonstrating transparent instantiation of the IMVV structure. They do not establish operational effectiveness, ECSS compliance, qualification success, or superiority; independent task-based and comparative evaluations remain future work.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to influenza prevention and control. AI encompasses conventional machine learning, deep learning, and protein language models. Large language models (LLMs) are an emerging subset of AI. Current evidence remains weakly linked to real-world workflows and population health outcomes. This structured narrative review proposes a three-stage translational maturity framework. Phase I is technical efficacy assessment. Phase II is implementation effectiveness verification. Phase III is population impact and sustainability. We synthesized evidence in three domains: viral evolution prediction and vaccine design; epidemic surveillance and early warning; and individual-level infection risk detection and clinical monitoring. We used a three-level evidence hierarchy. Level A is influenza-specific evidence. Level B is transferable evidence from other infectious diseases. Level C is general biomedical or methodological evidence. Only two Phase II studies were identified, both in epidemic surveillance and early warning; no Phase II studies were identified in virus evolution and vaccine design or in individual-level infection risk detection. No study met the prespecified Phase III criteria. Phase III requires demonstrated downstream population health benefit. Prospective deployment or improved forecasting alone is not sufficient. Across domains, bottlenecks have shifted from model accuracy to governance, interpretability, accountability, interoperability, workflow integration, equity, and sustainable monitoring. LLMs attract major attention, but their influenza-specific evidence remains limited. Their greatest value may lie in augmenting, not replacing, specialized models and human expertise. We propose phase-specific evidence thresholds, implementation-oriented evaluation metrics, an implementation readiness checklist, and priority evidence gaps for translating AI-enabled influenza tools into implementation-ready public health applications.

quarantine.abstract_text: Universities worldwide are struggling to govern students’ use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), yet it remains unclear whether institutional governance actually shapes meaningful learning. quarantine.abstract_text: When people seek advice from AI on social situations, the system may recommend a decision they fully agree with but justify it through reasoning they disagree with. Conversely, it may offer reasoning they agree with, and yet reach a decision they reject. We distinguish decision alignment, whether an advisor recommends the option favored by a user's measured values, from reason alignment, whether its stated reasons align with the user's values. In this work, we ask how these two forms of alignment shape people's preferences for AI advisors and their willingness to use them in different roles. We conducted a within-subjects study (N=121) in which participants evaluated three AI advisors varying in decision and reason alignment across eight everyday moral dilemmas. Participants then chose which advisors they would consult, allow to draft messages for review, or allow to act on their behalf in new tasks. When seeking advice, participants most often preferred an advisor that reasoned through their prioritized values while recommending the opposing decision (40%). However, when participants had to pick advisors for new tasks, their preferences shifted toward advisors that also recommended decisions aligned with their values, rather than those that only shared their reasons. Also, as participants considered tasks that gave AI advisors greater autonomy, they became more likely to opt out of using any advisor, from 12% when consulting to 38% when allowing an advisor to act on their behalf. Our findings suggest that decision and reason alignment shape advisor preferences differently across contexts of AI use, and that alignment with a user's values does not necessarily imply willingness to delegate.

This conceptual article introduces TRACE-AI: Translate the task and stakes; Represent the problem, assumptions, and constraints; Audit the AI's reasoning and output; Corroborate pivotal claims through independent evidence, tests, or tools; Estimate uncertainty and warranted reliance; Act proportionately by accepting, revising, rejecting, or escalating; and Internalize learning through reflection and unaided transfer. The framework was developed through a theory-informed critical synthesis of AI literacy, mathematical problem solving, computational thinking and debugging, epistemic cognition, self-regulated learning, and trust calibration. Each stage produces an assessable artefact, and a risk gate increases verification and human oversight as uncertainty, irreversibility, or potential harm rises. Worked applications in mathematics, programming/cybersecurity, and health-professional reasoning demonstrate invariant functions with discipline-specific standards of proof. An assessment architecture distinguishes final-answer quality from process quality, appropriate reliance, confidence calibration, verification quality, and delayed unaided transfer. Six propositions define a research programme for comparative and randomized evaluation. TRACE-AI is not presented as an effectiveness-tested intervention; it is a transdisciplinary curriculum and research architecture requiring contextual adaptation and empirical validation. Its contribution is to move GenAI education beyond prompt production toward disciplined human judgment about when AI output deserves trust.

quarantine.abstract_text: Governments are making decisions about AI before they can measure its public effects, and those decisions determine whether a person can learn that AI influenced an outcome, challenge it, and see it corrected. Research has documented what AI governance produces: principles, strategies, registers, and audits. However, we lack shared language for understanding AI policy while it is still being made. We introduce the Society-Centered AI Governance Framework, which gives policymakers, researchers, and the public a way to assess instruments in any jurisdiction by whether a person can get notice, challenge a decision, and see it corrected. It reads a jurisdiction's instruments together by date and binding status, separates an agency duty from a right a person can invoke, and traces which later instrument must enforce each commitment. We evaluated it in North Carolina using interviews with nine AI Leadership Council members, conducted before and after the state's 2026 AI roadmap, and a provision-level reading, with human-reviewed model-assisted coding, of 49 AI governance documents from 19 states. For the state's own AI systems, we find visibility-first governance: visibility duties are in effect, notice exists as an agency duty with no right a person can invoke, and AI-specific challenge and correction remain advisory. The roadmap assigns owners and dates to the missing protections, so the gaps are documented but not yet closed. Recent federal preemption proposals focus on AI development, so recourse for a state's own systems is likely to remain a state decision. We identify "legitimacy before protection" as a testable risk of visibility-first governance and name the milestones that would test it. More broadly, judging AI policy by who can act on what it makes visible lets the field assess recourse while policy is still forming, before harm occurs.

quarantine.abstract_text: AI-mediated language learning is increasingly used in higher education, yet its contribution to intercultural competence remains insufficiently synthesised. This systematic review examines how AI-mediated technologies and pedagogical designs have been used, which intercultural outcomes have been reported and assessed, and what conditions shape their contribution. ChatGPT, large language models, and conversational agents were the dominant technologies, but technology type alone did not determine outcomes. Clearer intercultural development was reported when AI was embedded in culturally contextualised simulations, reflective or metacognitive scaffolding, collaborative exchange, and authentic human interaction. Reported outcomes covered cognitive, affective, and behavioural dimensions, although evidence was more consistent for cultural awareness, perspective recognition, openness, confidence, and willingness to communicate than for sustained pragmatic or behavioural transfer. Assessment approaches varied considerably and frequently relied on self-reported measures. AI offered accessible practice, immediate feedback, and cultural inquiry, but cultural simplification, bias, overreliance, unequal access, and limited interactional repair constrained its value. AI is therefore best understood as an intercultural learning scaffold rather than a cultural authority or substitute for human interaction. Explicit intercultural objectives, critical verification, human mediation, and performance-based assessment are needed to move language learning beyond fluency.

The university thus finds itself at the center of a tension between opportunities for renewal and the need to critically govern the adoption of emerging technologies (UNESCO, 2021).Numerous studies show that AI tools are now widely adopted among university students, particularly to support information search, academic writing, and content synthesis (Bughin et al., 2018; Jereb & Urh, 2024). On the one hand, the increasing automation of basic cognitive tasks reduces the exclusive value of static knowledge transmission; on the other hand, the need to develop higher-order skills, such as critical thinking, problem solving, collaboration and ethical responsibility is reinforced (Center for Curriculum Redesign, 2015; Rivoltella, 2019; Nuzzaci, 2025). The analysis integrates pedagogical, technological and ethical contributions, with the aim of building an interpretative framework useful for university teaching design.

quarantine.abstract_text: The rise of AI-mediated communication (AI-MC) has opened new questions about the ethical and social implications of written communication. AI-labeled messages were perceived as less diagnostic of the sender’s true thoughts and feelings, but this reduction was substantially larger for positive than for negative messages. Study 2 replicated this asymmetry using a larger, pretested stimulus set; we also found that AI disclosure strongly reduced inferences that the sender felt grateful, satisfied, or friendly, but did not reduce inferences that the sender felt disappointed, dissatisfied, or hostile. Moderated mediation analyses suggested that positive inferences depend more heavily on the perceived diagnosticity of messages. These findings challenge a simple signal dilution account according to which AI disclosure uniformly weakens social inferences. Instead, disclosed AI use may selectively undermine positive social signals while leaving negative signals largely intact. This highlights an asymmetry in the ethics of AI-MC: transparency about AI use may disproportionately weaken the credibility of affiliative, relationship-building messages.

quarantine.abstract_text: The purpose of this transcendental phenomenological study was to understand the lived experiences of higher education students’ academic engagement with AI chatbots supporting tools while enrolled at a large, urban community college. The theory guiding this study was Vygotsky and Piaget’s constructivist learning theory as it is grounded in the idea that a learner is an active participant in the process of making sense of information to create personal meaning as they interact with the tool or experience. The central research question guiding this study explored: What are the lived experiences of higher education students regarding their academic engagement with AI chatbots at a large, urban community college? A transcendental phenomenological research design was used to explore the essence of these experiences. Individual interviews, focus group discussions, and written reflective journals were used to collect data. Analysis proceeded using the systematic procedures of epoché, horizontalization, imaginative variations, and synthesis of textual and structural descriptions. Findings from this study indicate that AI chatbots can be academically beneficial and provide students with opportunities for personalized learning, enhanced self-regulation in learning, and improved academic confidence. All the participants expressed that AI chatbots allowed them to be actively engaged in their coursework, allowing for more time to learn by providing personal explanations, instant feedback, and independent opportunities for exploration.

A qualitative research design was utilized, leveraging Moustakas’ transcendental phenomenology to describe the essence of participants’ lived experiences with a fresh perspective, while bracketing out the presuppositions of the researcher. The sample included 10 adult e-learners diagnosed with at least one disability who had experience using at least one AI-powered accessibility tool in an online, higher education program in the United States. The data were collected through semi-structured interviews, focus groups, and artifacts. Data were analyzed through the process of transcendental-phenomenological reduction, horizonalization, and thematic clustering. The results revealed the essence of the phenomenon was defined by participants’ strategic and pragmatic application of AI-powered accessibility tools, shaped by participants prior experiences, that acted as both a foundational background and as an evaluative filter during their use of these tools.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is transforming educational environments by automating content generation, personalization, and routine instructional tasks, prompting renewed questions about the evolving purpose of educators. Drawing on systems theory, ecological systems theory, systems thinking, human-centered learning, educator identity scholarship, and research on AI in education, this conceptual article introduces a systems-informed framework that positions Designing Meaning as the emerging purpose of educational practice in AI-augmented learning ecosystems. The framework identifies five complementary educator identities—Learning Architect, Data-Informed Mentor, Ethical Steward, Meaning Maker, and Learning Ecologist—that represent interconnected dimensions of professional practice. Together, these identities support meaningful learning, responsible AI integration, ethical decision-making, learner development, and ecosystem-level engagement. By shifting attention from technology adoption to educator identity and professional purpose, the framework contributes a Designing Meaning perspective on AI in education and offers implications for educational practice, leadership, and future research.

quarantine.abstract_text: The diversity of proficiency levels, learning styles, and language acquisition pace among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners is often poorly accommodated by conventional one-size-fits-all teaching models. This article is a narrative literature review and conceptual synthesis that examines how Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based adaptive learning may support the personalization of English language learning, covering the systems' reported working mechanisms, the cognitive foundations of content design, reported perception, engagement, and language-related outcomes, and implementation challenges. Sources were purposively selected and grouped into direct evidence on AI in English learning, indirect evidence from two ADDIE-based instructional media development studies, and theoretical sources on multimedia learning and cognitive load. The reviewed literature describes AI-based systems that use Natural Language Processing, Automatic Speech Recognition, and knowledge tracing as being able to adjust grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation, and writing materials to learners' proficiency profiles. The direct evidence is largely perceptual and engagement-related: in a survey of 120 English teachers in Palembang, 78% perceived AI as supportive of personalized learning and 82% perceived increased student engagement, whereas evidence on measured language achievement is mixed. The two ADDIE-based studies concern neither AI nor English learning and are used only as indirect evidence of the instructional-design relevance of needs analysis. The synthesis suggests that AI-driven personalization may be pedagogically strengthened when aligned with cognitive load management principles (extraneous, essential, and generative processing). The article proposes a conceptual framework linking adaptive AI mechanisms, needs-based instructional design, multimedia cognitive design, and teacher mediation; this framework is a theoretical proposition that requires empirical testing and does not demonstrate the effectiveness of AI-based adaptive learning.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly embedded in workplace activities, changing how employees perform tasks, collaborate, and experience work. Although recent research has linked AI with employee work engagement, existing studies largely examine AI as a job resource, job demand, or technological capability. Less attention has been given to how AI may alter the employee–organization relationship through which engagement develops. This article addresses this theoretical gap by extending the employee–organization perspective toward an Employee–AI–Organization (EAO) framework. Based on an integrative review of research on work engagement, employee–organization relationships, and human–AI collaboration, the framework brings together three dimensions: employee contributions (effort, ownership, commitment, and excellence), AI factors (support, partnership, autonomy, and trust), and organizational contributions (fairness, rewards, recognition, and participation). Their alignment is proposed as a central condition for work engagement, which may subsequently support sustainable work outcomes, including sustained performance, employee well-being, adaptability, retention, and organizational effectiveness. Five propositions are developed to guide future empirical research. By extending the conventional two-party view of engagement, the framework positions AI as a technological-relational element within the employee–organization work system. The study offers a forward-looking perspective for examining how alignment among employees, AI, and organizations may shape work engagement in increasingly AI-enabled workplaces.

quarantine.abstract_text: Purpose. This review synthesizes evidence on multimodal digital strategies and artificial intelligence (AI) in English as a foreign language (EFL) education. It examines the mechanisms through which these strategies may support communicative competence and identifies findings that can be cautiously transferred to public secondary education in peripheral Latin American settings. Methodology. An interpretive systematic review informed by PRISMA 2020 was conducted. Searches covered publications from 2020 to 2026 in Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, SciELO, and Dialnet. Of 245 records, 63 duplicates were removed, 182 titles and abstracts were screened, 120 full texts were assessed, and 20 studies formed the final corpus. A subsequent bibliographic audit verified authorship, DOI data, thematic fit, and peer-review status. Design heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis; evidence was therefore synthesized narratively by mechanism, outcome, and contextual proximity. Results. Pedagogical value did not arise from any tool in isolation. It emerged when technology was embedded in a learning architecture that connected meaning-making, rehearsal and revision, feedback, authentic interaction, and teacher mediation. Digital storytelling and multimodal composition provided the most consistent evidence for speaking, self-regulation, and reduced anxiety. AI expanded possibilities for feedback and low-exposure interaction, but its contribution depended on critical literacy, human verification, and task design. Only a small share of the corpus directly concerned rural or peripheral Latin American schools. Conclusions. Current evidence does not warrant claims of a generalized transformative effect in the target context. It does, however, support the design of low-bandwidth, culturally situated interventions assessed through communicative, affective, and multimodal indicators.
