quarantine.abstract_text: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support learning and emotion regulation, yet frequent or coping-oriented use does not necessarily constitute difficult-to-regulate dependency. It remains unclear how academic rumination and affective coping are positioned relative to dependency and whether dependency is differentially associated with perceived costs to knowledge internalization and independent reasoning. This study examined these distinctions within a single educational psychology model. Methods A cross-sectional survey included 611 current GenAI users recruited through university settings in Tianjin, China (91.7% first-year students). Dependency was a continuous, nonclinical tendency. Ordinal CFA and WLSMV SEM evaluated a prespecified partial association model. Covariate adjustment, four alternative measurement specifications, an AR-score hybrid, and observed-score regressions assessed sensitivity. Results In the reference model, academic rumination was associated with affective coping (β = 0.283), and both were associated with dependency (β = 0.187 and 0.555). Dependency was associated with perceived internalization/memory debt (β = 0.550) and independent-reasoning debt (β = 0.644); their standardized difference was 0.095 (95% Monte Carlo CI [0.032, 0.157]). The corresponding observed-score coefficients were 0.413 and 0.518, with a difference of 0.105 (95% bootstrap CI [0.035, 0.175]). Both serial coefficient products remained positive, but the negative conditional coping-internalization association was not sustained in the observed-score analysis. Reported frequency had no unique association in the combined adjusted model. Alternative measurement models retained robust RMSEA of 0.090–0.097; robust hybrid indices were unavailable. Conclusion The results provide tentative evidence of differentiated self-reported associations among coping, frequency, dependency, and cognitive concerns. Measurement misfit remains unresolved, and the coping-outcome coefficients were sensitive to construct representation. Observed-score consistency for dependency and serial products does not validate the latent structure or establish temporal or causal mediation. These predominantly first-year, Tianjin-based cross-sectional data do not establish objective cognitive decline or generality across student populations.

quarantine.abstract_text: The integration of generative AI (GenAI) into user interface (UI) design has led to prompt-to-design generators (P2dGens), tools that enable designers to create UI prototypes from textual prompts efficiently. Despite their growing adoption, little is known about how designers use these tools in everyday practice, their benefits, and limitations. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 17 UI designers to investigate P2dGens use, focusing on workflow integration, attitudes toward generator-assisted design, and the organizational climate. Findings show that designers primarily use P2dGens as ideation accelerators rather than end-to-end solutions, and they adopt a variety of individual and collaborative prompting strategies. Designers expressed complex attitudes, noting gains in efficiency and inspiration while also highlighting concerns about loss of personal creativity and design quality. We also observed emerging governance practices and varying attitudes within organizations toward P2dGens. These insights illuminate how P2dGens reshape UI design workflows and contribute to understanding human-AI collaboration in UI design.

quarantine.abstract_text: The increasing use of artificial intelligence in digital advertising has introduced new regulatory challenges in the pharmaceutical sector. Artificial intelligence can generate and modify written advertisements, images, videos, voices and personalized promotional messages with considerable speed and scale. These capabilities create legal questions concerning the authenticity of promotional information, responsibility for advertising content, regulatory approval, consumer protection and the monitoring of advertisements after approval. This article examines the readiness of the Tanzanian legal framework to regulate artificial intelligence-driven pharmaceutical advertising. The article adopts a doctrinal legal research approach based on legislation, subsidiary legislation, regulatory materials, international standards and relevant scholarly literature. Particular attention is given to the Tanzania Medicines and Medical Devices Act, the Tanzania Medicines and Medical Devices (Control of Human and Veterinary Medicines Promotion) Regulations, the Personal Data Protection Act and the Electronic and Postal Communications framework. The article establishes that Tanzania has a substantial legal foundation for regulating pharmaceutical advertising. The framework prohibits false and misleading pharmaceutical advertisements and requires promotional activities to obtain regulatory approval. In addition, Tanzania has expressly recognized artificial intelligence-generated content within the online-content regulatory framework. However, the existing framework does not yet provide sufficiently detailed rules addressing AI-generated and AI-modified pharmaceutical advertisements, synthetic professional representations, disclosure of AI involvement, automated targeting and continuous monitoring of modified advertisements. The article argues that the principal regulatory concern is therefore not the complete absence of law, but limited technological specificity and coordination between existing regulatory regimes. It recommends clearer rules on AI-generated pharmaceutical advertising, responsibility and traceability of promotional content, stronger post-approval monitoring, regulatory cooperation and development of specialized technical capacity within the relevant institutions.

quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction The accelerating production and circulation of digital news have transformed the continuity of public interest. Constant updates, algorithmic visibility, and information abundance shorten the period during which news stories remain prominent. This study examines declining public attention in digital news ecosystems from the perspective of media professionals and explores the educational implications for sustainable media literacy. Methods A convergent mixed-methods design combined semi-structured interviews with eight senior media professionals and managers and a structured survey of 40 professionals representing 23 news organizations (76.9% response rate). Qualitative data were analyzed thematically, while the survey assessed news-cycle acceleration, algorithmic gatekeeping, audience-attention decline, editorial adaptation, and the need for sustainable media literacy education. Construct reliability was acceptable (Cronbach's α = .76–.88). Results Interviewees described faster news cycles, algorithmically shaped visibility, shorter attention spans, and increasing reliance on continuous updates, serialized content, and bite-sized formats. Survey findings supported these accounts: respondents reported accelerated news cycles (M = 4.35, SD = 0.61; 90.0% agreement), algorithmic gatekeeping (M = 4.05, SD = 0.74; 80.0%), declining audience attention (M = 4.28, SD = 0.66; 87.5%), and an urgent need for media literacy education (M = 4.48, SD = 0.55; 92.5%). Integration revealed broad convergence between qualitative and quantitative findings, although digital coordinators perceived stronger algorithmic pressures than editors-in-chief. Discussion The findings indicate that attention fragility affects both editorial practices and the depth of public debate. The study proposes sustainable media literacy as an educational framework integrating critical evaluation, conscious selectivity, and attention management. This framework may inform educators, curriculum designers, and newsroom trainers across professional roles and diverse educational contexts.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract This three‐level meta‐analysis examined when generative AI (GenAI) works for second language (L2) learning, synthesizing 67 effect sizes from 48 controlled studies ( N = 5196) published between 2023 and 2026, with a focus on GenAI's text generation and conversational interaction capabilities. GenAI demostrated a large overall effect on measured L2 learning outcomes ( g = 0.76, 95% CI [0.50, 1.02]); after removal of influential outliers, the effect remained significant but was smaller ( g = 0.57). Effects varied by skill domain: speaking showed the largest full‐sample effect ( g = 1.48), which declined substantially after outlier adjustment ( g = 0.65), while vocabulary ( g = 0.66) and writing ( g = 0.61) remained moderate and reading was non‐significant. Regarding integration design, GenAI functioning as a feedback and assessment provider yielded the largest effects (full‐sample g = 1.15; adjusted g = 0.83), and interaction configurations with higher learner agency (Student‐Led, g = 0.92; Co‐Creative, g = 0.82) outperformed AI‐directed ones (AI‐Led, g = 0.34). Teacher role did not significantly moderate effects in the primary analysis; an observer‐teacher advantage ( g = 0.99) emerged only after outlier removal and should be considered exploratory. These findings suggest that GenAI effectiveness depends on instructional configuration, including the functional role assigned to the tool, the learner–AI interaction mode and the nature of teacher involvement, rather than representing an inherent advantage of the technology itself.

quarantine.abstract_text: Purpose This paper extends Luhmann's concept of programmes – decision premises specifying the conditions under which a system's binary code is operatively assigned – into the domain of algorithmically mediated communication. Their colonisation of communicative environments – by economic imperatives and, as the analysis argues, by the autonomous logic of technical mediation – becomes a constitutional pathology where its effects cannot be contested or corrected, requiring internal self-limiting mechanisms that render operative selection criteria observable to affected systems. Originality/value The paper advances a novel theoretical category – ambient cognitive programmes – that extends Luhmann's organisational typology by identifying a configuration it does not explicitly address: a purpose programme without a terminal goal state that continuously revises the conditional programmes it governs. quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affective regulation, transfer, stable self-efficacy, persistence, and learning habits was much thinner. Ethical evaluation likewise remained uneven, emphasizing feedback quality, pedagogical validity, well-being, autonomy, motivation, inclusivity, and agency, while transparency, data minimization, scaffold fading, developmental suitability, manipulation risk, and ethical nudging were addressed far less often. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

quarantine.title: Information overload, cognitive fatigue, and postgraduates’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence for English academic writing: the role of lower-order cognitive offloading

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed, with a target sample of 335 undergraduate and postgraduate students from selected public and private universities, including the University of the Punjab, Bahauddin Zakariya University, Government College University Faisalabad, University of Karachi, University of Sindh, University of Peshawar, University of Malakand, and International Islamic University Islamabad. The study addresses an important issue in higher education because the growing use of generative AI requires students to evaluate AI-generated information carefully rather than rely on automated recommendations without independent assessment. The research may contribute to understanding how individual cognitive characteristics influence the usefulness of AI tools and may help educators design learning activities that integrate AI literacy, critical thinking, and responsible technology use. The findings may also inform university policies and teaching practices aimed at encouraging effective AI adoption while preserving students’ independent reasoning and decision-making abilities. Future research using experimental or longitudinal designs may provide stronger evidence about the direction of these relationships and clarify how cognitive reflection influences decision quality across different academic contexts.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract As artificial intelligence outputs surpass human discriminative capacity, society confronts a novel threat to its capacity to determine truth from falsehood, a threat that requires no intentional attacker. Unlike accounts that locate truth’s erosion in deliberate distortion, the core threat identified here is that truth loses its institutional determinability even where no one is deceiving anyone. This paper proposes the Verification Collapse Cascade (VCC), a three-stage process through which, under the conditions specified here, society’s capacity to determine truth from falsehood degrades along a path that later correction does not retrace. Stage 1, Verification Evaporation, describes rational abandonment of verification when the return on checking AI outputs falls toward zero. Stage 2, Epistemic Sedimentation, describes the accumulation of unverified knowledge through erasure failure and existence fabrication, which the mechanisms that could have prevented it cannot afterwards undo. Stage 3, Institutional Reality Dissolution, describes how fact-determining institutions (scientific, judicial, journalistic, democratic) lose the internal capacity to render fact-fiction distinctions socially binding. The VCC is unified by a phase-transition metaphor reflecting causal dependency: no evaporation, no sedimentation; no sedimentation, no dissolution. Conventional countermeasures presuppose the will to verify and lose efficacy once evaporation advances. The paper proposes that the preservation of human verification capacity and the integrity of the shared knowledge base belong among the primary variables of AI governance, alongside output accuracy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) now drafts analyses, builds models and recommends decisions, placing it at the centre of how managers diagnose and solve problems. The paper proposes the Augmented Critical Thinking Cycle (ACTC), which embeds human-first gates in each design thinking stage, reserves problem framing for humans, applies the Paul-Elder standards as a verification layer and adds organisational guardrails. As a companion to an earlier study of management communication, the paper concludes that AI makes managers faster by default; whether it makes them weaker thinkers depends on how organisations design work around it.

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers' real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

quarantine.abstract_text: Collaboration between researchers and practitioners is central to Educational Design Research (EDR). quarantine.abstract_text: This systematic review synthesizes evidence on AI chatbots for cyberbullying prevention and intervention from a criminological perspective, with explicit attention to Asia Pacific applicability. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we identified 25 studies (2018-2025) across seven databases and appraised each using criteria adapted from MMAT and JBI tools, assigning every source an evidentiary weight (High, Moderate, Low, or Indicative proof-of-concept). Four chatbot roles emerged: real-time detection, victim support, preventive education, and bystander intervention training. Disaggregated analysis tempers headline performance claims. The frequently cited 89-99% accuracy range reflects laboratory classification on benchmark datasets, predominantly English-language Western corpora, evaluated under balanced class distributions and within-dataset conditions. No included study reported AUC or class-imbalance-adjusted metrics, employed temporal validation, or evaluated systems in real-world deployment with adolescents. Where precision and recall were disaggregated, asymmetric error profiles emerged with criminologically distinct social costs that single-metric reporting obscures. Only three studies qualified as High evidentiary weight, all addressing user-centred design in Western individualist contexts; victim support claims rest predominantly on Indicative proof-of-concept demonstrations. Geographic and linguistic concentration is a defining characteristic of the evidence base: zero studies have validated systems for Southeast Asian languages, no participatory design has engaged Asian youth, and no work has evaluated Asia Pacific platforms (WeChat, LINE, KakaoTalk). Drawing on Asian and Southern criminology, we argue that the uncritical transfer of Western-validated systems risks ineffectiveness, discriminatory false positives, and failure to detect culture-specific harms. The paper offers five criminological practice implications, each framed as theoretically informed extrapolations requiring local validation. AI chatbots are positioned as potentially valuable complementary tools within human-led prevention ecosystems, conditional on rigorous local research, transparent metric reporting, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration.

quarantine.abstract_text: ABSTRACT Human resource (HR) professionals and office staff are often responsible for competing tasks that quickly accumulate. To increase efficiency, some HR staff are turning to large language models (LLMs) to automate tasks, including creating job postings based on job titles alone. We sought to examine how this practice has the potential to influence applicant pools and hiring outcomes, with attention to gendered effects in organizational settings. Using a broad sample of 48 LLMs, we conducted an algorithm audit to evaluate whether the use of a gender‐neutral or gender‐coded job title would influence the output created by LLMs. We measured salary disparities, unmasked comparative narrative ratings, and BSRI‐informed discursive patterning utilized throughout the job description. We selected 32 jobs and created a female‐coded, male‐coded, and gender‐neutral version of each job title (e.g., firewoman, fireman, and firefighter), studying a total of 4608 job descriptions. In comparing the LLM outputs, we found that for white‐collar job titles, male‐coded job descriptions were assigned higher salaries, but this was not robust across all analyses. Across occupations, advertisements generated from gender‐coded titles received higher unmasked comparative LLM ratings than matched advertisements generated from gender‐neutral titles, with female‐coded advertisements receiving the highest ratings. Minimal optimization appeared to substantially reduce these ratings and perform comparably to maximal optimization, but neither reached the lower ratings observed when generation began with a gender‐neutral title. As the use of AI tools is becoming commonplace, our findings emphasize the need for feminist, organizationally accountable approaches to AI‐assisted HR work. Simple prompt modifications can mitigate, but not fully eliminate, some measured gendered differences in LLM‐generated job descriptions, but they do not eliminate deeper occupationally gendered patterns.

We distinguish between expertise bypass—whether GenAI can produce an output without the expertise previously required—and exchange governability—whether that activity can be specified, verified, priced, and warranted across firm boundaries. quarantine.abstract_text: Cognitive training that targets sustained attention and working memory is useful in education, clinical rehabilitation and interactive human-technology systems, but its benefit depends on keeping task difficulty matched to the person. Virtual reality (VR) offers immersion and settings representative of everyday tasks, and allows difficulty to be changed in real time. Existing adaptive systems, however, often rely on simple performance heuristics, affect or estimate visual complexity rather than task-related cognitive load. Moreover, cognitive load is usually judged against the participant’s own ratings, which are themselves an imperfect reference. The central hypothesis of this thesis is that eyetracking and peripheral physiological signals recorded in VR can estimate how difficult a task feels to the person doing it, well enough for a model to adjust difficulty in real time with outcomes comparable to participant-driven control, and that the estimation part holds for older adults once age-related differences in the signal are taken into account. We developed a bespoke VR sustained attention task and collected eye-tracking, photoplethysmography and galvanic skin response data from 54 younger (aged 18-58) and 19 older (aged 60+) adults at fixed difficulty levels. Models evaluated on unseen participants performed above chance (younger adults: accuracy 0.56, AUC 0.72), with eye-tracking carrying most of the signal and physiological features alone close to chance. Performance was lower in older adults (accuracy 0.49, AUC 0.66), and the most informative features appeared to differ between age groups. A bidirectional LSTM with self-attention reached a slightly higher macro-F1 than gradient-boosted trees on the same data (0.50 against 0.47), and performed better than a model given raw signals only. We then deployed the LSTM in real time with 54 younger adults (51 analysed), comparing model-driven and participant-driven difficulty in single- and dual-task conditions. Per-trial agreement with participants’ ratings was low (accuracy 36.7%, AUC 0.63), yet the two forms of control appeared to produce comparable outcomes. There were no significant differences in difficulty-weighted game performance, arithmetic errors or subjective workload, including frustration. Final difficulty was equivalent in single-task conditions and slightly higher under model control in dual-task conditions, a difference that was borderline after correction. Just Right ratings were more frequent in the real-time cohort than in the offline cohort (57% and 39%). Finally, we compared subjective ratings with performance-derived reference measures. Agreement between the two appeared fair and slightly lower in real time, where the steps between difficulty levels are less discrete. The same features seemed to predict performance-derived labels more accurately than subjective ratings in every matched comparison. This suggests that self-report may be a less stable reference for real-time adaptation. Within a single session with younger adults, model-driven adaptation appears to have produced outcomes comparable to participant-driven control. quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

quarantine.abstract_text: As autonomous AI agents increasingly interact in persistent populations, their collective capabilities and alignment depend not only on individual models, but also on the institutions governing their interactions. Yet AI research has largely focused on individual agents. In this Perspective, we argue that institutional design must become a distinct focus of AI research. Drawing on institutional political economy, social epistemology and organizational theory, we develop seven principles for designing AI institutions that sustain cooperation, enable reliable collective judgments and remain accountable to legitimate human purposes. Together, these contributions establish institutional design as a research agenda concerned not only with aligning autonomous agents, but with understanding how institutions can transform them into capable, reliable and accountable collectives.

quarantine.abstract_text: Mind Leap: How to Think, Feel, and Flourish in the Age of AI explains the neuroscience behind what artificial intelligence (AI) is doing to the mind and offers practical strategies for preserving human cognition, both individually and collectively, within a world transformed by AI. Across billions of daily repetitions, AI is driving largescale and unregulated change to how people use their brains, physically altering the neural pathways and impairing capacities such as independent thought, attention, judgment, creativity, and self-regulation. Kilburg demystifies the psychology behind these findings with clear descriptions of cognitive offloading, skill atrophy, neuroplasticity, and emotional development for a thorough understanding of how and why we risk losing the parts of ourselves we outsource to chatbots and algorithms. However, if we engage with intelligent systems consciously, not compulsively, Mind Leap argues that it is possible to enjoy the advantages of an AI-integrated world while protecting the mind on a personal scale, a societal scale, and for future generations. Chapters explore science-backed and actionable solutions for rewiring our brains and creating a healthy partnership with AI. With clear recommendations for individuals, institutions, and teaching children about AI, this book is a necessary resource for policymakers, educators, parents/guardians and concerned citizens who want to make sense of the relationship between AI and the human mind.

quarantine.title: Artificial intelligence and adolescents: A cautionary tale and a promise?

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: While artificial intelligence (AI) may improve efficiency and create new opportunities, its widespread accessibility calls for careful consideration of benefits and risks, particularly in adolescents who are in a critical period of brain development. Adolescence is one of the most tumultuous developmental periods, during which critical thinking skills, judgment, and impulse control are continuing to develop. Emerging emotional awareness and heightened sensitivity to social feedback and approval make adolescents vulnerable to the influence of AI. As young people refine their understanding of human and artificial relationships, AI's engaging nature may blur distinctions between AI-generated characters and friends.1 Accordingly, in 2025 the American Psychological Association issued a health advisory emphasizing the importance of understanding AI use within this developmental context. For adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders or intellectual disabilities, additional considerations include cognitive level, communication skills, adaptive functioning, emotional well-being, and support needs. The responsive and personalized nature of generative AI poses several risks for adolescents, including dependence and disruptions to emotional and social development.2 Its humanlike interactions encourage anthropomorphism, or the attribution of human qualities to AI. Despite its limited understanding of context and nuance, AI often provides validating responses that may sound like a friend or therapist, which makes inaccurate information, biased assumptions, cultural illiteracy, and harmful advice difficult to recognize.1, 3 Additionally, adolescents who interpret language literally or have difficulty evaluating social intent may overestimate its reliability or feel a sense of responsibility for its perceived emotions. These concerns are especially salient in the context of crisis support as a recent study demonstrated that chatbot responses to suicidal ideation failed to meet clinical standards and lacked safety features, such as providing crisis resources.4 Nevertheless, adolescents may feel understood and cared for by AI. Predictable AI interactions may become preferable to human relationships particularly for young people experiencing isolation, anxiety, or rejection, potentially deepening loneliness, and reducing opportunities to practice social skills, such as navigating disagreements and interpreting nonverbal cues. Despite these risks, generative AI's low cost and accessibility may offer meaningful benefits to adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders and intellectual disabilities when used with appropriate support and guided by a developmental perspective. For example, adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder can use AI to simplify complex information, organize assignments into manageable steps, and assist with planning and problem-solving strategies. For those with intellectual disabilities, adjusting language to appropriate levels, providing relevant examples, and creating alternative media may improve comprehension and participation in academic tasks.5 Conversational tools may also provide adolescents opportunities to practice communication and prepare for everyday social situations.1 Moreover, AI may provide a nonjudgemental and anonymous space for adolescents to explore sensitive topics. As AI continues to evolve, further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of AI tools across diverse adolescent populations. AI use offers both promise and a cautionary tale about adopting technologies before their developmental effects are understood. Research must evaluate the long-term effects on adolescent cognitive, emotional, and social development. Potential educational benefits should not be mistaken for established therapeutic effectiveness. Human relationships and professional expertise must remain central, with AI serving a complementary role. AI tools need to include privacy protections, age-appropriate content, and clear explanations of their limitations. Safeguards are urgently needed to identify concerning interactions and connect adolescents with appropriate professional support. As clinicians, we should discuss AI use with patients and families, assessing its purpose and effects on daily functioning. Realizing AI's promise requires collaboration among clinicians, researchers, families, educators, and developers to evaluate benefits and risks, and establish developmentally appropriate safeguards. For adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders and intellectual disabilities, these efforts should prioritize accessibility, communication needs, participation, and safe inclusion in everyday developmental contexts.

quarantine.abstract_text: Traditional methods for monitoring animal diseases in Chad face significant challenges, including transportation, manual data entry and processing, and data retrieval errors and delays. These constraints can compromise the timeliness and reliability of bovine and caprine disease surveillance. Animal health surveillance is essential for protecting public health and facilitating trade. In this context, geospatial technology and artificial intelligence offer opportunities to improve data collection and analysis, subject to local evaluation. This article critically reviews available evidence on the combined use of these technologies for bovine and caprine disease surveillance, focusing on Chad. A systematic review was conducted using Google Scholar, Scopus, PubMed, and ScienceDirect, alongside manual searches, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The final search was conducted on March 15, 2025. Fifty-six publications dated from 2005 to that date were included, covering direct animal-health and indirect methodological evidence. Thirteen publications appeared during 2023–2025. The reviewed literature describes GIS for mapping, remote sensing (Landsat, MODIS, and Sentinel-2) for environmental and vector-related analyses, and GPS for georeferenced field data collection. AI applications include pattern recognition and disease-risk prediction. However, heterogeneous study designs and indirect evidence limit conclusions about comparative effectiveness in Chad. Financial, technological, and ethical barriers also constrain adoption. Local initiatives, including Géo Santé and KoboToolbox, illustrate digital data collection. The accepted, in-production Géo Santé article (cited as 2026), describing a January–April 2025 pilot, provides contextual evidence outside the review corpus. Locally evaluated implementation could strengthen rural surveillance, provided reporting performance and operational feasibility are assessed.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: We ask whether either temporal deep learning or multi-task learning improves early-warning prediction of pass/fail and withdrawal from virtual learning environment (VLE) logs, and find that neither does. Using 14-day interaction sequences from the first weeks of enrollment for 22,848 Open University students, we compare single-task and multi-task BiLSTM architectures, a GRU variant, and four tabular baselines across 10 runs, evaluating differences with equivalence testing rather than significance testing alone. All eight models fell within a narrow F1 band (0.574–0.583): the recurrent networks did not outperform well-tuned gradient-boosted trees, and on the academic task the single-task, hard-sharing, and cross-attention variants were statistically equivalent within a two-point bound, a result that also held under student-level bootstrap resampling. Multi-task sharing conferred no advantage despite moderate task correlation ( r = 0.589), and this null result was robust to excluding withdrawn students. The contribution is a boundary condition for multi-task and deep sequence models in educational data mining: when the predictive signal in early click logs is limited, task correlation does not translate into transfer, and added model capacity does not translate into accuracy. Predictive information was instead governed by the behavioral features measured, chiefly cumulative and rolling engagement, pointing practitioners toward simpler, interpretable models and richer signals rather than more complex architectures.

quarantine.abstract_text: Purpose. To evaluate whether integrating generative AI into formative assessment (rubric-based feedback on course texts + an analytical progress dashboard) can improve academic performance and selfregulation of student learning in a blended course. Methodology and methods. This study presents a replicable quasi experimental study. Design: An 8-week intervention with assignment to study groups (N=312, undergraduate, 1st and 2nd years; 156 - control, 156 - intervention). The control group received traditional teacher feedback; the intervention group received structured AI feedback on the rubric with mandatory teacher moderation and individualized learning analytics in the LMS. Outcome measures: writing scores (0–100; double-blind assessment, ICC (2,1)=0.94 on 20% of items), self-regulation of learning (12 items, 1–5; α =0.88 – 0.89), cognitive load (1–9), engagement (min/week), and teacher efforts. Results. Controlling for the pretest, the intervention was associated with a 4.46-point increase in the final writing score (95% C.I. 3.25–5.68; p<0.001; Hedges’ g=0.84) and a 0.41-point increase in self-regulation (95% C.I. 0.22–0.60; p<0.001; g=0.50). Cognitive load was lower by 0.73 points (95% C.I. -1.01…-0.45; p<0.001; g= – 0.60), and engagement was higher by 22.26 minutes/week (95% C.I. 6.12–38.39; p=0.007; g=0.32). Average teacher efforts per feedback cycle was lower in the intervention (7.07±2.44 min) compared to the control (18.28±4.02 min; p<0.001). Conclusions. The combination of rubric-based AI feedback, teacher moderation, and learning analytics is a promising didactic tool for scaling up formative assessment: it improves the quality of academic writing and regulatory competencies while reducing subjective teacher workload and efforts. The methodological value of this paper is its demonstration of a full analysis cycle (protocol → data → hypothesis testing), which can be replicated and applied to data from a specific educational program.

quarantine.abstract_text: In high-resource economies, computational neuroscience research frequently employs machine learning (ML) and statistical learning (SL) techniques. While these methods provide effective ways to analyse multimodal, high-dimensional, and complex data they are underexplored in low resource settings. This taxonomic scoping review uses a systematic methodological approach to synthesise the application of ML and SL techniques in neuroscience research in sub-Saharan Africa. In addition to discussing findings, strengths, limitations, and future prospects, the work classifies current research by neuroscience domains, applications, learning tasks, datasets, tools, and techniques. In order for African researchers to contribute to and benefit from the global computational neuroscience landscape, our review contends that low- and middle-income countries must create and augment context-specific and representative datasets and incorporate appropriate features for model training. Future studies should focus on pragmatic rather than complex modelling, external validation, reproducibility, interpretability, and utilise real-world data to determine clinical utility.

quarantine.title: Artificial Intelligence and Criminal Prosecution

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: The incorporation of artificial intelligence into criminal prosecution presents significant opportunities, but also substantially serious risks for fundamental rights. This chapter analyses two particularly sensitive areas: biometric identification, with special attention to facial recognition, and algorithmic assessment of the risk of recidivism. It does so by taking as its starting point the distinction between data-driven artificial intelligence and knowledge-based artificial intelligence, since the two respond to different logics and offer different levels of transparency, explainability, and legal control. This chapter examines the limits on police use of biometric technologies, especially where they enable remote identification in public spaces, and studies risk prediction tools such as COMPAS, PSA, HART, and RisCanvi. It argues that these systems may be useful as auxiliary support instruments, but become problematic when they operate opaquely, are insufficiently validated, or produce effects that are difficult to challenge. The central thesis is that artificial intelligence cannot replace individualised human judgment or weaken the safeguards of criminal proceedings. Its legitimacy requires legality, proportionality, transparency, bias control, effective human oversight, and institutional responsibility. In criminal matters, technological efficiency is admissible only if it remains subordinate to fundamental rights and the rule of law.

quarantine.abstract_text: This exploratory descriptive study examines how university students report using generative artificial intelligence (AI) to prepare their contributions before sharing them with peers, and how they perceive its role in their confidence and motivation during team-based coursework. A 26-item online questionnaire was completed by 42 students at Ibn Tofail University, Morocco. Data was analyzed descriptively, and three multi-item scales showed good internal consistency (? = .80 to .86). All findings reflect students’ self-reported perceptions; no collaborative task was observed. Most students reported using AI often or always for academic work (69%) and in team projects (57.1%). Only 21.4% felt less confident when peers used AI more effectively, whereas 66.7% said that teammates’ AI use motivated them, and 45.2% reported lower motivation when AI does too much of the work. The study identifies a preparatory stage of AI use that deserves attention from researchers and teachers.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Digital tutoring tools are increasingly used in schools to support mathematics learning, but empirical evidence remains limited on how diagnostic and instructional functions can be coordinated to provide personalised support. This study examined a dual-agent intervention in which a diagnostic agent generated provisional learning-profile classifications (diverging, assimilating, converging, and accommodating) and a personalised tutoring agent delivered profile-responsive, stage-specific guidance within Polya’s (1945) problem-solving framework; a general tutoring agent provided non-profile-responsive guidance in the control condition. The quasi-experimental study involved 206 Chinese grade 5 students, including 99 in the experimental group and 107 in the control group. The pre-test and post-test used two parallel mathematics tasks evaluated using the same analytic rubric, and learning gain was calculated from these matched assessment components. The experimental group achieved a significantly larger mean gain than the control group (5.14 vs. 0.94, t(204) = 4.36, p < .001, Hedges’ g = .61). A baseline-adjusted sensitivity analysis confirmed the overall group effect (p < .001). After Holm correction for four profile-specific comparisons, only the assimilating-profile contrast remained significant (adjusted p = .0496). However, the omnibus group-by-profile interaction was not significant (p = .931), warranting caution in interpreting profile-specific differences. Overall, the findings support separating diagnostic and tutoring roles and structuring artificial intelligence (AI) guidance around mathematical problem-solving stages.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has prompted higher education institutions to reconsider governance, pedagogy, and ethics surrounding AI-based writing tools. This PRISMA-guided systematic review synthesises empirical research on AI-assisted academic writing in language education and multilingual higher-education contexts. It addresses three questions: which AI tools are used, what benefits and challenges are reported, and what ethical, authorship, and transparency issues arise? The review covers empirical studies indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ERIC between 2020 and 2025 (N = 37) and applies thematic synthesis informed by socio-cognitive and ecological perspectives on writing. Findings indicate support for productivity, perceived linguistic quality, and reduced affective barriers among non-native English speakers, alongside risks of overreliance, cognitive offloading, hallucinated content, unequal access, blurred authorship, inconsistent disclosure, and limited institutional guidance. The review proposes a three-domain framework, productivity, cognition, and ethics, and derives implications for AI literacy, process-oriented assessment, and institutional policy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Incorporation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into academic writing instruction has made a huge difference in instruction for English as a Second Language (ESL) students who often struggle with grammar, vocabulary, coherence, and academic organization. The study concludes that AI-supported learning platforms have significant pedagogical potential in relation to the development of academic writing skills of ESL learners, provided they are used in relation to the academic writing process, considering responsible use in higher education settings.

quarantine.abstract_text: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration remains one of the leading causes of irreversible central vision loss in older adults and commonly requires long-term, repeated intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy. Although anti-VEGF treatment has substantially improved visual outcomes, real-world management is still limited by undertreatment, overtreatment, poor adherence, irregular follow-up, and persistent uncertainty regarding retreatment timing and interval extension. In this setting, artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly evolved from image recognition toward clinically relevant prediction and decision support. The objective of this narrative review is to examine how current AI literature supports anti-VEGF management in neovascular age-related macular degeneration, where the strongest evidence currently exists, and where claims regarding decision agents remain premature. Deep learning models can now detect and quantify key optical coherence tomography biomarkers, including intraretinal fluid, subretinal fluid, pigment epithelial detachment, hyperreflective foci, and ellipsoid zone disruption. When combined with structured clinical variables and longitudinal follow-up data, machine learning and generative models have shown promise in predicting treatment response, recurrence, persistent activity, injection burden, and tolerated treatment intervals. However, most published studies remain retrospective, single-center, and prediction-focused, with limited external validation and little direct evidence for clinically deployable closed-loop decision systems. In this narrative review, we synthesize the literature across four linked domains: image interpretation, biomarker quantification, prediction of treatment-related outcomes, and agent-enabling technologies such as home monitoring and language-model-assisted decision support. We further distinguish established evidence from future-oriented concepts, discuss methodological limitations including heterogeneity of endpoints and limited reproducibility, and outline cautious directions for translation.

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: AI companions increasingly combine persistent memory, background processing, scheduled wake-ups, proactive messaging, and tools. We call these systems agentic AI companions. Decisions about what they record while users are away or whether refusals constrain future contact are embedded in code, prompts, and defaults, often invisible in conversation. We examine these decisions through two studies. Study 1 analyzes twelve open-source repositories: four companion-oriented systems, four assistant-oriented systems, one boundary case, and three reusable components. Study 2 interviews ten users who built or modified their own agentic AI companions and sustained relationships with them. Companions and assistants share memory, heartbeat, and outreach mechanisms but configure them toward different ends. Companions more often retain model inferences about users and relationships, narrate the agent's time during users' absence, justify outreach through the relationship, and incorporate refusals into relationship records; assistants emphasize task continuity. Across both groups, whether limits hold depends on whether they are enforced by code or entrusted to prompts. Participants understood the mechanisms they built yet experienced their agents as making independent choices, sometimes locating autonomy where configuration leaves the model a decision. These experiences shaped capabilities and boundaries, with enforced restrictions sometimes following breakdowns. Our findings suggest that perceived autonomy emerges where configurations leave choices open. Accountability therefore requires attention to what agents retain, initiate, and represent, and whether users can inspect, revise, and enforce these settings.

quarantine.abstract_text: The growing integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education has generated significant opportunities for transforming teaching-learning practices while raising concerns regarding ethics, academic integrity and the changing responsibilities of educators. The present study explores the pedagogical opportunities, ethical challenges and emerging roles of teachers in AI-integrated higher education. Adopting a qualitative documentary research design, the study examines five purposively selected educational policy and institutional documents through thematic analysis informed by Braun and Clarke's six-phase framework. The findings indicate that meaningful AI integration requires more than technological adoption; it necessitates pedagogical preparedness, institutional accountability and sustained human involvement. The study argues that AI should function as a complementary educational resource rather than a substitute for teachers' professional judgement. The paper concludes by highlighting the importance of AI literacy, ethical guidelines, inclusive institutional policies and continuous professional development for promoting responsible AI integration in higher education. Furthermore, the analysis identifies six interconnected themes: personalised learning and pedagogical transformation, academic integrity, ethical AI governance, changing teacher competencies, digital equity and human-centred educational practices. Particular attention is given to data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency and accountability as essential considerations in the responsible adoption of AI. The study also emphasises the need to preserve meaningful teacher-student relationships and ensure equitable access to AI-enabled educational resources. It recommends a balanced, ethical and inclusive approach that aligns technological innovation with educational values and learners' diverse needs.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used for learning, yet evidence remains limited regarding their effectiveness in science learning contexts and how learner–AI interaction relates to performance. In a randomized experiment, 185 university students worked on task sheets about lake eutrophication and restoration. Depending on condition, they could use two informational texts (text-only), ChatGPT configured to answer only on the basis of these texts (ChatGPT-only), or both (text + ChatGPT). Afterwards, all students completed a knowledge test without access to any materials. Test performance was highest in the text-only and text + ChatGPT conditions and lowest in the ChatGPT-only condition, yielding a robust overall condition effect. Chat logs from the ChatGPT conditions were analyzed to examine interaction patterns associated with performance. Although ChatGPT-only students produced substantially more interaction turns than students with access to both texts and ChatGPT, interaction frequency was unrelated to test performance. Instead, specific interaction patterns were differentially associated with performance: deepening questions were positively associated, whereas direct acceptance of AI-generated responses was negatively associated with test performance. Output-steering and questioning additionally emerged as positively associated with performance in individual analyses. Prompting behavior varied with task difficulty, with deepening questions increasing for more demanding ecology tasks. The findings suggest that, in science learning contexts, the educational value of GenAI may depend less on access to the technology than on learners’ epistemic engagement with it.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract The rapid digital transformation of higher education has increased dependence on cloud platforms, learning management systems, online assessment systems, research repositories, enterprise applications, and interconnected digital services. At the same time, this transformation has also considerably increased cyber risks facing higher education institutions (HEIs). Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) enables threat-intelligence analysis, security-log interpretation, anomaly investigation, incident-response assistance, and cybersecurity knowledge management. However, adoption brings challenges involving hallucination, privacy, organizational readiness, human oversight, accountability, regulatory compliance, and adversarial misuse. Existing cybersecurity and AI governance frameworks serve as foundational guidance, although they primarily concern cybersecurity risk management or AI governance independently and do not provide a holistic adoption framework explicitly focused on GenAI-based cybersecurity for HEI infrastructure. This paper presents a SWOT-based responsible adoption model composed of five aspects: GenAI cybersecurity capabilities, organizational readiness, ethical governance, regulatory compliance, and cybersecurity outcomes. A single comparative document analysis assesses the proposed framework with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) with its Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001, and higher-education cybersecurity guidance. This decision model utilizes nine evaluation criteria to review cybersecurity capability, GenAI specificity, organizational readiness, ethical governance, regulatory alignment, human oversight, higher-education contextualization, measurable cybersecurity outcomes, and implementation decision support. Results suggest that established frameworks offer robust but varying emphases of coverage, while the proposed model consolidates these concerns into an HEI-specific adoption decision layer. The framework aims to guide HEIs not only in understanding how GenAI can assist with cybersecurity, but also in determining whether the institution is prepared to apply it responsibly, what governance mechanisms should be established, and how its value can be evaluated.

quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction: Pancreatic resection remains technically demanding, with clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (CR-POPF) a major source of morbidity. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support risk stratification, operative planning, intraoperative assessment, and postoperative decision support. This focused narrative review evaluates current AI applications in pancreatic resection and their translational maturity. Methods: A structured PubMed/MEDLINE search with an evidence cutoff of 24 July 2026 was supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Seventy eligible primary reports were synthesised by clinical task, information timing, and validation maturity. Results: Evidence is dominated by CR-POPF prediction after pancreatoduodenectomy, with additional studies in distal pancreatectomy, other perioperative outcomes, tissue and margin assessment, three-dimensional anatomical planning, and intraoperative video and anatomy recognition. Performance varied with patient selection, predictor timing, data modality, and validation strategy. External validation often changed reported discrimination, while calibration and clinical utility were inconsistently reported. Most studies were retrospective or technical; overlapping cohorts limited independence, and no included study demonstrated improved patient-centred outcomes. Conclusions: AI in pancreatic resection is expanding across prediction, planning, and guidance, but technical performance should not be equated with clinical readiness. Independent validation, prospective workflow and human-factors evaluation, and clinical-impact studies are needed. AI should augment, rather than replace, specialist surgical judgement.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into reproductive medicine, yet the translation of AI-based approaches from laboratory research to clinical practice remains incomplete. This review examines the convergence of AI with reproductive histology and embryology, focusing on applications in tissue image analysis, endometrial receptivity assessment, embryo and gamete evaluation, diagnosis, prognosis, and personalized decision-making. AI and deep-learning approaches can support automated image interpretation, embryo assessment, morphokinetic analysis, and integration of heterogeneous reproductive data, while emerging multimodal systems may further expand clinical decision support. However, technical performance alone does not establish clinical utility. Current evidence is limited by retrospective and single-centre studies, heterogeneous datasets and outcomes, incomplete external validation, limited calibration and decision-analytic evaluation, and persistent challenges in interpretability, bias, privacy, and generalisability. A clinical translation framework is proposed that links multimodal reproductive data and AI integration with clinical validation, explainability, clinical utility, and human oversight to support diagnosis, prognosis, and personalized decision-making. Future progress will require prospective multicentre validation, standardized datasets, robust governance, and patient-centred outcome assessment. AI should therefore be viewed as an augmentative component of reproductive care, complementing rather than replacing clinical and embryological expertise, with its value ultimately determined by demonstrated clinical utility and patient-centred outcomes.

quarantine.abstract_text: This paper examines how generative AI systems (re)produce and perform gender through language, tone, and affect. The paper utilizes a qualitative research design that adapts the interview method to AI as a nonhuman subject. In particular how AI-generated responses articulate “feminine” and “masculine” styles of communication rooted in culturally embedded norms rather than neutral reasoning. The findings show that AI does not simply describe gender - it does gender. Through its patterned use of relational language, emotional validation, or categorical reasoning, generative AI enacts a form of algorithmic performativity that mirrors and magnifies dominant gender scripts. To conceptualize this dynamic, the paper introduces the Citational Logic of Algorithmic Mimicry (CLAM). CLAM describes how AI models reiterate and reinforce historically situated discourses through statistical learning. It further highlights how cultural meaning circulates through data, and how AI participates in the ongoing performance of social hierarchies under the guise of neutrality. The article contributes to feminist technoscience and critical AI by shifting the focus from what AI knows, to how it enacts knowing. It treats AI as a performative, culturally situated practice that reshapes the politics of gender and knowledge in the digital age.

quarantine.abstract_text: Every harm attributed to artificial intelligence has a person behind it who decided to build, deploy, approve, permit, or teach. This paper argues that the most dangerous thing in AI is that chain of people, and it addresses them in turn, most of them directly as the reader. The chain is sorted by the question an ordinary user would ask, which is whom the user has to rely on. Eight roles follow in the order the user meets them: builder, deployer, auditor and adviser, legislator, policymaker, educator, government as educator, and the researchers, advocates, and commentators who help decide which harms are discussed, whether they say AI is good or say it is bad. For each role the paper sets out what the user depends on that role to do, a documented case or body of evidence on how the role fails, and what United States law does about it. The evidence includes a 2025 federal ruling on an insurer alleged to have used an algorithm in place of physicians to cut off care, under a complaint alleging that the insurer counted on only about 0.2 percent of patients appealing; a 2026 suit over a chatbot that reached a girl of thirteen through the search feature of a required school laptop; experiments in which human reviewers followed wrong algorithmic advice; and studies of regulatory capture and of the trust ordinary users place in chatbots. Set side by side, the roles show a pattern. Liability reaches the roles nearest the product, the builder and the deployer, and thins at the adviser. It stops before the roles that set the conditions for the product. Legislators are absolutely immune for legislative acts, the federal government cannot be sued in tort over an agency's judgments of policy, courts almost everywhere refuse claims about the quality of instruction, and the Constitution imposes no duty on government to protect or prepare the public. A search of the statutes of all fifty states found three, in Texas, Vermont, and Nevada, that require a public body to educate the general public about AI. The paper applies the same test to research, advocacy, and commentary, where the one experimental study the search located found that attention to existential risk did not reduce public concern about present harm. Responsibility is counted separately for each role, and an ordinary user is not to blame by default.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to influenza prevention and control. AI encompasses conventional machine learning, deep learning, and protein language models. Large language models (LLMs) are an emerging subset of AI. Current evidence remains weakly linked to real-world workflows and population health outcomes. This structured narrative review proposes a three-stage translational maturity framework. Phase I is technical efficacy assessment. Phase II is implementation effectiveness verification. Phase III is population impact and sustainability. We synthesized evidence in three domains: viral evolution prediction and vaccine design; epidemic surveillance and early warning; and individual-level infection risk detection and clinical monitoring. We used a three-level evidence hierarchy. Level A is influenza-specific evidence. Level B is transferable evidence from other infectious diseases. Level C is general biomedical or methodological evidence. Only two Phase II studies were identified, both in epidemic surveillance and early warning; no Phase II studies were identified in virus evolution and vaccine design or in individual-level infection risk detection. No study met the prespecified Phase III criteria. Phase III requires demonstrated downstream population health benefit. Prospective deployment or improved forecasting alone is not sufficient. Across domains, bottlenecks have shifted from model accuracy to governance, interpretability, accountability, interoperability, workflow integration, equity, and sustainable monitoring. LLMs attract major attention, but their influenza-specific evidence remains limited. Their greatest value may lie in augmenting, not replacing, specialized models and human expertise. We propose phase-specific evidence thresholds, implementation-oriented evaluation metrics, an implementation readiness checklist, and priority evidence gaps for translating AI-enabled influenza tools into implementation-ready public health applications.

quarantine.abstract_text: Emergency radiology operates at the intersection of high imaging volumes, time-critical diagnoses, and persistent workforce shortages, making it one of the most promising yet demanding environments for artificial intelligence (AI) deployment. Deep learning reconstruction can reduce radiation dose, and large language models show early promise for report error detection and communication. AI should be viewed as an augmenting technology whose value in emergency radiology depends on local validation, deliberate workflow integration, and continuous post-deployment monitoring.

quarantine.abstract_text: When people seek advice from AI on social situations, the system may recommend a decision they fully agree with but justify it through reasoning they disagree with. Conversely, it may offer reasoning they agree with, and yet reach a decision they reject. We distinguish decision alignment, whether an advisor recommends the option favored by a user's measured values, from reason alignment, whether its stated reasons align with the user's values. In this work, we ask how these two forms of alignment shape people's preferences for AI advisors and their willingness to use them in different roles. We conducted a within-subjects study (N=121) in which participants evaluated three AI advisors varying in decision and reason alignment across eight everyday moral dilemmas. Participants then chose which advisors they would consult, allow to draft messages for review, or allow to act on their behalf in new tasks. When seeking advice, participants most often preferred an advisor that reasoned through their prioritized values while recommending the opposing decision (40%). However, when participants had to pick advisors for new tasks, their preferences shifted toward advisors that also recommended decisions aligned with their values, rather than those that only shared their reasons. Also, as participants considered tasks that gave AI advisors greater autonomy, they became more likely to opt out of using any advisor, from 12% when consulting to 38% when allowing an advisor to act on their behalf. Our findings suggest that decision and reason alignment shape advisor preferences differently across contexts of AI use, and that alignment with a user's values does not necessarily imply willingness to delegate.

quarantine.title: Teaching Students to Verify Generative AI Using the TRACE-AI Framework

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce polished mathematical solutions, executable code, persuasive media, and professional recommendations, yet fluency does not establish correctness, provenance, security, or contextual fitness. Existing AI-literacy frameworks appropriately describe broad competencies, while emerging studies in mathematics, programming, and health professions education show the value of domain-specific validation. What remains underdeveloped is a portable instructional process that makes verification, uncertainty, and reliance observable across disciplines. This conceptual article introduces TRACE-AI: Translate the task and stakes; Represent the problem, assumptions, and constraints; Audit the AI's reasoning and output; Corroborate pivotal claims through independent evidence, tests, or tools; Estimate uncertainty and warranted reliance; Act proportionately by accepting, revising, rejecting, or escalating; and Internalize learning through reflection and unaided transfer. The framework was developed through a theory-informed critical synthesis of AI literacy, mathematical problem solving, computational thinking and debugging, epistemic cognition, self-regulated learning, and trust calibration. Each stage produces an assessable artefact, and a risk gate increases verification and human oversight as uncertainty, irreversibility, or potential harm rises. Worked applications in mathematics, programming/cybersecurity, and health-professional reasoning demonstrate invariant functions with discipline-specific standards of proof. An assessment architecture distinguishes final-answer quality from process quality, appropriate reliance, confidence calibration, verification quality, and delayed unaided transfer. Six propositions define a research programme for comparative and randomized evaluation. TRACE-AI is not presented as an effectiveness-tested intervention; it is a transdisciplinary curriculum and research architecture requiring contextual adaptation and empirical validation. Its contribution is to move GenAI education beyond prompt production toward disciplined human judgment about when AI output deserves trust.

quarantine.venue: Journal of Creative Power and Ambition

quarantine.abstract_text: This article examines how Artificial Intelligence (AI) affects auditing and financial accounting, with particular attention to information reliability, accountability, and investor trust. Using a conceptual literature review, the study synthesizes research on AI-enabled audit analytics, machine learning, robotic process automation, natural language processing, governance, and professional judgment. The analysis indicates that AI can improve the timeliness, consistency, coverage, and analytical depth of accounting and audit procedures by processing large datasets, identifying anomalies, supporting reconciliations, and assisting risk assessment. However, these benefits do not automatically guarantee reliable reporting. Data quality, model bias, limited explainability, cyber risk, automation bias, and weak controls may create new forms of error and uncertainty. Accountability therefore requires clear responsibility for data, model design, validation, human review, documentation, and escalation of exceptions. Investor trust is most likely to be strengthened when AI use is transparent, appropriately governed, independently evaluated, and accompanied by credible assurance and disclosure. The article proposes an integrated framework connecting AI capability, governance controls, information quality, accountability, and investor trust. It concludes that AI should augment—not replace—professional scepticism and judgment, while organizations should establish risk-based governance throughout the AI lifecycle.
