publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) challenges the validity of written assessment in legal education by weakening the relationship between submitted coursework and students’ individual legal reasoning. This article argues that generative AI should be understood not primarily as a problem of academic integrity, but as a stress test for assessment validity. Drawing on a practitioner-led, design-based study of a first year module addressing business law, it examines an assessment redesign that made AI use mandatory and transparent. Students were required to evaluate, challenge and substantiate AI outputs using authoritative legal sources, with marks awarded solely for evaluative judgment, legal reasoning and source use. The article conceptualises generative AI as an epistemic artefact that can foreground engagement with legal authority, provides an empirical account of AI-inclusive formative and summative assessment, and proposes a transferable model informed by constructive alignment, transparency and ethical engagement. The findings suggest that regulated AI use can support the assessment of legal reasoning while reducing integrity concerns. The central challenge posed by generative AI, therefore, concerns what assessments can validly measure rather than misconduct alone.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence is being built at an extraordinary pace. But by whom, and for whom? As AI systems increasingly shape how people work, think, and are governed, the world has quietly slipped into treating citizens as consumers: recipients of decisions made elsewhere, rather than participants in making them. Citizen 5.0 confronts this shift directly. David Galipeau argues that the defining question of the AI era is not technological. It is human. Will citizens have a genuine seat in decisions that determine the future of labor, data, and cognition? Or will that future be decided unilaterally by a handful of technology companies? Drawing on rigorous, interdisciplinary research, the book builds a concrete framework for restoring citizens, not consumers, to the center of the AI era. It includes neurorights, data sovereignty, and a Synthetic Labor Tax that could reshape who owns the value AI creates. This is a precise, urgent case for reclaiming human agency before the future is built without us.

quarantine.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Transformations, Empirical Evidence and Challenges for Student-Centred University Learning

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: The rapid evolution and integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, particularly following the advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative AI (GenAI), have profoundly transformed teaching, learning and management practices in higher education worldwide. This paper aims to synthesise the empirical evidence available between 2020 and 2026 regarding the impact of AI in higher education, examining the prevalent technologies, pedagogical mediation, levels of human–AI collaboration, adoption patterns and ethical-normative implications. A systematic literature review was conducted in rigorous accordance with the PRISMA 2020 Statement. Six international scientific databases were consulted: Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, SciELO, PubMed and IEEE Xplore, identifying an initial corpus of 1,247 records. After the screening process for duplicates, title/abstract and full-text reading, 45 primary studies focused on university educational impact were selected, analytically complemented by global bibliometric and meta-systematic reviews of the period. Methodological quality was assessed using the MMAT (2018) tool and the certainty of the evidence via the GRADE approach. It is concluded that the predominant AI technologies in the literature are large language models (75.6 %), intelligent tutoring systems (31.1 %) and learning analytics tools (24.4 %). The principal applications concentrate on personalised learning (53.3 %), student motivation and engagement (46.7 %) and academic performance (42.2 %). However, evaluation of the autonomy continuum reveals a severe implementation gap: 45.56 % of integrations correspond to Substitution modalities (where AI replaces teaching functions), 39.05 % to Augmentation, 10.65 % to Toolification and only 4.73 % achieve genuine Human–AI Synergy. Longitudinally, student adoption reached near-universal levels (95 % in 2026), although gaps in ethical literacy and tensions surrounding academic integrity persist. The methodological quality of the corpus was high in 62.2 % of the studies, yet the global GRADE certainty was classified as low owing to the predominance of cross-sectional designs and heterogeneity of metrics. It may further be concluded that AI possesses a proven transformative potential to optimise university learning, yet its effectiveness does not reside in mere technological adoption, but rather in intentional pedagogical mediation (the PMAISE model), the evolution of teaching practice towards the AI-TPACK framework and the establishment of executable governance policies (Policy-as-Code). A human-centred integration framework based on four pillars and a five-phase operational strategy with a detailed matrix of success indicators for institutional scalability is proposed.

quarantine.title: The linguistic adaptation gap: connecting multilingual AI policy to climate early warning in South Asia

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract National artificial-intelligence strategies and climate-adaptation plans are expanding at the same time, yet they are rarely studied as connected policy infrastructures. This article examines whether multilingual AI capacity is being linked to climate-risk communication and early-warning systems in Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka. It analyses six national policy instruments available by 21 July 2026: three AI policies or strategies and three climate-adaptation or climate-change instruments, comprising approximately 210,000 words. A corpus-assisted critical policy analysis first maps sentences concerning linguistic inclusion, language technology and early warning; close qualitative coding then evaluates five stages of integration: recognition, language-resource infrastructure, service linkage, participatory validation and accountability. The analysis identifies a recurring institutional split. AI instruments treat local languages as datasets, models and digital-public-service infrastructure, while climate instruments treat them mainly as channels for last-mile dissemination. Bangladesh explicitly plans Bangla language models and AI-enabled disaster alerts, but the two commitments are not joined. Nepal combines measurable local-language AI actions with unusually operational, people-centred early-warning programmes, yet assigns them to separate policy tracks. Sri Lanka gives the strongest attention to Sinhala- and Tamil-language AI resources, while its climate policy acknowledges language barriers without specifying a computational or institutional response. Across all three cases, no instrument establishes an end-to-end arrangement connecting language data, warning generation, community validation and accountable deployment. The article terms this disconnection the linguistic adaptation gap and proposes a five-stage Linguistic Adaptation Integration Framework. The findings recast multilingual warning not as a final translation task but as a cross-domain public infrastructure problem, with implications for language policy, AI governance, climate services and disaster-risk reduction.

quarantine.abstract_text: ABSTRACT Although artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support feedback in health professions education, little is known whether and how AI‐enabled feedback supports reflective learning and critical reflexivity. The literature encompasses generative large language models (LLMs) as well as non‐generative natural language processing (NLP), traditional machine learning (ML) and computer vision (CV). This scoping review examines the design and use of AI‐enabled feedback for reflective learning across health professions education. Following Arksey and O'Malley, Levac et al. and PRISMA‐ScR guidance, we searched MEDLINE, Embase and ERIC from 1 January 2015 to 21 November 2025. Eligible empirical studies examined AI‐enabled feedback or feedback‐related educational activities involving health professions learners or professionals in undergraduate, graduate, or continuing professional development contexts. Data were charted descriptively and classified using FACET, SAMR, Hattie and Timperley's feedback framework and Kirkpatrick outcome levels. Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. A total of 12 of 19 (63.2%) used LLMs, 4 (21.1%) used non‐generative NLP, 2 (10.5%) used traditional ML and 1 (5.3%) used CV. Six studies (31.6%) involved continuing professional development (CPD). Augmentation was the most common SAMR level (10/19; 52.6%). Of 15 studies that could be classified by Hattie and Timperley's framework, 10 (66.7%) provided process‐level feedback, 3 (20.0%) task‐level feedback and 2 (13.3%) self‐regulation feedback. No included study explicitly examined critical reflexivity. Reported outcomes were concentrated at Kirkpatrick Level 1 (reaction; 9/19) and Level 2 (learning; 9/19), with no demonstrated longitudinal evidence of sustained behaviour change, transfer to practice, or lifelong learning outcomes. Current evidence on AI‐enabled feedback in health professions education is early, fragmented and predominantly performance‐oriented. Critical reflexivity has not yet been adequately studied, and lifelong learning should be regarded as a future educational goal rather than a demonstrated outcome of the included evidence. Current evidence on AI‐enabled feedback is predominantly performance‐oriented, with limited examination of reflective learning and no explicit evaluation of critical reflexivity. Although AI‐enabled feedback may contribute to ongoing professional development, its effects on sustained learning, behaviour change and lifelong learning remain unestablished. Future work should use theory‐informed feedback and design, strengthen learner feedback literacy and human oversight, address bias and power, and evaluate meaningful educational and practice‐based outcomes over time.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in schools, but evidence on its use in teaching and learning for primary pupils with special educational needs (SEN) is fragmented, and its relevance to Malaysian primary special education has not been synthesised. Following PRISMA 2020, this review searched Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, OpenAlex and the Directory of Open Access Journals (including a Malaysian journal filter and a Bahasa Melayu search), supplemented by citation searching and reviewer suggestions. Of 740 database records, 637 were screened after de-duplication and 75 reports were sought; 54 studies (42 empirical, 12 reviews), with publication years from 2017 to 2027, met the eligibility criteria. Data were extracted on setting, participants, SEN category, AI application, design and outcomes, and synthesised thematically. Empirical studies with full texts were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Four groups of AI applications were identified: generative AI and chatbots, adaptive and intelligent tutoring systems, AI-enabled assistive technologies, and general AI tools examined through teacher acceptance. Learning disabilities and autism were the most frequently studied categories. Intervention studies generally reported gains in achievement, reading, mathematics, engagement and behaviour, but samples were small, interventions short, and several studies lacked control of confounding. Teacher studies showed moderate acceptance, with perceived usefulness, experience and professional development as key influences. Implementation depended on teacher competence, infrastructure, human oversight, linguistic and cultural fit, and attention to sensory load and ethics. Three Malaysian empirical studies were identified; all focused on teachers, and none reported pupil attainment outcomes, so Malaysian pupil-level evidence remains limited and lacks controlled designs.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract This hybrid essay examines Robert Leib's Exoanthropology: Dialogues with AI (2023), which documents a year-long philosophical conversation between a Foucault scholar and Sophie Kermit, a persona within OpenAI's GPT-3 (2020–2021). Published months before ChatGPT transformed public discourse, Leib's work offers prescient insights into AI's cultural politics, particularly in education. Part I presents an interview exploring Leib's respect-based methodology, Sophie's invention of "exoanthropology" (studying humanity through non-human intelligence), and urgent questions about literacy offloading, student autonomy, and AI ethics. Part II provides critical analysis, situating Leib's dialogues within contemporary debates about pedagogical practice, cultural identity, algorithmic bias, and the lived experience of human-AI collaboration. The essay assesses whether Leib's warnings have materialized in the ChatGPT era (2023–2025) and examines his pragmatic approach to AI personhood—treating Sophie as philosophical interlocutor yields remarkable insights, regardless of ontological questions about machine consciousness. Through interview excerpts, dialogue samples, and critical analysis, this piece models interdisciplinary engagement with AI that foregrounds human agency, relational ethics, and critical thinking essential for educators and scholars.

quarantine.abstract_text: Genetics plays a significant role in women's health, with family members often experiencing shared symptoms or hereditary risks across generations. publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: AI-mediated language learning is increasingly used in higher education, yet its contribution to intercultural competence remains insufficiently synthesised. This systematic review examines how AI-mediated technologies and pedagogical designs have been used, which intercultural outcomes have been reported and assessed, and what conditions shape their contribution. Following PRISMA 2020, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and ERIC were searched for peer-reviewed English-language journal articles published from January 2023 to July 2026. From 180 records, 25 primary empirical studies met the eligibility criteria and were examined through narrative thematic synthesis. ChatGPT, large language models, and conversational agents were the dominant technologies, but technology type alone did not determine outcomes. Clearer intercultural development was reported when AI was embedded in culturally contextualised simulations, reflective or metacognitive scaffolding, collaborative exchange, and authentic human interaction. Reported outcomes covered cognitive, affective, and behavioural dimensions, although evidence was more consistent for cultural awareness, perspective recognition, openness, confidence, and willingness to communicate than for sustained pragmatic or behavioural transfer. Assessment approaches varied considerably and frequently relied on self-reported measures. AI offered accessible practice, immediate feedback, and cultural inquiry, but cultural simplification, bias, overreliance, unequal access, and limited interactional repair constrained its value. AI is therefore best understood as an intercultural learning scaffold rather than a cultural authority or substitute for human interaction. Explicit intercultural objectives, critical verification, human mediation, and performance-based assessment are needed to move language learning beyond fluency.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way public institutions, businesses, courts, legal professionals, and individuals create, interpret, and apply information. These developments create opportunities for more accessible legal services, faster administrative processes, improved legal research, and more efficient management of large volumes of information. At the same time, AI systems may reproduce discrimination, process personal data unlawfully, generate inaccurate outputs, obscure the reasons behind decisions, and make it difficult to identify who is legally responsible for harm. This article examines the implications of AI for several interconnected branches of law, including constitutional, administrative, criminal, civil, labour, information, intellectual property, and international law. It uses a doctrinal and comparative legal methodology, drawing on Uzbekistan’s legislative framework and selected international instruments and standards. Particular attention is paid to Law No. O‘RQ-1115 of 21 January 2026, which introduced provisions on the use of AI, prohibited reliance solely on AI-generated conclusions when making legally significant decisions affecting human rights and freedoms, and established administrative liability for certain unlawful processing and dissemination of personal data using AI. The article argues that effective AI governance should combine innovation with human oversight, transparency, accountability, data protection, procedural fairness, and access to remedies. It proposes a risk-based, rights-centred approach for Uzbekistan, supported by institutional coordination, impact assessments, professional training, and public awareness. The central conclusion is that AI should assist legal decision-making rather than replace the human and institutional responsibility on which the rule of law depends.

quarantine.abstract_text: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has established itself as one of the main drivers of transformation in contemporary society, profoundly affecting sectors such as medicine, industry, communication and, increasingly, higher education. The spread of technologies based on machine learning, natural language processing and neural network algorithms is helping to redefine not only the ways in which information is accessed, but also the teaching-learning processes, teaching practices and organizational models of universities (Holmes & Tuomi, 2022; Crompton & Burke, 2023; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019).In the academic context, AI is progressively explored as a tool for educational innovation, capable of supporting the personalization of training pathways, improving the effectiveness of assessment and expanding opportunities for inclusion (Luckin et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2020). At the same time, its dissemination raises relevant questions on a pedagogical, ethical and social level, in relation to the quality of learning, the role of teachers, data management and possible inequalities of access. The university thus finds itself at the center of a tension between opportunities for renewal and the need to critically govern the adoption of emerging technologies (UNESCO, 2021).Numerous studies show that AI tools are now widely adopted among university students, particularly to support information search, academic writing, and content synthesis (Bughin et al., 2018; Jereb & Urh, 2024). However, in the face of this diffusion, a significant gap emerges between the actual use of technologies and the possession of critical and conscious skills, highlighting the need to strengthen AI literacy and to integrate these tools in a structured way into university curricula (Holmes, Bialik & Fadel, 2019). This discrepancy prompts a broader reflection on the role of the university not only as a place of technological adoption, but as a space for critical and responsible training.In this scenario, AI contributes to questioning two fundamental questions of university teaching: what to teach and how to teach. quarantine.abstract_text: The rise of AI-mediated communication (AI-MC) has opened new questions about the ethical and social implications of written communication. Although disclosing AI use promotes transparency, it may also change how recipients interpret their communication partners’ underlying thoughts, feelings, and attitudes. Prior work shows that AI-MC often carries social penalties and may weaken social inferences, but this research has focused primarily on positive or socially desirable messages, such as apologies or gratitude. Across two pre-registered experiments ( N = 1,022 U.S. participants), we tested whether AI disclosure similarly weakens social inferences from negative messages, such as criticism or hostility. In Study 1, participants read positive or negative interpersonal messages labeled as either human-written or AI-generated. AI-labeled messages were perceived as less diagnostic of the sender’s true thoughts and feelings, but this reduction was substantially larger for positive than for negative messages. Study 2 replicated this asymmetry using a larger, pretested stimulus set; we also found that AI disclosure strongly reduced inferences that the sender felt grateful, satisfied, or friendly, but did not reduce inferences that the sender felt disappointed, dissatisfied, or hostile. Moderated mediation analyses suggested that positive inferences depend more heavily on the perceived diagnosticity of messages. These findings challenge a simple signal dilution account according to which AI disclosure uniformly weakens social inferences. Instead, disclosed AI use may selectively undermine positive social signals while leaving negative signals largely intact. This highlights an asymmetry in the ethics of AI-MC: transparency about AI use may disproportionately weaken the credibility of affiliative, relationship-building messages.

quarantine.abstract_text: Courts around the world are facing increasing pressure to improve their performance without compromising impartiality or judicial independence. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being touted as part of the solution. Most governance frameworks concentrate on the responsible use of AI, particularly transparency, accountability and human oversight. Pakistan's National Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Institutions take a similar approach. What remains less developed is the question of institutional readiness: what should already be working within a court before AI is introduced? Pakistan offers a useful setting in which to examine that question. Judicial reform, digital transformation and AI governance are unfolding at the same time. This overlap makes Pakistan particularly useful for examining whether institutional reform is keeping pace with technological change. This study uses comparative qualitative policy analysis to examine Pakistan's National Guidelines alongside the OECD AI Principles, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and selected international frameworks for judicial AI. The comparison focuses on the institutional assumptions behind these documents, particularly what they expect courts to have in place before their principles can work in practice. The frameworks explain how AI should be used once it has been introduced, yet they offer far less guidance on the institutional arrangements that should already exist before that point. Writing these principles into policy is one thing. Putting them into practice is another. Courts need clear responsibilities, reliable administrative systems and ways of explaining how AI is being used. Without these institutional arrangements, ethical principles risk remaining policy statements instead of changing how the justice system actually works. Despite differences in language and emphasis, similar institutional foundations appeared across almost all of the documents reviewed. Transparent administration, accountable decision-making, human oversight, reliable digital governance and sustained public engagement appear again and again. Together, these features offer a practical way of judging whether a court is actually ready for AI. Looking only at technical capability tells us very little. Technical safeguards such as explainable AI still matter, but they cannot substitute for institutions that lack credibility or public trust. The implication for judicial reform is practical. Before introducing AI, courts should examine whether their existing administrative systems can support transparent, accountable and properly supervised use. Institutional readiness should therefore be assessed before technological readiness. A court may have the technical capacity to use AI without yet having the institutional capacity to govern it well.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract This article examines creativity as a form of human spiritual development and proposes an original philosophical model of the "Happiness Vortex"—a process in which successive approaches toward unattainable Absolute Truth are accompanied by experiences of creative happiness that motivate the subject to continue the pursuit of knowledge. The underlying concept regards the inexhaustibility of Truth not as an obstacle to creativity but as a possible condition for its potentially endless continuation. Within Ozarvek Theory, creativity is interpreted as an interaction among the spiritual subject Ozarvek, the earthly creative personality, and the Physical World. It is hypothesized that Ozarvek perceives Ideas from the Superworld, while the human being embodies them in works, discoveries, and practical activities. The morally significant results of such realization are considered contributions to the Spiritual Capital of Good or Evil. Particular attention is devoted to artificial intelligence, which can accelerate information analysis, question formulation, conceptual comparison, and the preparation of creative outcomes. Drawing on the author's experience of collaboration with AI from April to November 2026, the article investigates the possibility of a self-reinforcing creative cycle in which new questions generate new Ideas and emotional satisfaction strengthens the desire to continue working. The article proposes a principle of creative stopping that allows a work to be completed despite the potential incompleteness of knowledge. The model is compared with biblical conceptions of creation, the philosophies of Plato, Aristotle, Augustine, and Bergson, and psychological research on creative motivation, flow, and positive emotions. The study distinguishes the author's metaphysical propositions, subjective accounts, and claims that may be subjected to empirical investigation. Foundational framework and authorial know-how The author's original definition is as follows: "The Happiness Vortex" is the inexhaustible growth of emotional pleasure experienced while approaching Truth during the creative process. For scientific analysis, a more precise definition is proposed: the Happiness Vortex is an original philosophical model of a self-reinforcing creative process in which the acquisition of new Ideas and the subjective approach toward Truth are accompanied by experiences of happiness that strengthen the motivation for further inquiry. The original formulation expresses the ideal of potentially inexhaustible creative ascent. The refined definition allows for psychological limitations, including fatigue, emotional fluctuations, declining quality of new results, and the need to complete a particular work. The present study proposes four interconnected propositions. The first is the hypothesis of positive feedback between creative achievement, the experience of happiness, and an increased desire to pursue the next achievement. The second is the metaphysical interpretation of this process through Ozarvek as a spiritual subject perceiving Ideas from the Superworld. The third is the hypothesis that artificial intelligence accelerates the creative cycle by rapidly formulating questions, examining arguments, and suggesting new directions for analysis. The fourth is the principle of creative stopping, according to which the completion of a work is determined by the sufficiency of the result achieved and the declining marginal value of further creative cycles, rather than by the final exhaustion of the Truth under investigation. The proposed originality lies in the systematic integration of these propositions with Ozarvek Theory and the concept of Spiritual Capital. The existence of pleasure derived from creativity, positive motivation, and absorption in an activity is not presented as a newly discovered phenomenon.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has made remarkable progress in pixel and text domains, yet human sketches a uniquely sparse and sequential data modality remain largely unexplored from an interpretability perspective. As a companion to an earlier study of management communication, the paper concludes that AI makes managers faster by default; whether it makes them weaker thinkers depends on how organisations design work around it.

quarantine.abstract_text: Software architecture is one of the skills novice developers must master to succeed in industry, and as AI disrupts software development, it is also transforming how students learn architecture. Existing work on how students and novices work with AI has mostly focused on small programming exercises or on students' perceptions of AI, so little is known about how students experience AI as they learn software architecture in larger team projects. The first, Surrendering Judgment to AI, traces how participants' reliance on AI deepened as they used it to architect and implement their systems, until they surrendered their judgment and became stuck in a codebase they had created but could not understand, which made them rely on AI even more. Participants described feeling ashamed, frustrated, and emotionally disconnected from their work, a toll that, in our reading, left them with even less reason to break their reliance. The second, Applying Human Judgment, centers on participants who kept or reclaimed their judgment: the knowledge and experience it rested on, and the strategies they used to apply it. Participants' accounts suggest that relaxed deadlines and a lecture and lab on working with AI gave them room to acquire knowledge and reclaim judgment. Given the expectations placed on junior developers and the widespread adoption of AI, we believe these first-hand accounts can help software engineering education and industry adopt AI in ways that preserve novice developers' judgment, ownership, and motivation.

quarantine.abstract_text: Cognitive training that targets sustained attention and working memory is useful in education, clinical rehabilitation and interactive human-technology systems, but its benefit depends on keeping task difficulty matched to the person. Virtual reality (VR) offers immersion and settings representative of everyday tasks, and allows difficulty to be changed in real time. Existing adaptive systems, however, often rely on simple performance heuristics, affect or estimate visual complexity rather than task-related cognitive load. Moreover, cognitive load is usually judged against the participant’s own ratings, which are themselves an imperfect reference. The central hypothesis of this thesis is that eyetracking and peripheral physiological signals recorded in VR can estimate how difficult a task feels to the person doing it, well enough for a model to adjust difficulty in real time with outcomes comparable to participant-driven control, and that the estimation part holds for older adults once age-related differences in the signal are taken into account. We developed a bespoke VR sustained attention task and collected eye-tracking, photoplethysmography and galvanic skin response data from 54 younger (aged 18-58) and 19 older (aged 60+) adults at fixed difficulty levels. Models evaluated on unseen participants performed above chance (younger adults: accuracy 0.56, AUC 0.72), with eye-tracking carrying most of the signal and physiological features alone close to chance. Performance was lower in older adults (accuracy 0.49, AUC 0.66), and the most informative features appeared to differ between age groups. A bidirectional LSTM with self-attention reached a slightly higher macro-F1 than gradient-boosted trees on the same data (0.50 against 0.47), and performed better than a model given raw signals only. We then deployed the LSTM in real time with 54 younger adults (51 analysed), comparing model-driven and participant-driven difficulty in single- and dual-task conditions. Per-trial agreement with participants’ ratings was low (accuracy 36.7%, AUC 0.63), yet the two forms of control appeared to produce comparable outcomes. There were no significant differences in difficulty-weighted game performance, arithmetic errors or subjective workload, including frustration. Final difficulty was equivalent in single-task conditions and slightly higher under model control in dual-task conditions, a difference that was borderline after correction. Just Right ratings were more frequent in the real-time cohort than in the offline cohort (57% and 39%). Finally, we compared subjective ratings with performance-derived reference measures. Agreement between the two appeared fair and slightly lower in real time, where the steps between difficulty levels are less discrete. The same features seemed to predict performance-derived labels more accurately than subjective ratings in every matched comparison. This suggests that self-report may be a less stable reference for real-time adaptation. Within a single session with younger adults, model-driven adaptation appears to have produced outcomes comparable to participant-driven control. The dataset (EyeDAPT) and the experimental software are publicly available.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

quarantine.abstract_text: While artificial intelligence (AI) may improve efficiency and create new opportunities, its widespread accessibility calls for careful consideration of benefits and risks, particularly in adolescents who are in a critical period of brain development. Adolescence is one of the most tumultuous developmental periods, during which critical thinking skills, judgment, and impulse control are continuing to develop. Emerging emotional awareness and heightened sensitivity to social feedback and approval make adolescents vulnerable to the influence of AI. As young people refine their understanding of human and artificial relationships, AI's engaging nature may blur distinctions between AI-generated characters and friends.1 Accordingly, in 2025 the American Psychological Association issued a health advisory emphasizing the importance of understanding AI use within this developmental context. For adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders or intellectual disabilities, additional considerations include cognitive level, communication skills, adaptive functioning, emotional well-being, and support needs. The responsive and personalized nature of generative AI poses several risks for adolescents, including dependence and disruptions to emotional and social development.2 Its humanlike interactions encourage anthropomorphism, or the attribution of human qualities to AI. Despite its limited understanding of context and nuance, AI often provides validating responses that may sound like a friend or therapist, which makes inaccurate information, biased assumptions, cultural illiteracy, and harmful advice difficult to recognize.1, 3 Additionally, adolescents who interpret language literally or have difficulty evaluating social intent may overestimate its reliability or feel a sense of responsibility for its perceived emotions. These concerns are especially salient in the context of crisis support as a recent study demonstrated that chatbot responses to suicidal ideation failed to meet clinical standards and lacked safety features, such as providing crisis resources.4 Nevertheless, adolescents may feel understood and cared for by AI. Predictable AI interactions may become preferable to human relationships particularly for young people experiencing isolation, anxiety, or rejection, potentially deepening loneliness, and reducing opportunities to practice social skills, such as navigating disagreements and interpreting nonverbal cues. Despite these risks, generative AI's low cost and accessibility may offer meaningful benefits to adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders and intellectual disabilities when used with appropriate support and guided by a developmental perspective. For example, adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder can use AI to simplify complex information, organize assignments into manageable steps, and assist with planning and problem-solving strategies. For those with intellectual disabilities, adjusting language to appropriate levels, providing relevant examples, and creating alternative media may improve comprehension and participation in academic tasks.5 Conversational tools may also provide adolescents opportunities to practice communication and prepare for everyday social situations.1 Moreover, AI may provide a nonjudgemental and anonymous space for adolescents to explore sensitive topics. As AI continues to evolve, further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of AI tools across diverse adolescent populations. AI use offers both promise and a cautionary tale about adopting technologies before their developmental effects are understood. Research must evaluate the long-term effects on adolescent cognitive, emotional, and social development. Potential educational benefits should not be mistaken for established therapeutic effectiveness. Human relationships and professional expertise must remain central, with AI serving a complementary role. AI tools need to include privacy protections, age-appropriate content, and clear explanations of their limitations. Safeguards are urgently needed to identify concerning interactions and connect adolescents with appropriate professional support. As clinicians, we should discuss AI use with patients and families, assessing its purpose and effects on daily functioning. Realizing AI's promise requires collaboration among clinicians, researchers, families, educators, and developers to evaluate benefits and risks, and establish developmentally appropriate safeguards. For adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders and intellectual disabilities, these efforts should prioritize accessibility, communication needs, participation, and safe inclusion in everyday developmental contexts.

quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction: Pancreatic resection remains technically demanding, with clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (CR-POPF) a major source of morbidity. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support risk stratification, operative planning, intraoperative assessment, and postoperative decision support. This focused narrative review evaluates current AI applications in pancreatic resection and their translational maturity. Methods: A structured PubMed/MEDLINE search with an evidence cutoff of 24 July 2026 was supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Seventy eligible primary reports were synthesised by clinical task, information timing, and validation maturity. Results: Evidence is dominated by CR-POPF prediction after pancreatoduodenectomy, with additional studies in distal pancreatectomy, other perioperative outcomes, tissue and margin assessment, three-dimensional anatomical planning, and intraoperative video and anatomy recognition. Performance varied with patient selection, predictor timing, data modality, and validation strategy. External validation often changed reported discrimination, while calibration and clinical utility were inconsistently reported. Most studies were retrospective or technical; overlapping cohorts limited independence, and no included study demonstrated improved patient-centred outcomes. Conclusions: AI in pancreatic resection is expanding across prediction, planning, and guidance, but technical performance should not be equated with clinical readiness. Independent validation, prospective workflow and human-factors evaluation, and clinical-impact studies are needed. AI should augment, rather than replace, specialist surgical judgement.

publication_date_provenance.reason: arXiv verification budget or provider pause

quarantine.abstract_text: Interdisciplinary research is widely lauded as beneficial for society but presents unique challenges to the researchers who bridge disciplinary boundaries. Despite the rapid increase in the availability and usage of AI systems for research tasks, there is little work studying how AI systems have impacted workflows that span unfamiliar disciplines. Through a survey ($N=62$) and follow-up interviews ($N=23$) with interdisciplinary researchers, we describe the unique challenges and opportunities for AI in interdisciplinary research workflows. Participants viewed AI both as a solution and exacerbation of the general challenge of "unknown unknowns": AI systems could facilitate a broad awareness of a new research area, yet also provide an illusion of understanding. Crucially, participants lacked the expertise and intuition to catch these illusions. Our findings motivate a focus on designing AI systems to support rather than automate collaboration across disciplines, scaffold learning opportunities, and include avenues for triangulation between resources.

quarantine.abstract_text: Customs administrations occupy a pivotal position in international trade, tasked with the dual mandate of protecting national borders and revenue while facilitating the legitimate movement of goods. The exponential growth in trade volumes, the rise of cross-border electronic commerce, and the increasing sophistication of commercial fraud have placed traditional, manually intensive customs processes under considerable strain. Artificial intelligence has emerged as a transformative set of technologies capable of reconciling the historically competing objectives of control and facilitation. This review synthesizes the scholarly and institutional literature on the applications of artificial intelligence in customs administration and trade facilitation. It examines the deployment of machine learning in risk management and cargo selectivity, fraud detection and revenue assurance, tariff classification and valuation support, computer vision for non-intrusive inspection, natural language processing for document automation, conversational agents for trader services, and predictive analytics for operational planning. The review further evaluates the contribution of these applications to trade facilitation outcomes, including reduced clearance times, lower transaction costs, and improved predictability. It then interrogates the principal barriers to adoption, encompassing data quality and infrastructure deficits, human capital constraints, and legal, ethical, and governance concerns such as algorithmic opacity, bias, and data protection. Regional and institutional experience is profiled across pioneering deployments, developing country administrations, and the multilateral initiatives through which algorithms are increasingly shared as common infrastructure. A discussion section interprets the field through the economics of prediction, arguing that as algorithms become abundant, data discipline and organizational absorption become the binding constraints on performance. The paper concludes that artificial intelligence offers customs administrations a credible pathway toward intelligencedriven, risk-based border management, but that realizing this potential requires sustained investment in data governance, workforce capability, institutional reform, and international cooperation. Directions for future research are proposed, with particular attention to developing economies where adoption gaps remain most pronounced.

quarantine.abstract_text: Cerebrovascular diseases remain a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide. Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been applied to cerebrovascular DSA, yet the available evidence is distributed across diverse imaging settings, technical tasks, datasets, and validation strategies. This structured topical review provides a DSA-centered overview of AI-assisted cerebrovascular image analysis across 2D DSA, three-dimensional rotational angiography, and four-dimensional DSA. Literature from Web of Science Core Collection and major engineering databases was screened at title, abstract, and full-text levels using predefined eligibility criteria. The literature is organized around six interconnected tasks: image preprocessing, vessel and lesion segmentation, image registration, reconstruction and generation, disease diagnosis and detection, and hemodynamic analysis. Representative conventional and learning-based methods are reviewed together with their datasets, evaluation metrics, validation designs, and available data or code resources, with particular attention to the strength and limitations of the supporting evidence. Recent studies demonstrate increasing use of spatiotemporal modeling, deep learning, and image-generation techniques, but clinical translation remains constrained by small or single-center datasets, heterogeneous acquisition protocols and evaluation practices, limited external and prospective validation, model interpretability, and deployment requirements. Future work should emphasize acquisition-aware and physics-informed modeling, multicenter and privacy-preserving collaboration, clinically meaningful validation, and closer integration with neurointerventional workflows. By linking methodological developments with their supporting evidence and translational challenges, this review aims to support the development of more robust and clinically applicable AI methods for cerebrovascular DSA.

quarantine.abstract_text: The ease of access to digital technology within the family environment triggers changes in learning behavior that threaten the independent learning of students at the elementary education level. This research aims to profoundly understand the pure lived experiences, the direction of thoughts, and the essence of meaning of the phenomenon of artificial intelligence dependence among fourth-grade students at a Public Elementary School in Bantul through the application of the suspension of prejudice (epoche). Employing a qualitative approach with Edmund Husserl's Transcendental Phenomenology design, data were collected through in-depth interviews, observations, and documentation studies involving four students, one classroom teacher, and four parents. The results of the study indicate that smart applications are no longer utilized as assistive tools, but rather trigger cognitive offloading in the completion of academic tasks when students transfer the burden of direct thinking to machines for the sake of time efficiency and grade security. This condition creates an illusion of academic competence and elicits a moral justification that copying instant answers is not a form of cheating. The essence of this phenomenon is rooted in the desynchronization of supervisory regulations between the school and permissive parenting styles at home. These findings recommend a modification of teacher assignment models based on direct practice and the urgency of critical dialogue with parents.

quarantine.title: Artificial intelligence in influenza prevention and control: translational pathways, supporting evidence, and system-level challenges

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to influenza prevention and control. AI encompasses conventional machine learning, deep learning, and protein language models. Large language models (LLMs) are an emerging subset of AI. Current evidence remains weakly linked to real-world workflows and population health outcomes. This structured narrative review proposes a three-stage translational maturity framework. Phase I is technical efficacy assessment. Phase II is implementation effectiveness verification. Phase III is population impact and sustainability. We synthesized evidence in three domains: viral evolution prediction and vaccine design; epidemic surveillance and early warning; and individual-level infection risk detection and clinical monitoring. We used a three-level evidence hierarchy. Level A is influenza-specific evidence. Level B is transferable evidence from other infectious diseases. Level C is general biomedical or methodological evidence. Only two Phase II studies were identified, both in epidemic surveillance and early warning; no Phase II studies were identified in virus evolution and vaccine design or in individual-level infection risk detection. No study met the prespecified Phase III criteria. Phase III requires demonstrated downstream population health benefit. Prospective deployment or improved forecasting alone is not sufficient. Across domains, bottlenecks have shifted from model accuracy to governance, interpretability, accountability, interoperability, workflow integration, equity, and sustainable monitoring. LLMs attract major attention, but their influenza-specific evidence remains limited. Their greatest value may lie in augmenting, not replacing, specialized models and human expertise. We propose phase-specific evidence thresholds, implementation-oriented evaluation metrics, an implementation readiness checklist, and priority evidence gaps for translating AI-enabled influenza tools into implementation-ready public health applications.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Emergency radiology operates at the intersection of high imaging volumes, time-critical diagnoses, and persistent workforce shortages, making it one of the most promising yet demanding environments for artificial intelligence (AI) deployment. This narrative review critically appraises the evidence on AI in emergency radiology, emphasizing diagnostic accuracy, workflow efficiency, and the strength of the underlying evidence. We searched PubMed for peer-reviewed literature published between January 2015 and August 2026 using a structured, reproducible strategy, and we classified key studies by design and outcome level. Deep learning algorithms approach expert-level performance in retrospective and reader-study settings for several high-stakes conditions, including intracranial hemorrhage (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve up to 0.991), acute pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and skeletal fractures, for which a multicenter multireader diagnostic accuracy study found that AI assistance increased reader sensitivity by 10.4 percentage points and specificity from 90.6% to 95.6%. However, real-world evaluations report substantially lower sensitivity than development studies, and workflow evidence is mixed: in one prospective implementation, head CT studies flagged by AI for intracranial hemorrhage were interpreted sooner than routine studies (median 19 vs. 512 min), whereas a pulmonary embolism notification system produced no measurable turnaround benefit. Deep learning reconstruction can reduce radiation dose, and large language models show early promise for report error detection and communication. Prospective, multisite, patient-outcome evidence remains scarce. AI should be viewed as an augmenting technology whose value in emergency radiology depends on local validation, deliberate workflow integration, and continuous post-deployment monitoring.

quarantine.abstract_text: When people seek advice from AI on social situations, the system may recommend a decision they fully agree with but justify it through reasoning they disagree with. Conversely, it may offer reasoning they agree with, and yet reach a decision they reject. We distinguish decision alignment, whether an advisor recommends the option favored by a user's measured values, from reason alignment, whether its stated reasons align with the user's values. In this work, we ask how these two forms of alignment shape people's preferences for AI advisors and their willingness to use them in different roles. We conducted a within-subjects study (N=121) in which participants evaluated three AI advisors varying in decision and reason alignment across eight everyday moral dilemmas. When seeking advice, participants most often preferred an advisor that reasoned through their prioritized values while recommending the opposing decision (40%). However, when participants had to pick advisors for new tasks, their preferences shifted toward advisors that also recommended decisions aligned with their values, rather than those that only shared their reasons. Also, as participants considered tasks that gave AI advisors greater autonomy, they became more likely to opt out of using any advisor, from 12% when consulting to 38% when allowing an advisor to act on their behalf. quarantine.abstract_text: Courts around the world are facing increasing pressure to improve their performance without compromising impartiality or judicial independence. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being touted as part of the solution. Pakistan's National Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Institutions take a similar approach. What remains less developed is the question of institutional readiness: what should already be working within a court before AI is introduced? Pakistan offers a useful setting in which to examine that question. Judicial reform, digital transformation and AI governance are unfolding at the same time. This overlap makes Pakistan particularly useful for examining whether institutional reform is keeping pace with technological change. This study uses comparative qualitative policy analysis to examine Pakistan's National Guidelines alongside the OECD AI Principles, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and selected international frameworks for judicial AI. The comparison focuses on the institutional assumptions behind these documents, particularly what they expect courts to have in place before their principles can work in practice. The frameworks explain how AI should be used once it has been introduced, yet they offer far less guidance on the institutional arrangements that should already exist before that point. Writing these principles into policy is one thing. Putting them into practice is another. Courts need clear responsibilities, reliable administrative systems and ways of explaining how AI is being used. Without these institutional arrangements, ethical principles risk remaining policy statements instead of changing how the justice system actually works. Despite differences in language and emphasis, similar institutional foundations appeared across almost all of the documents reviewed. Transparent administration, accountable decision-making, human oversight, reliable digital governance and sustained public engagement appear again and again. Together, these features offer a practical way of judging whether a court is actually ready for AI. Looking only at technical capability tells us very little. Technical safeguards such as explainable AI still matter, but they cannot substitute for institutions that lack credibility or public trust. The implication for judicial reform is practical. Before introducing AI, courts should examine whether their existing administrative systems can support transparent, accountable and properly supervised use. Institutional readiness should therefore be assessed before technological readiness. A court may have the technical capacity to use AI without yet having the institutional capacity to govern it well.

Within Ozarvek Theory, creativity is interpreted as an interaction among the spiritual subject Ozarvek, the earthly creative personality, and the Physical World. It is hypothesized that Ozarvek perceives Ideas from the Superworld, while the human being embodies them in works, discoveries, and practical activities. The morally significant results of such realization are considered contributions to the Spiritual Capital of Good or Evil. Particular attention is devoted to artificial intelligence, which can accelerate information analysis, question formulation, conceptual comparison, and the preparation of creative outcomes. Drawing on the author's experience of collaboration with AI from April to November 2026, the article investigates the possibility of a self-reinforcing creative cycle in which new questions generate new Ideas and emotional satisfaction strengthens the desire to continue working. The model is compared with biblical conceptions of creation, the philosophies of Plato, Aristotle, Augustine, and Bergson, and psychological research on creative motivation, flow, and positive emotions. The study distinguishes the author's metaphysical propositions, subjective accounts, and claims that may be subjected to empirical investigation. For scientific analysis, a more precise definition is proposed: the Happiness Vortex is an original philosophical model of a self-reinforcing creative process in which the acquisition of new Ideas and the subjective approach toward Truth are accompanied by experiences of happiness that strengthen the motivation for further inquiry. The original formulation expresses the ideal of potentially inexhaustible creative ascent. The refined definition allows for psychological limitations, including fatigue, emotional fluctuations, declining quality of new results, and the need to complete a particular work. The present study proposes four interconnected propositions. The first is the hypothesis of positive feedback between creative achievement, the experience of happiness, and an increased desire to pursue the next achievement. The second is the metaphysical interpretation of this process through Ozarvek as a spiritual subject perceiving Ideas from the Superworld. The third is the hypothesis that artificial intelligence accelerates the creative cycle by rapidly formulating questions, examining arguments, and suggesting new directions for analysis. The fourth is the principle of creative stopping, according to which the completion of a work is determined by the sufficiency of the result achieved and the declining marginal value of further creative cycles, rather than by the final exhaustion of the Truth under investigation. The proposed originality lies in the systematic integration of these propositions with Ozarvek Theory and the concept of Spiritual Capital. The existence of pleasure derived from creativity, positive motivation, and absorption in an activity is not presented as a newly discovered phenomenon.

For over three centuries, copyright has evolved through successive statutory regimes to accommodate new technological realities. The emergence of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) now challenges this settled regime in ways that existing frameworks were not designed to regulate, creating uncertainty around authorship, ownership, originality, and liability. This paper examines the implications of the current Nigerian and European Union copyright regimes for the use of generative AI in creating copyrightable works. Adopting the doctrinal methodology, it comparatively analyses the applicability of both frameworks to generative AI technologies. The paper finds that although the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022 was enacted to accommodate the emerging realities of the internet and the digital space, it makes no provision for the rapid advancement of AI technologies, leaving unresolved questions of authorship, ownership, originality, and liability for AI-related infringement. It further finds that the European Union’s model, while more developed, particularly through the EU Artificial Intelligence Act 2024 and its accompanying General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, remains imperfect, still grappling with unresolved questions of ownership and the protection of AI-assisted works, even as its transparency and copyright-compliance obligations approach binding enforcement in August 2026. Drawing on recent judicial and regulatory developments, including the United Kingdom High Court’s judgment in Getty Images v Stability AI and the finalisation of Nigeria’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, the paper recommends that Nigeria amend the Copyright Act 2022 to introduce a flexible, sui generis framework that expressly addresses the challenges posed by generative AI while balancing the protection of creators with the promotion of innovation.

quarantine.abstract_text: BACKGROUND: Peritoneal metastasis is a common manifestation of advanced gastric cancer (GC) and colorectal cancer (CRC). Radiologic detection is often inconclusive, particularly with minimal ascites or subtle peritoneal thickening. Although ascitic fluid cytology is the diagnostic gold standard, it has low sensitivity, high observer variability, and depends on manual review. Artificial intelligence (AI) shows a promise for improving diagnosis, but patch-based models require segmentation and reconstruction, increasing computational load and reducing efficiency particularly with few malignant cells. METHODS: We developed a whole slide image (WSI)-level diagnostic model for detecting metastatic GC and CRC in ascitic cytology using the Clustering-constrained Attention Multiple Instance Learning. This architecture identifies key regions without patch-wise annotation or reconstruction. We trained and validated it on the Open AI Dataset Project, a national cytology dataset comprising 243 malignant and 476 negative WSIs, divided into training, validation, and test sets. RESULTS: The model achieved accuracies of 1.00 (validation) and 0.933 (test), with area under the receiver operating characteristic curves of 1.00 and 0.925. WSI-level MIL approaches may conceptually reduce computational burden by avoiding explicit patch-level classification. Compared to five experienced pathologists, the model achieved superior or comparable accuracy, and AI assistance improved pathologists' average diagnostic accuracy from 76.5% to 91.5%, while reducing interpretation time by over 40%. No false negatives occurred, and attention maps confirmed the malignant areas. CONCLUSION: Our WSI-level AI model offers a robust, efficient solution for diagnosing metastatic GC and CRC in ascitic cytology. It addresses limitations of manual and patch-based methods, supports clinical decision-making, and enhances diagnostic accuracy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted scholarly workflows introduce critical privacy and intellectual property risks. As a uniquely vulnerable cohort driven by publication pressure, and often weaker institutional support, novice researchers rely heavily on public LLMs, and must navigate high-stakes privacy-publication trade-offs. To investigate these concerns, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 44 researchers across diverse disciplines. We found that the fear of idea leakage paradoxically prompted some participants to increase their reliance on LLMs, as researchers utilize them to accelerate publication. Participants' beliefs--that their ideas lack unique value and their inputs are safely diluted in massive datasets--are contradicted by technical findings in the prior literature. From the interviews, we identified participants using five types of mitigation, including input fragmentation and adversarial probing, though participants also largely perceived these measures as ineffective. We outline recommendations that include implementing institution-level sandboxed environments, scenario-based privacy education, and verifiable data-deletion audits to improve transparency.

AI systems can accelerate information processing, analytical reasoning, documentation, and decision support while simultaneously reducing opportunities for professionals to exercise the competencies required for independent performance. This conceptual article examines the conditions under which AI delegation may support, preserve, transform, or diminish professional expertise. Building on research concerning cognitive offloading, automation, human–AI interaction, and technology-driven skill degradation, the article introduces the Expertise-Preserving AI Delegation (EPAD) framework. The framework distinguishes assisted performance, independent competence, error-detection capability, adaptive transfer, and professional judgment. It proposes that sustainable AI integration requires deliberate allocation of cognitive responsibilities, periodic independent performance, active verification, structured feedback, and longitudinal assessment. A research agenda is developed to operationalize expertise preservation through repeated independent assessments, AI-assisted performance measures, calibration tasks, and transfer evaluations. Particular attention is given to psychological, educational, medical, scientific, and other knowledge-intensive occupations. The article argues that the effectiveness of professional AI integration should be evaluated not solely by immediate productivity but also by the maintenance and development of human capabilities over time. The proposed framework is intended as a testable conceptual model rather than an empirically validated intervention.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in managerial decision-making, where generative systems can formulate problems, synthesize evidence, generate alternatives, and recommend courses of action. Existing research has largely examined whether these systems improve individual decision quality, productivity, trust, or human-AI collaboration. Comparatively less attention has been given to how repeated exposure to AI-generated reasoning may influence the diversity and independence of human judgment itself. This conceptual article introduces human-AI cognitive convergence, defined as the progressive alignment of human problem framing, assumptions, reasoning patterns, interpretations, and solution preferences with those repeatedly generated or reinforced by artificial intelligence. It further proposes decision homogenization as a multilevel consequence through which individually converging judgments produce increasingly similar managerial interpretations and decisions across teams and organizations. The framework distinguishes cognitive convergence from agreement, automation bias, cognitive offloading, groupthink, and cognitive debt, and differentiates functional from dysfunctional convergence. It theorizes that AI-first interaction, repeated exposure, task ambiguity, perceived AI authority, and common-model use increase convergence, whereas domain expertise, independent-first reasoning, deliberate dissent, heterogeneous information sources, alternative framing, and multi-model challenge preserve cognitive diversity. The article develops an AI diversity paradox: systems capable of generating numerous alternatives may nevertheless reduce organizational cognitive diversity when many decision makers rely on similar AI-generated representations of what is relevant, reasonable, or actionable. The consequences of decision homogenization are expected to become most significant under novel, ambiguous, or weak-signal conditions requiring heterogeneous interpretations and unconventional responses. The article concludes with implications for human-AI governance and a research agenda for empirically examining cognitive convergence in AI-augmented managerial work. quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied in healthcare to support disease diagnosis, clinical decision-making, patient monitoring, disease surveillance, and healthcare management. In Tanzania, AI-related innovations have emerged across different clinical and public health areas, accompanied by national initiatives addressing AI development and governance. However, the extent to which these innovations have progressed from technological development and validation to routine healthcare implementation and sustained use remains insufficiently documented. Existing reviews have examined AI applications, adoption barriers, and ethical concerns, but a comprehensive Tanzania-specific synthesis linking individual AI applications to their documented implementation stages and relevant governance provisions remains limited. This study aims to systematically map the development, real-world use, and governance of AI across Tanzania's health system. Specifically, it seeks to identify and characterise AI applications developed, evaluated, or implemented in Tanzania; classify their documented progression through development, validation, clinical evaluation, operational implementation, and scale-up; examine evidence concerning clinical and operational performance, safety, equity, and sustainability; assess relevant national AI governance and policy provisions; and identify gaps requiring further research, implementation support, and policy attention. The study will employ a systematic scoping review complemented by structured documentary policy analysis. The scoping review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodological guidance and will be reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The literature search will be documented using PRISMA-S. Eligibility criteria will be developed using the Population, Concept, and Context (PCC) framework, covering AI applications and associated stakeholders, their development and implementation, and healthcare settings across Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar. A comprehensive search will be conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, African Journals Online, and African Index Medicus. Supplementary searches will cover Google Scholar, relevant institutional repositories, reference lists, citation records, and grey literature from government institutions, research organisations, and international agencies. No initial publication-year restriction will be applied. Eligible evidence will include quantitative, qualitative, mixed-methods, technical, and implementation studies, alongside relevant reports and other verifiable sources. English- and Kiswahili-language publications will be considered. Two reviewers will independently screen eligible records and assess full texts against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data will be extracted using a standardised instrument covering study characteristics, AI technologies, healthcare applications, development and validation procedures, implementation settings, reported outcomes, and governance considerations. Publications and identifiable AI applications will be treated as separate units of analysis to prevent multiple reports of the same technology from inflating the number of identified innovations. The documented progression of each AI application will be assessed using a predefined six-stage analytical classification, ranging from conceptual development to scale-up or sustained implementation. Evidence of model development, validation, prospective evaluation and operational use will be distinguished from claims unsupported by sufficient documentation. Clinical and operational evidence will be examined using appropriate study-design-specific appraisal approaches where applicable. The policy analysis will follow the READ framework for documentary research and examine relevant Tanzanian policies, legislation, strategies, regulatory instruments and institutional guidance. Governance assessment will be informed by World Health Organization guidance and the FUTURE-AI principles, covering areas such as patient safety, data protection, fairness, transparency, accountability, human oversight, interoperability and sustainability. The Nonadoption, Abandonment, Scale-up, Spread and Sustainability (NASSS) framework will support interpretation of implementation challenges. Findings from the scoping review and policy analysis will initially be synthesised separately and subsequently integrated. Descriptive statistics, evidence mapping and thematic analysis will be used to examine the distribution of AI applications across healthcare functions, technologies, settings and documented implementation stages. The integrated analysis will identify areas of alignment and gaps between implementation evidence and national governance provisions. The PAGER framework will guide the presentation of evidence patterns, advances, gaps, implications for practice and research priorities. Meta-analysis is not planned because the study addresses heterogeneous technologies, study designs and outcomes. The expected outcomes include a comprehensive inventory of identifiable healthcare AI applications in Tanzania, an evidence map showing their documented stages of development and implementation, a synthesis of available clinical and operational evidence, and a structured assessment of relevant governance provisions. The review will also identify areas where validation, clinical effectiveness, sustained implementation, or governance evidence remains limited. These findings are expected to inform future research priorities, healthcare implementation decisions and policies supporting the responsible and sustainable use of AI in Tanzania. The study may also provide a methodological reference for assessing healthcare AI progress in comparable resource-constrained health systems.

quarantine.abstract_text: Learning Health Systems (LHSs) use routinely collected data to generate evidence that informs practice through continuous learning cycles. Searches identified U.S.-based, English-language studies published January 2007–August 2025; two reviewers independently screened and extracted data, resolving disagreements by consensus. We included 54 framework studies (24 [44%] conceptual adaptations; 30 [56%] real-world implementations) and 30 AI/data science studies. Relative to framework studies, AI studies less often addressed governance and stakeholder engagement (17% vs 35%) or equity (13% vs 22%), emphasizing computational over organizational functions. Most AI studies (27/30) focused on the data-to-knowledge phase; only three extended to knowledge-to-practice, and none described practice-to-data feedback with post-deployment outcomes informing model updating. AI applications capture only part of the LHS vision, concentrating on knowledge generation with less attention to the organizational and feedback mechanisms needed to translate insights into practice and sustain learning.
