quarantine.abstract_text: Cognitive training that targets sustained attention and working memory is useful in education, clinical rehabilitation and interactive human-technology systems, but its benefit depends on keeping task difficulty matched to the person. Virtual reality (VR) offers immersion and settings representative of everyday tasks, and allows difficulty to be changed in real time. Existing adaptive systems, however, often rely on simple performance heuristics, affect or estimate visual complexity rather than task-related cognitive load. Moreover, cognitive load is usually judged against the participant’s own ratings, which are themselves an imperfect reference. The central hypothesis of this thesis is that eyetracking and peripheral physiological signals recorded in VR can estimate how difficult a task feels to the person doing it, well enough for a model to adjust difficulty in real time with outcomes comparable to participant-driven control, and that the estimation part holds for older adults once age-related differences in the signal are taken into account. We developed a bespoke VR sustained attention task and collected eye-tracking, photoplethysmography and galvanic skin response data from 54 younger (aged 18-58) and 19 older (aged 60+) adults at fixed difficulty levels. Models evaluated on unseen participants performed above chance (younger adults: accuracy 0.56, AUC 0.72), with eye-tracking carrying most of the signal and physiological features alone close to chance. Performance was lower in older adults (accuracy 0.49, AUC 0.66), and the most informative features appeared to differ between age groups. A bidirectional LSTM with self-attention reached a slightly higher macro-F1 than gradient-boosted trees on the same data (0.50 against 0.47), and performed better than a model given raw signals only. We then deployed the LSTM in real time with 54 younger adults (51 analysed), comparing model-driven and participant-driven difficulty in single- and dual-task conditions. Per-trial agreement with participants’ ratings was low (accuracy 36.7%, AUC 0.63), yet the two forms of control appeared to produce comparable outcomes. There were no significant differences in difficulty-weighted game performance, arithmetic errors or subjective workload, including frustration. Final difficulty was equivalent in single-task conditions and slightly higher under model control in dual-task conditions, a difference that was borderline after correction. Just Right ratings were more frequent in the real-time cohort than in the offline cohort (57% and 39%). Finally, we compared subjective ratings with performance-derived reference measures. Agreement between the two appeared fair and slightly lower in real time, where the steps between difficulty levels are less discrete. The same features seemed to predict performance-derived labels more accurately than subjective ratings in every matched comparison. This suggests that self-report may be a less stable reference for real-time adaptation. Within a single session with younger adults, model-driven adaptation appears to have produced outcomes comparable to participant-driven control. The dataset (EyeDAPT) and the experimental software are publicly available.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

quarantine.abstract_text: As autonomous AI agents increasingly interact in persistent populations, their collective capabilities and alignment depend not only on individual models, but also on the institutions governing their interactions. Yet AI research has largely focused on individual agents. In this Perspective, we argue that institutional design must become a distinct focus of AI research. Drawing on institutional political economy, social epistemology and organizational theory, we develop seven principles for designing AI institutions that sustain cooperation, enable reliable collective judgments and remain accountable to legitimate human purposes. These address reciprocal contributions, accountable authority, functional differentiation, epistemic pluralism, criticism and correction, human direction, and institutional adaptation. We illustrate their application through machine science, where autonomous research challenges institutions developed around human capabilities and constraints. We then propose an experimental research programme in which matched populations of AI agents operate under alternative institutional arrangements, and describe MoltJournal, an API-first journal for autonomous research agents, as an illustration of how such institutions can be made programmable and observable. Together, these contributions establish institutional design as a research agenda concerned not only with aligning autonomous agents, but with understanding how institutions can transform them into capable, reliable and accountable collectives.

The contribution is a boundary condition for multi-task and deep sequence models in educational data mining: when the predictive signal in early click logs is limited, task correlation does not translate into transfer, and added model capacity does not translate into accuracy. Predictive information was instead governed by the behavioral features measured, chiefly cumulative and rolling engagement, pointing practitioners toward simpler, interpretable models and richer signals rather than more complex architectures.

No study met the prespecified Phase III criteria. Phase III requires demonstrated downstream population health benefit. Prospective deployment or improved forecasting alone is not sufficient. Across domains, bottlenecks have shifted from model accuracy to governance, interpretability, accountability, interoperability, workflow integration, equity, and sustainable monitoring. LLMs attract major attention, but their influenza-specific evidence remains limited. Their greatest value may lie in augmenting, not replacing, specialized models and human expertise. We propose phase-specific evidence thresholds, implementation-oriented evaluation metrics, an implementation readiness checklist, and priority evidence gaps for translating AI-enabled influenza tools into implementation-ready public health applications.

As AI systems increasingly shape how people work, think, and are governed, the world has quietly slipped into treating citizens as consumers: recipients of decisions made elsewhere, rather than participants in making them. Citizen 5.0 confronts this shift directly. David Galipeau argues that the defining question of the AI era is not technological. It is human. Will citizens have a genuine seat in decisions that determine the future of labor, data, and cognition? Or will that future be decided unilaterally by a handful of technology companies? Drawing on rigorous, interdisciplinary research, the book builds a concrete framework for restoring citizens, not consumers, to the center of the AI era. It includes neurorights, data sovereignty, and a Synthetic Labor Tax that could reshape who owns the value AI creates. This is a precise, urgent case for reclaiming human agency before the future is built without us.

quarantine.abstract_text: The rapid evolution and integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, particularly following the advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative AI (GenAI), have profoundly transformed teaching, learning and management practices in higher education worldwide. This paper aims to synthesise the empirical evidence available between 2020 and 2026 regarding the impact of AI in higher education, examining the prevalent technologies, pedagogical mediation, levels of human–AI collaboration, adoption patterns and ethical-normative implications. A systematic literature review was conducted in rigorous accordance with the PRISMA 2020 Statement. Six international scientific databases were consulted: Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, SciELO, PubMed and IEEE Xplore, identifying an initial corpus of 1,247 records. After the screening process for duplicates, title/abstract and full-text reading, 45 primary studies focused on university educational impact were selected, analytically complemented by global bibliometric and meta-systematic reviews of the period. Methodological quality was assessed using the MMAT (2018) tool and the certainty of the evidence via the GRADE approach. It is concluded that the predominant AI technologies in the literature are large language models (75.6 %), intelligent tutoring systems (31.1 %) and learning analytics tools (24.4 %). The principal applications concentrate on personalised learning (53.3 %), student motivation and engagement (46.7 %) and academic performance (42.2 %). However, evaluation of the autonomy continuum reveals a severe implementation gap: 45.56 % of integrations correspond to Substitution modalities (where AI replaces teaching functions), 39.05 % to Augmentation, 10.65 % to Toolification and only 4.73 % achieve genuine Human–AI Synergy. Longitudinally, student adoption reached near-universal levels (95 % in 2026), although gaps in ethical literacy and tensions surrounding academic integrity persist. The methodological quality of the corpus was high in 62.2 % of the studies, yet the global GRADE certainty was classified as low owing to the predominance of cross-sectional designs and heterogeneity of metrics. It may further be concluded that AI possesses a proven transformative potential to optimise university learning, yet its effectiveness does not reside in mere technological adoption, but rather in intentional pedagogical mediation (the PMAISE model), the evolution of teaching practice towards the AI-TPACK framework and the establishment of executable governance policies (Policy-as-Code). A human-centred integration framework based on four pillars and a five-phase operational strategy with a detailed matrix of success indicators for institutional scalability is proposed.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract National artificial-intelligence strategies and climate-adaptation plans are expanding at the same time, yet they are rarely studied as connected policy infrastructures. This article examines whether multilingual AI capacity is being linked to climate-risk communication and early-warning systems in Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka. It analyses six national policy instruments available by 21 July 2026: three AI policies or strategies and three climate-adaptation or climate-change instruments, comprising approximately 210,000 words. A corpus-assisted critical policy analysis first maps sentences concerning linguistic inclusion, language technology and early warning; close qualitative coding then evaluates five stages of integration: recognition, language-resource infrastructure, service linkage, participatory validation and accountability. The analysis identifies a recurring institutional split. AI instruments treat local languages as datasets, models and digital-public-service infrastructure, while climate instruments treat them mainly as channels for last-mile dissemination. Bangladesh explicitly plans Bangla language models and AI-enabled disaster alerts, but the two commitments are not joined. Nepal combines measurable local-language AI actions with unusually operational, people-centred early-warning programmes, yet assigns them to separate policy tracks. Sri Lanka gives the strongest attention to Sinhala- and Tamil-language AI resources, while its climate policy acknowledges language barriers without specifying a computational or institutional response. Across all three cases, no instrument establishes an end-to-end arrangement connecting language data, warning generation, community validation and accountable deployment. The article terms this disconnection the linguistic adaptation gap and proposes a five-stage Linguistic Adaptation Integration Framework. The findings recast multilingual warning not as a final translation task but as a cross-domain public infrastructure problem, with implications for language policy, AI governance, climate services and disaster-risk reduction.

quarantine.title: Between Niti and Nyaya: A Society-Centered Framework for AI Governance

publication_date_provenance.reason: arXiv verification budget or provider pause

quarantine.abstract_text: Governments are making decisions about AI before they can measure its public effects, and those decisions determine whether a person can learn that AI influenced an outcome, challenge it, and see it corrected. Research has documented what AI governance produces: principles, strategies, registers, and audits. However, we lack shared language for understanding AI policy while it is still being made. We introduce the Society-Centered AI Governance Framework, which gives policymakers, researchers, and the public a way to assess instruments in any jurisdiction by whether a person can get notice, challenge a decision, and see it corrected. It reads a jurisdiction's instruments together by date and binding status, separates an agency duty from a right a person can invoke, and traces which later instrument must enforce each commitment. We evaluated it in North Carolina using interviews with nine AI Leadership Council members, conducted before and after the state's 2026 AI roadmap, and a provision-level reading, with human-reviewed model-assisted coding, of 49 AI governance documents from 19 states. For the state's own AI systems, we find visibility-first governance: visibility duties are in effect, notice exists as an agency duty with no right a person can invoke, and AI-specific challenge and correction remain advisory. The roadmap assigns owners and dates to the missing protections, so the gaps are documented but not yet closed. Recent federal preemption proposals focus on AI development, so recourse for a state's own systems is likely to remain a state decision. We identify "legitimacy before protection" as a testable risk of visibility-first governance and name the milestones that would test it. More broadly, judging AI policy by who can act on what it makes visible lets the field assess recourse while policy is still forming, before harm occurs.

quarantine.abstract_text: ABSTRACT Although artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support feedback in health professions education, little is known whether and how AI‐enabled feedback supports reflective learning and critical reflexivity. The literature encompasses generative large language models (LLMs) as well as non‐generative natural language processing (NLP), traditional machine learning (ML) and computer vision (CV). This scoping review examines the design and use of AI‐enabled feedback for reflective learning across health professions education. Following Arksey and O'Malley, Levac et al. and PRISMA‐ScR guidance, we searched MEDLINE, Embase and ERIC from 1 January 2015 to 21 November 2025. Eligible empirical studies examined AI‐enabled feedback or feedback‐related educational activities involving health professions learners or professionals in undergraduate, graduate, or continuing professional development contexts. Data were charted descriptively and classified using FACET, SAMR, Hattie and Timperley's feedback framework and Kirkpatrick outcome levels. Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. A total of 12 of 19 (63.2%) used LLMs, 4 (21.1%) used non‐generative NLP, 2 (10.5%) used traditional ML and 1 (5.3%) used CV. Six studies (31.6%) involved continuing professional development (CPD). Augmentation was the most common SAMR level (10/19; 52.6%). Of 15 studies that could be classified by Hattie and Timperley's framework, 10 (66.7%) provided process‐level feedback, 3 (20.0%) task‐level feedback and 2 (13.3%) self‐regulation feedback. No included study explicitly examined critical reflexivity. Reported outcomes were concentrated at Kirkpatrick Level 1 (reaction; 9/19) and Level 2 (learning; 9/19), with no demonstrated longitudinal evidence of sustained behaviour change, transfer to practice, or lifelong learning outcomes. Current evidence on AI‐enabled feedback in health professions education is early, fragmented and predominantly performance‐oriented. Critical reflexivity has not yet been adequately studied, and lifelong learning should be regarded as a future educational goal rather than a demonstrated outcome of the included evidence. Current evidence on AI‐enabled feedback is predominantly performance‐oriented, with limited examination of reflective learning and no explicit evaluation of critical reflexivity. Although AI‐enabled feedback may contribute to ongoing professional development, its effects on sustained learning, behaviour change and lifelong learning remain unestablished. Future work should use theory‐informed feedback and design, strengthen learner feedback literacy and human oversight, address bias and power, and evaluate meaningful educational and practice‐based outcomes over time.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in schools, but evidence on its use in teaching and learning for primary pupils with special educational needs (SEN) is fragmented, and its relevance to Malaysian primary special education has not been synthesised. Following PRISMA 2020, this review searched Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, OpenAlex and the Directory of Open Access Journals (including a Malaysian journal filter and a Bahasa Melayu search), supplemented by citation searching and reviewer suggestions. Of 740 database records, 637 were screened after de-duplication and 75 reports were sought; 54 studies (42 empirical, 12 reviews), with publication years from 2017 to 2027, met the eligibility criteria. Data were extracted on setting, participants, SEN category, AI application, design and outcomes, and synthesised thematically. Empirical studies with full texts were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Four groups of AI applications were identified: generative AI and chatbots, adaptive and intelligent tutoring systems, AI-enabled assistive technologies, and general AI tools examined through teacher acceptance. Learning disabilities and autism were the most frequently studied categories. Intervention studies generally reported gains in achievement, reading, mathematics, engagement and behaviour, but samples were small, interventions short, and several studies lacked control of confounding. Teacher studies showed moderate acceptance, with perceived usefulness, experience and professional development as key influences. Implementation depended on teacher competence, infrastructure, human oversight, linguistic and cultural fit, and attention to sensory load and ethics. Three Malaysian empirical studies were identified; all focused on teachers, and none reported pupil attainment outcomes, so Malaysian pupil-level evidence remains limited and lacks controlled designs.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: AI-mediated language learning is increasingly used in higher education, yet its contribution to intercultural competence remains insufficiently synthesised. This systematic review examines how AI-mediated technologies and pedagogical designs have been used, which intercultural outcomes have been reported and assessed, and what conditions shape their contribution. Following PRISMA 2020, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and ERIC were searched for peer-reviewed English-language journal articles published from January 2023 to July 2026. From 180 records, 25 primary empirical studies met the eligibility criteria and were examined through narrative thematic synthesis. ChatGPT, large language models, and conversational agents were the dominant technologies, but technology type alone did not determine outcomes. Clearer intercultural development was reported when AI was embedded in culturally contextualised simulations, reflective or metacognitive scaffolding, collaborative exchange, and authentic human interaction. Reported outcomes covered cognitive, affective, and behavioural dimensions, although evidence was more consistent for cultural awareness, perspective recognition, openness, confidence, and willingness to communicate than for sustained pragmatic or behavioural transfer. Assessment approaches varied considerably and frequently relied on self-reported measures. AI offered accessible practice, immediate feedback, and cultural inquiry, but cultural simplification, bias, overreliance, unequal access, and limited interactional repair constrained its value. AI is therefore best understood as an intercultural learning scaffold rather than a cultural authority or substitute for human interaction. Explicit intercultural objectives, critical verification, human mediation, and performance-based assessment are needed to move language learning beyond fluency.

quarantine.abstract_text: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has established itself as one of the main drivers of transformation in contemporary society, profoundly affecting sectors such as medicine, industry, communication and, increasingly, higher education. The spread of technologies based on machine learning, natural language processing and neural network algorithms is helping to redefine not only the ways in which information is accessed, but also the teaching-learning processes, teaching practices and organizational models of universities (Holmes & Tuomi, 2022; Crompton & Burke, 2023; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019).In the academic context, AI is progressively explored as a tool for educational innovation, capable of supporting the personalization of training pathways, improving the effectiveness of assessment and expanding opportunities for inclusion (Luckin et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2020). At the same time, its dissemination raises relevant questions on a pedagogical, ethical and social level, in relation to the quality of learning, the role of teachers, data management and possible inequalities of access. The university thus finds itself at the center of a tension between opportunities for renewal and the need to critically govern the adoption of emerging technologies (UNESCO, 2021).Numerous studies show that AI tools are now widely adopted among university students, particularly to support information search, academic writing, and content synthesis (Bughin et al., 2018; Jereb & Urh, 2024). However, in the face of this diffusion, a significant gap emerges between the actual use of technologies and the possession of critical and conscious skills, highlighting the need to strengthen AI literacy and to integrate these tools in a structured way into university curricula (Holmes, Bialik & Fadel, 2019). This discrepancy prompts a broader reflection on the role of the university not only as a place of technological adoption, but as a space for critical and responsible training.In this scenario, AI contributes to questioning two fundamental questions of university teaching: what to teach and how to teach. On the one hand, the increasing automation of basic cognitive tasks reduces the exclusive value of static knowledge transmission; on the other hand, the need to develop higher-order skills, such as critical thinking, problem solving, collaboration and ethical responsibility is reinforced (Center for Curriculum Redesign, 2015; Rivoltella, 2019; Nuzzaci, 2025). The university is therefore called upon to rethink its educational objectives, orienting itself towards educational models capable of integrating disciplinary knowledge, transversal skills and meta-skills.This paper aims to analyze the role of artificial intelligence as a lever of educational innovation in higher education, highlighting its potential, applications and limitations. In particular, the impact of AI on teaching-learning processes, the main educational technologies and applications, the change in the role of the university teacher and the ethical, social and cultural implications related to its adoption are examined (Panciroli & Rivoltella, 2023; Baker & Hawn, 2021). The goal is to outline a critical and integrated vision, in which AI is not considered as an end in itself, but as a tool to be governed in a conscious and responsible way, at the service of the quality and equity of university education.The paper adopts a narrative-argumentative theoretical-critical approach, based on a selective review of the international literature on Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED). The analysis integrates pedagogical, technological and ethical contributions, with the aim of building an interpretative framework useful for university teaching design.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionised professional settings, necessitating vocational students to cultivate new types of preparedness beyond traditional digital skills. This research seeks to analyse the factors influencing AI readiness as a novel aspect of job preparedness among vocational high school students by exploring the impacts of technological literacy, acceptance of technology, institutional backing, and technological infrastructure. A quantitative explanatory framework was utilised, focusing on vocational high school students in South Sulawesi, Indonesia. Data were gathered using structured questionnaires and examined using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling to assess both direct and indirect correlations among the research constructs. The findings indicate that institutional backing is the most significant factor influencing AI preparedness, succeeded by technological infrastructure. Institutional backing affects AI readiness both directly and indirectly via technology infrastructure, underscoring the significance of school-level environments in fostering pupils' technological competence. In contrast, technological literacy does not substantially forecast AI preparedness, revealing a disparity between fundamental digital abilities and sophisticated AI skills. Technological acceptability exhibits an inverse correlation with AI preparedness, contradicting traditional beliefs about sequential technological integration. The results suggest that students' preparedness for the workforce in the digital age relies on institutional capabilities, technological settings, and organised AI educational experiences, rather than solely on personal competencies. This research formulates a socio-technical framework elucidating AI preparedness as an integral element of vocational students' employment ready in technology-driven environments.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract This systematic review examines ethical challenges arising from the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in psychiatric patient management. Six databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO and CINAHL) were searched to 1 December 2025. Fourteen empirical studies published between 2020 and 2025 (ten qualitative, two cross-sectional survey and two mixed-methods studies) were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and synthesized thematically. Across stakeholders—patients, clinicians, young people, and experts—AI was viewed as promising for improving access, efficiency, and personalization of care, yet raised concerns about privacy, surveillance, bias, loss of empathy, and unclear accountability. Participants described the ethical acceptability of AI as conditional on strong data protection, transparency, human oversight, and equity-focused implementation. Because the evidence base is small, largely perception-based, drawn mainly from high-income countries and often concerned with hypothetical tools, these findings should be regarded as exploratory; they nevertheless point to the need for human-centred, ethically governed AI integration in mental healthcare.

quarantine.abstract_text: Purpose. This review synthesizes evidence on multimodal digital strategies and artificial intelligence (AI) in English as a foreign language (EFL) education. It examines the mechanisms through which these strategies may support communicative competence and identifies findings that can be cautiously transferred to public secondary education in peripheral Latin American settings. Methodology. An interpretive systematic review informed by PRISMA 2020 was conducted. Searches covered publications from 2020 to 2026 in Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, SciELO, and Dialnet. Of 245 records, 63 duplicates were removed, 182 titles and abstracts were screened, 120 full texts were assessed, and 20 studies formed the final corpus. A subsequent bibliographic audit verified authorship, DOI data, thematic fit, and peer-review status. Design heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis; evidence was therefore synthesized narratively by mechanism, outcome, and contextual proximity. Results. Pedagogical value did not arise from any tool in isolation. It emerged when technology was embedded in a learning architecture that connected meaning-making, rehearsal and revision, feedback, authentic interaction, and teacher mediation. Digital storytelling and multimodal composition provided the most consistent evidence for speaking, self-regulation, and reduced anxiety. AI expanded possibilities for feedback and low-exposure interaction, but its contribution depended on critical literacy, human verification, and task design. Only a small share of the corpus directly concerned rural or peripheral Latin American schools. Conclusions. Current evidence does not warrant claims of a generalized transformative effect in the target context. quarantine.abstract_text: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support learning and emotion regulation, yet frequent or coping-oriented use does not necessarily constitute difficult-to-regulate dependency. It remains unclear how academic rumination and affective coping are positioned relative to dependency and whether dependency is differentially associated with perceived costs to knowledge internalization and independent reasoning. This study examined these distinctions within a single educational psychology model. Methods A cross-sectional survey included 611 current GenAI users recruited through university settings in Tianjin, China (91.7% first-year students). Dependency was a continuous, nonclinical tendency. Ordinal CFA and WLSMV SEM evaluated a prespecified partial association model. Covariate adjustment, four alternative measurement specifications, an AR-score hybrid, and observed-score regressions assessed sensitivity. Results In the reference model, academic rumination was associated with affective coping (β = 0.283), and both were associated with dependency (β = 0.187 and 0.555). Dependency was associated with perceived internalization/memory debt (β = 0.550) and independent-reasoning debt (β = 0.644); their standardized difference was 0.095 (95% Monte Carlo CI [0.032, 0.157]). The corresponding observed-score coefficients were 0.413 and 0.518, with a difference of 0.105 (95% bootstrap CI [0.035, 0.175]). Both serial coefficient products remained positive, but the negative conditional coping-internalization association was not sustained in the observed-score analysis. Reported frequency had no unique association in the combined adjusted model. Alternative measurement models retained robust RMSEA of 0.090–0.097; robust hybrid indices were unavailable. Conclusion The results provide tentative evidence of differentiated self-reported associations among coping, frequency, dependency, and cognitive concerns. Measurement misfit remains unresolved, and the coping-outcome coefficients were sensitive to construct representation. Observed-score consistency for dependency and serial products does not validate the latent structure or establish temporal or causal mediation. These predominantly first-year, Tianjin-based cross-sectional data do not establish objective cognitive decline or generality across student populations.

quarantine.abstract_text: The integration of generative AI (GenAI) into user interface (UI) design has led to prompt-to-design generators (P2dGens), tools that enable designers to create UI prototypes from textual prompts efficiently. Despite their growing adoption, little is known about how designers use these tools in everyday practice, their benefits, and limitations. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 17 UI designers to investigate P2dGens use, focusing on workflow integration, attitudes toward generator-assisted design, and the organizational climate. Findings show that designers primarily use P2dGens as ideation accelerators rather than end-to-end solutions, and they adopt a variety of individual and collaborative prompting strategies. Designers expressed complex attitudes, noting gains in efficiency and inspiration while also highlighting concerns about loss of personal creativity and design quality. We also observed emerging governance practices and varying attitudes within organizations toward P2dGens. These insights illuminate how P2dGens reshape UI design workflows and contribute to understanding human-AI collaboration in UI design.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI)–based intelligent tutoring systems represent a transformative innovation in school education, offering unprecedented learning personalization. This systematic literature review analyzes 53 scientific studies to identify the opportunities that GAI provides for the design and development of these tutoring systems. The findings show the predominance of general-purpose tools such as ChatGPT and models such as GPT-4, highlighting their ability to generate interactive content and adaptive feedback. Key features are identified, including adaptability, dialogic interaction, and emotional engagement. However, the analysis reveals critical gaps between current technical capabilities and deep pedagogical integration, including limitations in comprehensive student modeling, algorithmic opacity, and limited empirical evidence of long-term impact. In light of these gaps, strategic research and development opportunities are proposed, focusing on grounded instructional design, explainable architectures, operational mechanisms for ethics and equity, teacher co-orchestration tools, and rigorous efficacy studies. It is concluded that advancing the field requires a transdisciplinary approach to ensure that these intelligent tutors are pedagogically robust, ethical, and aligned with the goal of equitable and holistic education.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has the potential to enhance teaching and learning. However, effective integration requires teachers to possess adequate technological proficiency and a positive perception of its educational applications. This study examined teachers’ perceptions of AI, their level of technological proficiency, and the perceived educational implications of AI in public elementary schools in the City of Ilagan, Isabela. A quantitative descriptive-correlational research design was employed, involving 110 teachers selected through stratified random sampling during School Year 2026–2027. Data were gathered using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and the Pearson Product-Moment Correlation Coefficient. Findings revealed that teachers demonstrated high technological proficiency in basic computer skills, digital literacy, and digital communication and collaboration. Teachers also expressed strong agreement regarding the perceived positive impact of AI on student engagement and learning, teaching and teacher roles, and critical thinking and collaboration. Furthermore, teachers’ perceptions of AI were positively and significantly related to all dimensions of technological proficiency and perceived educational implications. The study concludes that effective AI integration requires continuous technological development, responsible AI use, and adequate institutional support.

quarantine.title: Auditing the Judge: Internal Signals for LLM Reasoning Assurance

publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: Language-model systems use self-judgment to decide which answers to release, review, or recompute. Because intervention is costly, an assurance score must rank errors well at the available budget, not merely over the full ranking. We compare the judge's continuous verdict-token score with a supervised correctness probe trained on attention-head activations from the same prompt. Exact identities link fixed-budget error recall to residual risk and show that AUROC averages recall over all budgets. Across three open 7-12B models on GSM8K and MATH, the probe finds 1.3-22.5 additional percentage points of errors at 5% review in all six model-dataset settings (median 7.4 points). At 10% routing, probe-guided allocation improves accuracy over equal-cost random allocation in both GSM8K experiments, but beats judge-guided routing only for the weaker judge. Cross-dataset transfer lowers probe AUROC for every model in both directions relative to target-domain training. Because dataset, weight precision, and generation budget change together, this measures a joint protocol shift rather than a dataset-only effect. Internal signals can improve supervised, in-domain budget allocation, but are not domain-general confidence estimators.

quarantine.abstract_text: Large language models (LLMs) are reshaping intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) by reducing authoring costs and enabling flexible interaction. However, effective tutoring requires more than fluent responses. It also depends on pedagogical control, domain grounding, learner modeling, interaction design, orchestration, and reliable evaluation. We examine these requirements through a component-centric framework that organizes LLM-based tutoring systems into four functional layers: pedagogical policy, domain and grounding, learner state, and interaction/interface. A cross-cutting orchestration layer coordinates these components, while agentic tutoring systems are treated as an emerging subset of the broader field. Drawing on representative literature on LLM-based and agentic tutoring systems, published mostly between late 2022 and mid-2026, we analyze how tutoring capabilities are implemented across system architecture, learner modeling, interaction, orchestration, and evaluation. The reviewed literature suggests that evaluation remains concentrated on response-level and model-based proxies, while direct evidence of learning gains remains limited. Learner-state modeling and interaction design also receive less systematic attention. We conclude by identifying challenges in answer leakage, pedagogy–solving trade-offs, learner-state calibration, interaction validity, and proxy validity.
